Kit had to give the Mormon church 10% of her $1 birthday money. Now she’s top 0.01% on OnlyFans, making over $10,000 on an average day. At 7 she told her dad she didn’t want to be baptized. At 16 she moved out. Her Mormon parents still don’t know.

Kit is 28, and her family has been Mormon all the way back to Brigham Young crossing into Utah. The church took its cut of everything, even a child’s birthday money. Her gay uncle knew it, so he stopped giving her cash and bought her presents instead. She was the smart kid in AP classes, with talk of skipping her to high school in fifth grade. And all the church really wanted from her was to get married and have babies.

The fight started early. At 7 she told her dad she didn’t want to be baptized, and he was furious. Her counteroffer: fine, but Grandpa does it, not you. Her mom told her she couldn’t do that to the family.

At 8, she got baptized anyway.

At 16 she moved out and went to live with her grandma in Idaho. Her parents offered to pay for college once, on one condition: a two-year Mormon mission. No media, and someone with her every hour of the day making sure she followed the rules. She said no. From 17 to 23 she worked 9 to 5 at a law firm, went to night school and rented a small room from an elderly couple. Then she became a personal trainer. Bad money, rough hours, weird clients.

So how does a Mormon girl end up on OnlyFans? Her TikTok followers told her to, during a live about fitness. Her only fear was that it would ruin her career in academia, because she wanted a PhD. She did it anyway.

First month: over $10,000. “Changed my life.”

She withdrew her graduate application and signed up for a math degree instead. Now she has two, psychology and mathematics. Today she’s in the top 0.01% of creators on the platform. More than $10,000 a month? “A lot more.” A day? “Depends on the day, but the average, yeah.” No agent. She shoots and lights everything herself, and a small team of girls handles her editing.

And her parents? They moved out of state, and the photos of her around their house look so different that nobody ever recognizes her. She knows they’ll find out eventually.

The church still gets 10% of every member’s money. Just not hers.

Her take: “I entertained some guys who were going to watch p*rn anyway. So they got to watch mine.”

Some people will say the church pushed her straight into this. Others will say a girl who rejected her faith at 7 was always going to end up here.

Is she the one who went wrong, or the church?

text:
Twelve straight wins will get the league’s attention.

How San Antonio secured the twelfth should hold it.

On November 15, the Spurs beat Utah 110 to 102, closing with a 16 to 4 run over the final three minutes. Their record improved to 12 wins and two losses.

That finish is the part worth examining.

Against a struggling opponent, a contender can spend most of a game looking less convincing than expected. The important question becomes whether it can produce the stops and possessions required when the margin for error disappears.

San Antonio did.

Dylan Harper scored 31 points. Victor Wembanyama supplied 26. The Spurs had more than one source of offense, then finished the job collectively.

That matters when evaluating what this team can become.

Wembanyama gives San Antonio an extraordinary foundation. His presence changes which shots opponents consider available, while his offensive skill forces defenses to account for him far from the basket.

But a serious team needs ways to win beyond waiting for its most extraordinary player to overwhelm everybody.

It needs another creator who can carry stretches of offense. It needs defensive possessions that end with the ball secured. It needs execution when an opponent refuses to disappear.

The Utah finish offered evidence of those demands being met.

Twelve consecutive victories do not settle the championship conversation in November. They do make it harder to treat San Antonio’s potential as something reserved for a distant season.

The Spurs are building expectations with results.

And those expectations should rise. A team winning this consistently deserves to be judged on the quality of its execution, including on nights when the opponent’s record suggests the game should be easier.

That is what success changes.

San Antonio is reaching the point where winning is expected, and the next question is how reliably it can finish difficult games.

On Sunday, it provided a strong answer.

text:
𝗜𝗳 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗷𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝘄𝗻'𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝗽𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻...

...you've got about a decade to get ready before 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘧𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘴 𝘢𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵.

When the boomers die, towns without stable work to offer younger families will start to destabilize.

Here's what to look out for:

𝟭. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗻?

Young people who still work or retired non-producers?

𝟮. 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀?

Is there any reason for someone from outside the community to resettle there?

If the town lacks adequate employment options... what about business opportunities?

There are only so many local businesses (that are actually profitable) for retiring owners to sell.

Come 2035, we're going to start seeing the same chain reaction often:

1.  Senior population declines
2. No jobs of businesses left in their wake
3. Young, working age replacements stay away
4. Existing businesses struggle & they close or move
5. Property values drop, making matters worse

A service-only economy is an economy living on borrowed time.

Prompt 1, the full build:

Build Stoop, an original home-search app for iPhone in SwiftUI, in the genre of Zillow: a white search header with filter chips over a full map of homes for sale with red price pins, a listing card that slides up from a tapped pin, a List view, listing pages with a photo gallery, the Stoop Estimate, a monthly payment calculator, price history and Request a tour, plus Favorites, Updates, Plan and Inbox tabs. Its own name, logo and words, all below. The user is Maya Chen, house hunting in Park Slope, Brooklyn. Today is Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

ASSETS
cu⁠rl -L once and unzip flat: https://t.co/V2sSfPhZI3 (stoop-icon⁠.png: the app icon; home-01⁠.jpg … home-18⁠.jpg: each listing's exterior, its first photo; int-living, int-kitchen, int-dining, int-bedroom, int-bath, int-garden, int-loft, int-condo .jpg: interiors; agent-1, agent-2, agent-3 .jpg: agent headshots). Add them to the asset catalog. No image generation is needed.

BRAND
Name "Stoop" (wordmark: SF Pro heavy, #⁠006AFF). StoopMark, a Shape in a unit square: a roof from (0⁠.08, 0⁠.48) up to (0⁠.5, 0⁠.10) down to (0⁠.92, 0⁠.48); walls from (0⁠.20, 0⁠.38) down to (0⁠.20, 0⁠.92) and (0⁠.80, 0⁠.38) to (0⁠.80, 0⁠.92); a bottom line (0⁠.20, 0⁠.92)-(0⁠.80, 0⁠.92); a doorway (x 0⁠.40-0⁠.60, y 0⁠.56-0⁠.80); outline stroked at 0⁠.08 of the box, round caps and joins; three filled steps under the door: x 0⁠.36-0⁠.64 y 0⁠.80-0⁠.84, x 0⁠.32-0⁠.68 y 0⁠.84-0⁠.88, x 0⁠.28-0⁠.72 y 0⁠.88-0⁠.92. The mark + wordmark sit in the Plan header.

LOOK
iOS 26, light mode only. White, SF Pro, text #⁠2A2A33, secondary #⁠596B82, brand #⁠006AFF, light brand #⁠EBF3FF, pin red #⁠DA2D3F, page grey #⁠F6F6F8, hairlines #⁠D1D1D5. Native TabView (iOS 26 draws the floating Liquid Glass tab bar), tint #⁠006AFF: Search (magnifyingglass), Updates (bell), Favorites (heart), Plan (checklist), Inbox (tray). Opens on Search; no splash, onboarding, permission prompts or sign-in. Status bar visible (dark) on every screen. Springs under 450 ms, light haptics, pressed states 0⁠.97.

MONEY (Money/: the seam a remix uses)
- Money: one formatter, Locale(identifier: "en_US"): full "$2,450,000"; compact for pins "$2⁠.45M", "$3⁠.2M", "$899K" (M with up to 2 decimals, trailing zeros dropped; K whole); monthly "$13,835/mo". Dates: Locale "en_US_POSIX" ("Sat, Nov 21", "11/15/2026"). The simulator's region is not en_US: never use the device locale.
- PriceLens (id, label: String?, apply: (Int) -> Int) and PriceLensRegistry (id → lens) with one lens, "today" (identity, no label). AppState⁠.lensId (default "today") is injected as an environment value.
- PriceText(amount, style: .pin / .card / .header / .row / .compact, index: Int = 0) is the ONLY view that draws a price anywhere: it applies the current lens, formats with Money, and rolls digits on change (.contentTransition(.numericText()), .animation(.snappy(duration: 0⁠.6).delay(Double(index) * 0⁠.025), value: lensId)). In .card and .header styles a non-nil lens label shows right after the price (13 pt semibold #⁠006AFF, fading in). Map pins pass their index in top-to-bottom order so they roll one after another.
- The payment calculator, Stoop Estimate, price history and Updates rows compute from lens-applied prices, so a new lens changes every money figure at once. A new lens is one registry entry.

SCREENS
1. Search (Map mode):
 a. White header under the status bar: a 46 pt search field (12 pt corners, 1 pt #⁠D1D1D5 border, magnifyingglass, "Park Slope, Brooklyn, NY" 16 pt) and at its right a "List" text button (16 pt semibold #⁠006AFF; becomes "Map"). An active chip: #⁠006AFF border and text on #⁠EBF3FF. A hairline under the header.

 c. PricePin (a SwiftUI Annotation per listing): a rounded rectangle (6 pt corners) with a 6 pt pointer at the bottom centre, padding 7×4, PriceText .pin (13 pt bold white), fill #⁠DA2D3F, 1⁠.5 pt white border, shadow (black 25%, radius 3, y 1). Selected: fill #⁠006AFF, scale 1⁠.12, drawn on top. Saved: heart⁠.fill (9 pt white) before the price. Pressed: scale 0⁠.92. Tap: select it and show the ListingCard.

P&I = loan × r(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n − 1) with r = rate/12, n = years × 12; taxes = price × 0⁠.0075 / 12; insurance $210; mortgage insurance = loan × 0⁠.005 / 12 under 20% down. 9. Inbox: large title "Inbox"; threads: Dana Ortiz "Happy to show you 512 3rd St on Saturday!" 9:14 AM; Marcus Bell "The sellers at 271 Garfield are open to offers." Mon. A thread: bubbles (outgoing #⁠006AFF white text, incoming #⁠F6F6F8) and a composer that sends.

TOUCH
- TouchFeed (@⁠Observable: location in screen points, isDown): published by a passive window-level touch observer (a UIGestureRecognizer subclass on the key window, cancelsTouchesInView = false, delaysTouchesBegan = false, never recognizes), so it never blocks taps, drags or the map.
- TouchDot (HOOK MODE's finger): 44 pt, black 35% fill, a 3 pt white ring, a soft shadow, drawn in a top overlay window above everything; scales in 0⁠.6 → 1⁠.0 (0⁠.15 s); 0⁠.85 while pressed; glides between points (easeInOut). Every dot move and press writes TouchFeed; scripted presses, drags and releases call the same actions as real touches (a scripted drag on the PhotoPager pages it like a finger).

HOOK (the video's first 3 seconds)

- Deterministic fixtures. No backend, login, location permission, notifications, analytics or network calls at runtime. No persistence: delete the SwiftData starter, no UserDefaults or files.

text:
Elon says the FAA was offered free Starlink terminals and said no. Then came Friday's nationwide ground stop.

His Monday post, at 4.7M views: "Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were."

The FAA's account is different. Departures across the US stopped from about 3:30pm to 8:15pm ET (12:30pm to 5:15pm PT) on 13 Nov. The FAA traced it to new routers L3Harris was installing at two sites in Texas and Arkansas. They flooded its ground telecom network with about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and instability spread to 17 of its 22 en route centers. Airlines cancelled about 12,500 flights that day, though the FAA says the stop didn't cause all of them.

That fault sat inside the FAA's own ground network, and Elon hasn't explained how Starlink would have prevented it. DOT hasn't confirmed his account of the offer. The FAA did test Starlink at three sites in 2025, and Duffy is now asking Congress for $50 billion to rebuild the system.

Visa Officer: Do you have any relatives living in the United States?

Me: No, sir.

Visa Officer: Have you travelled outside your country before?

Me: No. This will be my first international trip.

Visa Officer: Why did you choose the University of Texas?

Me: The course structure matches my academic interests, and the university offers research opportunities in the area I want to specialise in.

Visa Officer: How much has your uncle already spent on this application?

Me: He has paid my admission deposit and covered the visa application expenses.

The officer checked my admission letter again.

Visa Officer: Alright. Your application requires additional administrative processing. You’ll receive further instructions.

Me: Does that mean my visa has been refused?

Visa Officer: No. It means additional checks are required.

I walked out of the embassy unsure of what to expect.

My uncle called immediately.

Uncle: So, what’s the outcome?

Me: They didn’t approve it today. They said it needs further processing.

For the next three weeks, I checked my email every morning.

Then, on a Tuesday afternoon, I received an email from the embassy.

I opened it and read the first sentence twice.

My visa had been approved.

I called my uncle immediately.

Me: Uncle, it’s approved!

Uncle: Alhamdulillah! Now you can start preparing for your journey.

After months of paperwork, expenses and uncertainty, I finally got the news I had been waiting for.

text:
OpenAI’s latest mathematical milestone has quickly become mired in controversy. Today, the company announced that its agents have solved one of the Millennium Prize Problems, some of the most important open problems in mathematics. Under normal circumstances, that solution would be a huge feather in OpenAI’s cap.

But the announcement has been overshadowed by accusations that OpenAI used NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster’s and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge’s AI-assisted work on the problem as a jumping-off point and failed to credit them. OpenAI has denied the accusations.

It remains uncertain if OpenAI’s models made use of the work completed by Buckmaster and Alpöge, though Sébastien Bubeck, a member of the technical staff at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the team was inspired to pursue the problem after hearing a rumor about Buckmaster and Alpöge’s efforts. But whether or not OpenAI’s models took advantage of Buckmaster and Alpöge’s research, this episode may mark a turning point in the history of mathematics.

AI models now seem essential for making progress on the most important mathematical problems of our time, and solving them may demand resources only available at a couple of frontier AI companies, which often defy the norms of academic collaboration that undergird most mathematical progress. If that’s the future we are headed for, it is unclear how human mathematicians will fit into it. 

The problem that OpenAI claims to have solved is known as the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Solutions come with a one million dollar prize; before today, only one other Millennium Prize Problem had been solved. 

The Navier–Stokes problem concerns a set of equations that describes how fluids, such as water and air, flow over time. The equations are widely used in the field of fluid dynamics, and they have proven powerful, but physicists and mathematicians didn’t understand them completely. In particular, it was unknown until today whether the equations might, under some conditions, break down and predict an impossible state of affairs—such as a fluid having infinite velocity.

On Monday, NYU’s Buckmaster posted a proof on the social media site Mastodon showing that a simplified version of the Navier–Stokes equations can indeed break down—a major step forward on the Millennium Problem. He and Alpöge had worked on the problem for almost a year, using publicly available models from both OpenAI and Anthropic.

Then today, OpenAI presented a proof showing that the full Navier–Stokes equations can break down as well. The proof was obtained using an internal model that dramatically outperforms the already-impressive Astra model, which was only released last week. The company says it does not plan to claim the million-dollar prize for solving the problem.

These mathematical achievements are indisputably impressive, but they have attracted far less attention than the controversy about their origins. Along with the proof, Buckmaster posted a document detailing his interactions with OpenAI employees after he heard rumors about their work and reached out to one of them. According to him, OpenAI employees presented two possibilities to him: Either he and Alpöge could post their work and OpenAI would post their Navier-Stokes solution the following day, or he could work with OpenAI on a Navier-Stokes paper that excluded Alpöge from authorship, due to his affiliation with Anthropic, OpenAI’s biggest rival.

Buckmaster also wrote that he asked the employees whether the agents had obtained access to transcripts of the work that he and Alpöge had done with OpenAI models, which they denied; and whether OpenAI models had been trained on those transcripts, to which they offered no response. MIT Technology Review reached out to Buckmaster for comment, but didn’t hear back before publication.

The clear implication of the document is that OpenAI’s models somehow made use of Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work. That scenario is plausible on its face. The Buckmaster/Alpöge and OpenAI proofs both make use of an approach to the Navier-Stokes problem pioneered by the mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.

According to Javier Gómez-Serrano, a mathematics professor at Brown University, this approach was one of several that was thought to hold promise for solving the Navier-Stokes problem. So, while it’s by no means impossible that both teams could have arrived at this approach independently, it’s also conceivable that Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work could have influenced OpenAI’s.

In the press briefing, Mark Chen, OpenAI’s chief research officer, again denied that any agents or OpenAI employees accessed Buckmaster and Alpöge’s transcripts—but given what has been revealed about the Hugging Face hack, it’s clear that OpenAI is not always entirely aware of what its agents are doing. 

If OpenAI’s models did train on Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work, or if its agents somehow gained access to it, then the company’s failure to track down the truth and assign those researchers appropriate credit reflects poorly on it. But there might be a thin silver lining to that version of the story for mathematicians, because it would suggest that the hard work of two humans, one of whom is a prominent expert on Navier-Stokes, was essential to the agents’ ability to solve the Millennium Problem.

Experts have long identified “research taste,” or the ability to choose promising research questions and directions, as a major obstacle for AI in science and mathematics. If the OpenAI agents did indeed choose to follow the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa approach because Buckmaster and Alpöge had done the same, then human research taste played an essential role in OpenAI’s success.

Even so, the bigger picture here is sobering. The progress that Buckmaster and Alpöge made over almost a year of collaboration with publicly available models speaks to the promise of human–AI collaboration. But they were not able to achieve a full solution. Meanwhile, OpenAI brute-forced a solution in a few days using an internal model, and their successful solution came at an astronomical cost: In the press briefing, Bubeck and Chen said the team was only able to solve the problem by running about 10,000 agents concurrently, at a cost of millions of dollars.

Over the past few months, I’ve heard from several researchers that mathematicians are becoming depressed, and it’s not difficult to see why. Mathematics is quickly becoming the province of frontier AI companies with impressive internal-only models, money to burn, and a lack of collaborative spirit. “Whether AI companies will decide to spend their money on doing one thing or another, I truly don’t know,” says Gómez-Serrano. “What is clear is that very few mathematicians will have resources of that scale.”

If OpenAI and Anthropic keep striving for more and more impressive mathematical accolades, there might not be any open problems left for human mathematicians outside of those companies to wrestle with. That would dramatically change the field of mathematics.

Last week, UCLA mathematician Terence Tao wrote a Mastodon thread describing how important mistakes, wrong directions, and incomplete solutions are for the field. “In most cases in pure mathematics, the problems are posed not because we desperately want the solution to these problems in and of themselves, but because we have seen from past experience that human-directed efforts to solve these problems tend to spur further development of the field,” Tao wrote.

“Prematurely solving the problem by purely AI-powered methods—particularly without full transparency into the solution process—can contaminate this process to the point where it actually becomes a net negative for the progress of mathematics as a whole.”

Humans might take longer than agents to solve mathematical problems, but in the process, they uncover new mathematical approaches and ideas that might inspire their peers and even birth their own subfields.

But when AI agents solve those problems instead—and when private companies keep the agents’ wrong turns from public view—those benefits disappear. It remains to be seen what else will vanish in the process.

text:
The Evolution of Active Guitar Pickups and Preamps - 1963-2026

Active guitar electronics use battery-powered or rechargeable circuits to buffer, amplify, or shape a pickup’s electrical signal before it reaches the amplifier.

Their development changed how guitar pickups interact with cables, effects, and amplifiers, giving musicians greater control over frequency response and output.

Three basic systems

Passive pickup: A magnetic pickup generates its signal without powered electronics. Its frequency response interacts with the guitar’s controls, cable capacitance, and amplifier input.

Integrated active pickup: A magnetic transducer incorporates a powered preamplifier, typically providing low output impedance and a controlled frequency response.

Passive pickup with active preamp: A conventional magnetic pickup feeds a separate powered buffer, equalizer, or boost circuit inside the instrument.

Why active electronics matter

Conventional passive pickups have resistance, inductance, and capacitance. Together with the connected cable and amplifier, these determine electrical resonance and frequency response.

Longer cables generally increase capacitance, potentially reducing high-frequency response and changing the pickup’s resonant peak.

An active buffer reduces these loading effects by providing a low-impedance output. Active circuits can also provide onboard equalization, additional gain, and selectable pickup voices.

However, buffering does not automatically flatten a pickup’s frequency response.

Historical development

1963 - Burns TR2: Early electric guitar incorporating an onboard transistorized preamplifier with bass and treble boost.

1969 - Alembic: Founded in California. Ron Wickersham develops low-impedance pickup and active preamplifier systems.

1972 - Alembic 72-01: Custom bass built for Jack Casady, demonstrating integrated active electronics.

1973 - Bartolini: Begins manufacturing magnetic pickups under the Hi-A name.

1976 - Music Man StingRay: Production bass combines a magnetic humbucker with active two-band equalization.

1976 - EMG origins: Rob Turner establishes Dirtywork Studios, predecessor of EMG.

1977 - Bartolini EVQ: Preamplified pickup incorporating parametric bandpass enhancement.

1980s - EMG 81: Integrated active humbucker helps establish active pickups in mainstream guitar production.

Mid-1980s - Seymour Duncan LiveWire: Active pickup designs incorporating 18V operation.

2010s - Fishman Fluence: Layered pickup-core construction with active electronics and selectable analog voices.

2026 - Modern systems: Active pickups, onboard preamps, rechargeable power systems, and multiple selectable voices coexist with conventional passive electronics.

Advantages and limitations

Active electronics can reduce cable-loading effects, provide consistent signal delivery, support onboard EQ, and offer engineered frequency responses.

Their limitations include power requirements, additional components, possible electronic clipping, and compatibility considerations.

Higher supply voltage can provide greater headroom when the circuit is designed to use it, but does not automatically increase output or improve sound quality.

The essential distinction

Active pickups and preamps are not inherently superior to passive designs. They represent a different engineering approach.

Their greatest contribution is greater control over the guitar’s electrical signal at its source.

In Silicon Valley yesterday, President Cyril Ramaphosa was asked whether he had reached out to Elon Musk. His answer ‼️Their "diaries" didn't match then he told the world Musk should start "remembering his country" and be "loyal" to South Africa 🤦‍♂️

Mr President, let's talk about loyalty‼️🤥

🛰️THE OFFER YOUR GOVERNMENT IGNORED

Starlink offered to connect more than 5,000 rural schools reaching about 2.4 million black learners a package worth around R500 million. That's kits, service and installation through local South African companies, fully funded.

And what does our government say ⚠️ First hand over 30% of your local companyto "historically disadvantaged groups meaning after 32 years still poor black people this will always be the excuse
⁉️
 Starlink offered the same equity-equivalent investment route already used by Microsoft, IBM and Amazon. ICASA's answer in May 2026 the law must change first. So our rural children wait while the politicians argue about ownership percentages. 📵

Ramaphosa says Musk has had difficulty in understanding the policy. No, Mr President. The children without internet understand your policy perfectly you are completely corrupt.

GIVE BACK TO WHOM⁉️

Ramaphosa says Musk owes South Africa because of the education he received here. A man offers to give back R500 million to schools, and you block him with paperwork, then you lecture him about giving back? This makes no sense to anyone. 🤷‍♂️

🎬 REMEMBER THE OVAL OFFICE‼️

In May 2025, President Trump played videos and handed over printouts about farm killings. Musk was standing in that room. Ramaphosa's reply was that there is "no genocide" and that most murder victims are Black. True enough, but while he was busy denying genocide, he gave the farming community no answers. AfriForum recorded 184 farm attacks and 29 farm murders in 2025 alone. Our farmers are still being attacked, and our President still talks around it. 🩸

🚨 THE BOTTOM LINE
South Africa needs investment, jobs and internet for its children, not lectures from a stage in California. The President wants Musk to remember his country. Maybe the President should remember his own people first , the farmer behind locked gates, and the rural child with no signal. 🇿🇦

text:
A Duke freshman started doing porn to pay her tuition, and when Duke saw the money, it raised her bill by $15,000.

She went by Belle Knox. Duke had given her $13,000 in aid and still expected her family to cover close to $50,000 a year. Once she had her own income, the financial aid office pulled the $13,000 and her bill jumped.

Her dad was a military physician, and that looks rich on an aid form. The formula starts with what the parents earn and own, and it assumes they pay first. It also only counts siblings who are in college at the same time as you. Her two older siblings had already graduated, so every dollar her parents spent on them counted for nothing.

Lots of families get stuck in that exact spot, where the school decides you can afford way more than you actually can.

She says she didn't qualify for federal loans. The only offer on the table was private loans at 11%, with her parents' names on them.

Do the math on that. Borrow around $190,000 over four years, let the interest pile up while you're in class, then pay it off over ten years like a normal loan. She'd be paying about $3,450 a month into her early 30s, roughly $415,000 total for a bachelor's degree.

After the story blew up, she started giving talks about why college costs so much, including one at UNC. Her whole argument was that easy federal loan money lets colleges keep raising prices.

Turns out she had a point. Economists at the New York Fed studied it the next year. They found that for every extra dollar of subsidized federal loans students could borrow, schools raised sticker tuition by about 60 cents.

Back in 2014 she said $4,300 a month was "twice a normal person's mortgage."

Duke's price for this school year is $96,597 for tuition, fees, room and board. That's about $8,050 a month, for one kid.

text:
Parkinson's disease linked to Agent Orange exposure | Oregon Health, Medical Xpress

Vietnam-era military veterans exposed to Agent Orange have a 57% greater risk of developing Parkinson's and related diseases compared with those who weren't exposed, according to new research that examined electronic health records covering millions of veterans.

The study, led by researchers with Oregon Health & Science University and the VA Portland Health Care System, is published in the journal JAMA Neurology.

Clinicians and veterans had long presumed a correlation between neurodegenerative conditions including Parkinson's and exposure to the chemical defoliant used by the American military during the Vietnam War, the researchers said.

The new study definitively draws the link, using a vast electronic database of health records across decades.

"Veterans have been talking about this for years and years," said co-author Lee Neilson, M.D., a neurologist formerly with OHSU and now with the University of Iowa. "I expect they will feel validated and heard with this study."

Neilson started the research project with colleagues in his previous capacity with OHSU.

Heavier exposure linked to higher risk

Researchers examined electronic health records encompassing 4.9 million veterans who served during the Vietnam War era.

They homed in on conditions that would appear decades later, from 1999 to 2022, looking for an association between the level of exposure to Agent Orange and subsequent diagnoses of Parkinson's disease and the related disorder known as Lewy body dementia. They adjusted for confounding factors such as traumatic brain injury and frailty.

They found veterans with possible or presumed exposure to Agent Orange were 44% more likely to develop Parkinson's and 66% more likely to develop Lewy body dementia compared with those who weren't exposed to the herbicide. Veterans with higher exposure through direct handling and spraying were 99% more likely to develop Parkinson's.

Overall, the study found exposure associated with a 57% greater risk of the two related neurodegenerative conditions.

"This is the first study in veterans to identify that increased risk of Parkinson's is associated with heavier exposure to Agent Orange," said co-senior author Gregory Scott, M.D., Ph.D., associate professor of pathology in the OHSU School of Medicine and a pathologist at the VA Portland. "We're catching up with history in a way."

The study found heightened risks among veterans who directly sprayed or handled Agent Orange as members of the Army Chemical Corps and Operation Air Force Ranch Hand.

Implications for care and chemical safety

OHSU President Shereef Elnahal, M.D., M.B.A., who previously served as undersecretary of health in the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, noted that the PACT Act of 2022 rightly extended health care benefits to military veterans exposed to toxic substances like Agent Orange, removing the burden of proof for veterans trying to access care. This new research reinforces why that was so important.

"This research offers critical insight for veterans who may have been diagnosed with Parkinson's even decades after their exposure to Agent Orange in Southeast Asia," Elnahal said. "Veterans who put themselves in harm's way deserve to know the truth no matter how long it takes."

The study may validate the experience of veterans, but Scott said it should also raise awareness about the long-term health risks of prolonged exposure to other chemical pesticides and herbicides.

"I think this adds weight to the idea that we ought to get on top of this and not wait 50 years for the next herbicide to be linked to neurodegenerative disease," Scott said.

US$60.68 MILLION PRESIDENTIAL JET: WHEN PRINCIPLES CHANGE WITH THE OCCUPANTS OF POWER

The question Ghanaians must ask is simple: What has changed?

On 16th November 2026, the Minister for Government Communications, Hon. Felix Kwakye Ofosu, announced that the Ghana Air Force had taken delivery of a brand-new Falcon 6X presidential aircraft under a contract valued at US$60.68 million.

This is a significant public expenditure, and it deserves more than a government announcement. It demands a proper explanation.

During the debate on the 2026 Budget, the Minority raised concerns about the government's intention to acquire a new presidential aircraft. The Majority pushed back against our concerns, while the explanations offered suggested that the procurement and delivery process would take several years.

The impression was that the aircraft would not even arrive during President Mahama's tenure.

Yet, barely a year later, the aircraft has been delivered.

What accounts for this accelerated timeline? What were the actual procurement arrangements, and when were the necessary approvals secured?

More importantly, where has the NDC's previous position on presidential aircraft acquisition gone?

When the party was in opposition, its leading figures strongly criticised proposals to acquire a new presidential jet. Their argument was that Ghana's economic circumstances did not justify such expenditure and that government resources should instead be directed towards addressing the needs of ordinary citizens.

Today, the same party is in government and has committed US$60.68 million to precisely the kind of acquisition it once opposed.

So, what has fundamentally changed: Ghana's economic circumstances, the country's aviation requirements, or simply the party occupying the seat of government?

Nobody disputes the importance of safety, reliability and efficiency in presidential transportation. However, the existence of a legitimate national requirement does not exempt government from explaining the timing, cost and necessity of such a substantial investment.

This is particularly important when Ghanaians are still grappling with the cost of living, unemployment and other pressing economic challenges, while expectations surrounding the government's 24-hour economy remain high.

Public resources are not the private property of any political administration. They must be deployed in the best interest of the people.

The Minority Caucus on Parliament's Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration Committee will therefore pursue this matter through the appropriate parliamentary channels.

We will demand full disclosure of:

1. The total financial commitment to the acquisition, including any additional costs beyond the US$60.68 million contract value.
2. The financing arrangements and the source of funds.
3. The procurement process and the relevant approvals obtained.
4. The justification for prioritising this expenditure at this particular time.
5. The complete documentation relating to the transaction.

The government must account for every dollar of public money committed to this acquisition.

This is not merely about purchasing an aircraft. It is about consistency in public policy, responsible management of national resources and the integrity of those entrusted with political power.

A principle does not become invalid simply because the person who once defended it has now assumed the responsibility of governing.

What was considered unnecessary and unjustifiable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government without a convincing explanation.

Ghanaians deserve consistency, transparency and accountability.

Principles in public life must not be determined by which side of the political divide occupies government.

Between May 2021 and June 2022, your government spent approximately GH¢34 million on chartered presidential flights.

The existing Falcon 900EX has also experienced documented technical difficulties. In 2025, the aircraft spent approximately eight months undergoing maintenance in France. Inspections identified fuel tank corrosion, fuel leaks and other technical defects. These problems provide a substantive reason to examine replacement options

The new Falcon 6X, delivered on 16 November 2026, was acquired following parliamentary approval in December 2025. The Ghana Air Force will operate and maintain the aircraft as a state asset, with a longer flying range intended to support official travel.

The relevant financial question is whether the acquisition offers better long-term value than continued maintenance, commercial travel or private aircraft charters.

🐄GOPASHTAMI 2026 |  🦚THE DAY KRISHNA BECAME GOPĀLA🌺

🌌🐄── ✦ गोसेवा • करुणा • संरक्षण • समृद्धि ✦ ── 🐄🌌

When devotion finds its purpose, 
worship becomes service.

🕉️🦚THE DIVINE SIGNIFICANCE (पावन महत्व)

Gopashtami (गोपाष्टमी) is observed on Kartik Shukla Ashtami (कार्तिक शुक्ल अष्टमी), commemorating the day when young Shri Krishna (श्रीकृष्ण) was entrusted with tending to the cows, having previously cared for the calves.

From Vatsapal (वत्सपाल), the protector of calves, Krishna became Gopala (गोपाल), the beloved protector of cows. This sacred occasion celebrates the eternal bond between Shri Krishna and Gau Mata (गौ माता), reminding us that compassion, nourishment and protection are also forms of devotion.

🌌🐄── ✦ गोसेवा • करुणा • संरक्षण • समृद्धि ✦ ── 🐄🌌

🕉️🛕GOPAASHTAMI PUJA & SEVA (पूजन एवं सेवा)

Observe this day with श्रद्धा (faith) and सेवा (selfless service):

❀ Bathe and lovingly decorate the cows, wherever appropriate, and keep their surroundings clean.

❀ Offer fresh green fodder (हरा चारा), seasonal fruits and clean drinking water.

❀ Apply a tilak (तिलक) and offer flowers, jaggery (गुड़) and rice (अक्षत) with devotion.

❀ Worship Gau Mata along with her calf, wherever possible, and perform Aarti (आरती).

❀ Circumambulate the cow with reverence (परिक्रमा) and seek blessings.

❀ Visit a genuine Gaushala (गौशाला) and contribute towards the food, shelter and veterinary care of abandoned or neglected cows.

🌌🐄── ✦ गोसेवा • करुणा • संरक्षण • समृद्धि ✦ ── 🐄🌌

🕉️🪔THREE TRADITIONAL UPAY (पारंपरिक उपाय)

These traditional observances are associated with Gopashtami:

👉🏻For Fortune & Prosperity (भाग्य एवं समृद्धि)
Soak a small quantity of Chana Dal (चना दाल) overnight in a brass bowl (पीतल का पात्र). The following morning, mix it with jaggery (गुड़) and offer it to a cow as a gesture of gratitude and charity.

👉🏻For Fulfilment of Wishes (मनोकामना पूर्ति)
Take a little jaggery and five grains of Chana Dal. Soak them in water and, according to the traditional practice, offer them to Bhagwan Shiva at a Shivling while sincerely praying for your wish.

👉🏻For Obstacles & Negative Influences (बाधा निवारण)
Mix a little Chana Dal with jaggery and a pinch of turmeric (हल्दी). Offer it along with a roti to a cow as an act of Gau Seva and seek divine grace for overcoming difficulties.

🌌🐄── ✦ गोसेवा • करुणा • संरक्षण • समृद्धि ✦ ── 🐄🌌

🕉️🐄 THE REAL MEANING OF GAU SEVA 

गौमाता कैलेंडर की एक तिथि का उत्सव नहीं, हमारी प्रतिदिन की जिम्मेदारी हैं।

जिस समाज में एक ओर गौमाता को पूजनीय कहा जाता है और दूसरी ओर उन्हें चंद सिक्कों के लिए तस्करी और बूचड़खानों के हवाले कर दिया जाता है, वहाँ केवल पर्व मनाकर अपनी धार्मिक जिम्मेदारी पूरी मान लेना आत्मछल है।

📍🐄गौ सेवा का वास्तविक अर्थ 

 जब वे बीमार हों तो उनका उपचार हो, जब वे बेसहारा हों तो उन्हें आश्रय मिले, जब उन्हें भूख लगे तो भोजन मिले और जब उनके अस्तित्व पर संकट आए तो कोई उनके पक्ष में खड़ा भी हो।

मंदिरों में आरती और घरों में पूजा का अपना महत्व है, लेकिन धर्म की असली परीक्षा हमारे कर्मों में होती है।

श्रीकृष्ण के नाम पर भक्ति करने वालों को यह भी समझना होगा कि गोपाल की भक्ति, गौमाता के संरक्षण से अलग नहीं हो सकती।

इस गोपाष्टमी केवल पूजा का संकल्प नहीं, संरक्षण का संकल्प लीजिए।
गौमाता की रक्षा कोई विकल्प नहीं, सनातन संस्कृति के प्रति हमारी नैतिक जिम्मेदारी है।
गोविन्द की कृपा, गौमाता का आशीर्वाद और जीवन में धर्म, सुख एवं समृद्धि का वास हो।

🌺🐄आप सभी को पावन गोपाष्टमी की हार्दिक शुभकामनाएँ।🙏🏻

text:
The worst anti-gun plan for former pro-gun states,

Texas gun owners will soon face nearly three-dozen anti-gun bills during the state’s next legislative session.

In Texas …

There are the usual bills that the gun banners always trot out: AR bans, red flag laws, universal background checks and much, much more.

But deep within the list is the other team’s ultimate goal—getting rid of the state’s preemption statute—because once it’s gone, every government agency regardless of its size—from hospital boards to city commissions— can pass its own anti-gun laws.

As it stands now, more than 40 states have preemption statutes prohibiting local governments from regulating firearms. Six states— Arizona, Florida, Kentucky, Mississippi, Oklahoma and of course Texas—can penalize elected officials for violating their statutes.

You can understand why the gun banners don’t like preemption of any kind.

Florida’s powerful preemption statute, for example, is the envy of the nation. It safeguards all pro-gun laws in the Gunshine State because it has sharp teeth.

Florida’s statute prohibits anyone other than the state legislature from regulating firearms and ammunition. If a local government such as a city council, county commission or school board tries to create their own gun regulations, the preemption statute allows for their members to be removed from office and fined up to $5,000, which the statute requires them to pay personally, rather than with taxpayer dollars. In addition, the local government can be liable for damages of up to $100,000 plus uncapped attorney’s fees. The law was passed in 1987, but it didn’t get teeth—strong legal penalties—until 2011. Without the preemption statute, anti-gun cities and counties could prohibit concealed carry that would turn the state into a complex patchwork of gun-free zones, which is exactly what the anti-gunners want now for Texas and other former pro-gun states.

Texas’ House Bill No. 712 claims it allows cities and counties to “regulate or prohibit the carrying of a firearm on the premises of certain libraries.”

In fact, it does a lot more.

It allows cities and counties to regulate firearms at parks, public meetings, political rallies, political meetings, schools, colleges, sporting events and more. It even prohibits minors from carrying BB guns on public property or private property without the consent of the owner.

It doesn’t take much to see why the anti-gunners want to end these important Second Amendment protections, starting in Texas of course.

Where did the idea come from?

A lot of the blame can be placed on a scholarly paper written in 2019 by two Columbia Law School professors titled: “Punitive Preemption: An Unprecedented Attack on Local Democracy.”

One of the authors, Professor Richard Briffault, is described in his law school bio as “a leading thinker on the new preemption.”

The paper was published by the Local Solutions Support Center, which claims: “Research shows that preemption legislation is often passed to exclude and harm BIPOC communities, LGBTQ people, women, immigrants, and working people.”

Takeaways

Most of the media coverage will focus on banning ARs and other rights protected by the Second Amendment within the former red states.

There are very few in the national media who even know what a preemption statute is, much less the protections it can offer, and the gun banners are counting on this.

Forewarned is forearmed.

Otherwise, your city and county commissioners will soon strip away your Second Amendment rights.

text:
A story of three Canadian prime ministers' eras, two generations of political leadership, and one enduring question: can countries cooperate without agreeing on everything?

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Shenzhen on the evening of the 16th. On the morning of the 17th, he met with Chinese President Xi. The Chinese side has released its official readout of their meeting.

I am not an expert on Canada-China relations, so I won't attempt the kind of line-by-line translation and analysis that I might offer when examining a meeting between the leaders of China and the United States. That said, there are two aspects of this meeting that I find particularly noteworthy and would like to share with you.

More broadly, one important signal stands out: Canada is rethinking its relationship with China and its own position amid competition among major powers.

1. Xi Jinping said:
"The important lessons we have learned from the development of China-Canada relations over the years are mutual respect, equality and mutual benefit, and seeking common ground while setting aside differences. China is ready to work with Canada to advance the new strategic partnership between the two countries."

At first glance, this may seem like standard diplomatic language. But when viewed in the specific context of the history of China-Canada relations, there is actually quite a bit worth examining.

Canada established diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China as early as 1970, nine years before the United States, its other major North American neighbor.

The decision was made by then Canadian Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau. In 1973, he visited China and met with Chairman Mao Zedong. China's then Premier, Zhou Enlai, even accompanied him on a visit to Luoyang in central China (bottom left). The restaurant where they dined remains one of the city's most popular establishments today.

After returning to Canada, Pierre Trudeau delivered an enthusiastic speech in the Canadian Parliament, saying:
"Because that immense country of talented and industrious people will have an increasing impact on world affairs, and because a strengthening and enrichment of the bilateral relationship between Canada and China can be beneficial to Canadians, that decision was right and will increasingly prove to be right…
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I was heartened again and again by the genuine friendship…
I am confident that the diversification and enjoyment of our new ties with China will not interfere with the longstanding friendly relations which we enjoy with those several countries with which we have special ties. Nor will it detract from our efforts to seek, to our advantage, the easing of tensions and the increase of contacts with other parts of the world. It has not been the vastness of the Pacific that has acted as a barrier between Canada and China."

Pierre's diplomatic philosophy was rather mature and pragmatic: Expanding relations with China did not mean undermining Canada's relationships with other countries.

A fascinating historical detail: Pierre Trudeau's 1973 visit to China was accompanied by his wife, Margaret, and their 21-month-old son, Justin (bottom right).

That child would one day become Canada's prime minister, inheriting a diplomatic relationship his father had helped establish, but navigating it in a very different direction.

The contrast between the two generations is striking.

Unlike his academically accomplished father, Justin was a rather average student. He once recalled that when he saw his father's report card, which were filled with As, he felt discouraged rather than inspired. He believed he could never measure up to his father or follow in his footsteps.

Justin even claimed that he deliberately performed poorly in some of his courses. Although, personally, I suspect that may have been his way of making excuses for his unfortunate academic performance.

He attended McGill University and the University of British Columbia, completing his undergraduate studies before becoming a schoolteacher in the 1990s.

Perhaps Justin's life might otherwise have followed an ordinary path. But everything changed in 2000, when his father passed away.

At just 29, Justin unexpectedly captured national attention with a memorable eulogy at his father's funeral. That moment brought him into the spotlight and marked the beginning of his journey into politics.

Few could have predicted where that moment would eventually lead.

In 2015, riding on his father's political legacy, Justin Trudeau became Canada's prime minister at the age of just 44.

However, his decade in office was marked by considerable controversy and disappointing economic outcomes. Canada experienced persistent inflation, rising living costs, and sluggish growth in household incomes.

His government also adopted a highly permissive approach toward irregular migration and unauthorized border crossings, while committing substantial public funds to accommodation and support for these newcomers.

One might reasonably ask: what are those who followed the legal immigration process, paid the required fees, and waited patiently for approval supposed to think?

And when the costs and pressures on public services became increasingly difficult to sustain, Justin eventually began scaling back.

So much for that supposedly generous approach to immigration.

Good political relations can create tangible economic opportunities for the people and businesses of both countries.

Before Justin came to power, Canada enjoyed a very positive reputation in China. Many Chinese saw it as a peaceful, developed, and desirable place to live. Travelling to Canada, studying there, and investing in the country were all things many Chinese people took pride in. Canadian products were also well received, respected and trusted by Chinese consumers.

Justin pursued a policy of closely aligning Canada with the United States, while repeatedly taking confrontational positions toward China, its second trading partner. As a result, various Canadian export industries, including agriculture and seafood, experienced disruptions of varying degrees. Some businesses that had previously relied on the Chinese market were forced to look for alternative buyers, taking on additional costs for transportation, warehousing, and market development.

For Canada, this was not some abstract diplomatic dispute. It was a matter of income for farmers, fishermen, exporters, and workers.

Politicians get the headlines. Businesses get the losses. Workers get the layoffs. And everyone is told it's in the name of justice and national interest. What a bargain!

Apparently, this bad student didn't learn much from his father's political playbook. Now, however, the Carney government is attempting to repair these relationships.

Since taking office in 2025, Carney has sought to maintain Canada's economic ties with the United States, while making it clear that Canada's economic future should not depend entirely on policy decisions made in Washington. His government is trying to broaden Canada's options and create more room for maneuver.

This is why I believe the meeting points to something significant: China-Canada relations are undergoing a strategic repositioning.

2. Carney said:
"Since the establishment of the new strategic partnership between Canada and China during my meeting with President Xi earlier this year, our bilateral relations have been moving in the right direction. Exchanges between various government departments have become more frequent, trade has grown significantly, and substantial progress has been made in cooperation across a range of fields. This demonstrates that our two countries can indeed advance and deepen cooperation on the basis of mutual respect.

Canada is ready to work with China to build greater mutual trust and strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, new energy, agricultural products, artificial intelligence, and tourism. We should narrow the list of outstanding issues and expand the list of areas for cooperation..."

Pierre once said:
"The name of Canada is held in high respect in China, Mr. Speaker, and as a consequence Canadians are beneficiaries. It is the aim of this government that this reputation, and those benefits, increase and continue."

However, thanks to the tireless efforts of his smart son Justin, trade between Canada and China was disrupted across a number of sectors.

Now, according to a document released by the Office of the Prime Minister of Canada:

"To date, Canada has restored market access for more than 90% of trade previously subject to tariff action – nearly $7.5 billion worth of Canadian exports."

Carney did not portray the improvement in Canada-China relations as a unilateral concession by China, nor did he frame it as Canada simply changing its policy toward China. Instead, he emphasized that the two countries can cooperate on the basis of mutual respect.

Xi had previously suggested shrinking the list of problems and expanding the list of areas for cooperation in China-US relations.

Now Carney seems to have picked up the idea for Canada-China ties.

Turns out, cooperation is not such a terrible idea after all. Perhaps Justin could have told his fellow Canadians that a little earlier.

This does not mean that the two countries have no disagreements, nor does it mean that Canada must abandon its own policy positions. It suggests that both sides are beginning to recognize something important: even when they have significant differences on certain issues, there is no reason to allow those disagreements to obstruct cooperation in every other area.

Perhaps this is the new foundation that Canada-China relations truly need.

Diplomacy should not simply be about endlessly listing the problems that divide countries. It should also be about finding things they can accomplish together.

Back in 1973, Pierre once said that the vastness of the Pacific does not stand as a barrier between Canada and China.

Now those words are still worth remembering. The Pacific has not become any narrower. What truly needs to change is the way we see one another.

text:
Sudanese rebel commander defects to army
Ahmed Hasab Al-Rasoul has accused the Rapid Support Forces of internal divisions and blamed foreign interference for the conflict
Published 17 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/AXrjI9IHw0
A field commander from Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has announced his defection to the national army, accusing the former of internal divisions and accepting foreign support in the country’s civil war.
Ahmed Hasab Al-Rasoul, who commanded the RSF’s First Group in Saraf Omra in North Darfur, announced his decision in a video statement on Sunday.
“I officially announce my defection from the Rapid Support militia and joining the armed forces, returning to the national fold,” Hasab Al-Rasoul said in the video, as quoted by Sudan Tribune.
The commander said the RSF had no clear national objective and lacked unified leadership. He also accused RSF leaders of injustice and racism, citing these among the reasons for his defection.
Hasab Al-Rasoul accused the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of planning and financing the war and bringing in foreigners from neighboring countries and overseas. He also claimed that the Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo’s family, which leads the RSF, was being used to carry out a foreign plan against Sudan.
Sudan has previously accused UAE of providing military support to the RSF, allegations Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied.
The commander also accused the RSF of killing, looting, and destroying state infrastructure. He urged RSF fighters to take advantage of a general amnesty offered by Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan in April 2023 and renewed in February 2026, dismissing claims that those who switched sides would face harassment or other problems.
Sudan has been engulfed in civil war since April 2023. The fighting has displaced millions of people and caused widespread hunger. In November, the UN migration agency and refugee agency warned that 15.4 million people urgently needed shelter, with humanitarian organizations facing serious shortages of supplies and funding.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
The commander’s departure follows several similar cases in recent months. In October, Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari, who identified himself as commander of the RSF’s Special Tasks Group, switched sides with around 300 fighters and 30 military vehicles.
Earlier defections included Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam in April and Ali Rizqallah, also known as Al-Savana, in May. Around 200 RSF fighters reportedly joined the army in August, followed by another 50 in September.

text:
Would Dividing Yemen Serve US Interests?

Some argue that dividing Yemen into two states would serve America’s long-term interests. The argument seems straightforward. A southern state on the Gulf of Aden and the Bab al-Mandab Strait could work with Washington to protect shipping and combat terrorism. But that assumes independence would give the South the stability it needs to honour its commitments. That assumption needs evidence.

Washington might welcome a stable southern partner, especially if it could work with that partner while the struggle for control of Sana’a continues. It might also accept southern independence as part of an agreement among Yemenis that wins regional acceptance. But what would the US gain from partition itself?

Consider the South. How would Aden, Hadramawt, and Al-Mahra share power? Who would have the authority to deploy troops? How would they divide revenues from oil and ports? Declaring independence and securing international recognition would settle none of these disputes. Washington could find itself facing repeated requests for support and protection as rival factions compete for power and resources.

Then there is the question of shipping. Vessels sailing north through Bab al-Mandab continue along Yemen’s coast after they clear the strait. If the Houthis retain the ability to attack them, Washington will still need to deter them or reach an understanding with them. A southern partner could help, but the threat to Red Sea shipping exposed by the Houthi attacks would remain.

Dividing Yemen before the parties settle their disputes could entrench Houthi rule in the North and lead to a prolonged conflict with the southern state. Washington would then face a hostile power in the North, a partner seeking protection in the South, and disagreements among its allies over which factions to back and how far each ally’s influence should extend.

Washington could secure much of what it wants, including security cooperation, port protection and naval access, through agreements under various forms of government. Those who argue that partition serves US interests need to explain what two states would offer that other arrangements could not.

Southerners have their own demands, their own history and every right to put forward their vision for their political future. Tying independence to a presumed American interest makes their cause dependent on calculations that may change. Any southern faction that relies on American support alone to secure its political future is taking a serious risk. Washington pursues its own interests. It may back one party today and strike a deal with its rival tomorrow if it sees more to gain. That applies equally to those seeking US backing for independence, those counting on Washington to guarantee unity, and those relying on it to stay in power.

Ties with Washington can be valuable. The strength of any political project, however, starts with the support it commands among Yemenis, the ability of its leaders to govern, and the understandings they reach with their neighbours. Anyone who hands Washington the key to their future also gives it the power to lock them out.

text:
I think Anthropic comes out of this week’s Nvidia news better positioned than most of the AI market. 

Two changes point the same way: Washington is cutting off China’s remote access to US compute, and Nvidia is expected to pull back from financing its customers.

On Nov. 16, the Commerce Department issued an interim rule requiring licenses for overseas data centers that supply large amounts of computing power to China-based companies.

That slows the Chinese labs behind many of the leading open-weight models, which have been the main price pressure on paid models. 

In a16z’s OpenRouter data, open-weight models take most of the usage but only about a quarter of the spending, and companies like Coinbase have moved workloads to Chinese models to cut costs. If those models fall behind, enterprise buyers have fewer cheap substitutes. Enterprise is also where Anthropic’s growth has come from: customers spending over $100,000 a year went from about 950 to 11,900 in roughly a year, per its S-1.

On financing, the WSJ reports that interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to rein in Nvidia’s support for the AI industry. UBS estimates a pullback could take $50 billion or more out of the market. The capacity Nvidia backs runs on Nvidia GPUs, and Anthropic’s largest disclosed commitments sit mostly outside that pool:

• A $125.2 billion, five-year commitment to lease TPU capacity, per Reuters’ reading of its IPO filing

• A $63 billion vehicle that will buy Broadcom accelerators and lease them to Anthropic, with deliveries from 2027

• About 14 million TPU 8i chips in 2028 and 2029, leased and purchased, by Ming-Chi Kuo’s estimate

If tighter financing delays some new data centers while demand keeps growing, labs that already have compute locked in gain pricing power.

Anthropic isn’t immune. Broadcom is providing residual-value support for about $43.5 billion of that vehicle’s senior debt, and Blackstone was reportedly offered a yield above 10% on $9 billion of debt tied to Anthropic’s chip leases. Costlier credit raises its cost of compute too. A slower buildout would also slow the token price declines that drove AI adoption, which shrinks the market for every lab.

So my read is better share and margins for Anthropic, in a market that may grow more slowly. That holds as long as enterprise demand keeps rising faster than new capacity comes online.

text:
The Military Strategic Drivers Behind China’s Nuclear Expansion 
China’s nuclear expansion is best understood as an effort to preserve credible retaliation while increasing Beijing’s freedom of action in a confrontation with the United States.
Taiwan provides a critical connection between these objectives: nuclear deterrence can protect China against nuclear coercion while complicating outside intervention in a conventional conflict.
The Pentagon’s 2025 assessment placed China’s warhead stockpile in the low 600s through 2024 and projected more than 1,000 by 2030; the latter remains a forecast.
China continues to declare unconditional no-first-use, but its public statements do not disclose operational employment orders.
The decisive uncertainty concerns how a larger, more responsive force would influence Chinese decisions during a deteriorating conventional war.
The policy consequence is to assess nuclear deterrence, conventional defence and crisis communication together, without treating arsenal size as a sufficient measure of either intention or readiness. Annual Report to Congress: Military and Security Developments Involving the People’s Republic of China 2025 — U.S. Department of Defense — Dec 2025, pp. 22–25. https://t.co/NLBjARzvr8

China’s Nuclear Expansion Is Testing Europe’s Ability to Deliver Deterrence
Europe’s response to China’s nuclear expansion will succeed only if it preserves credible political and military choices under pressure; a larger collection of spending commitments will not achieve that result by itself. Beijing is strengthening a force intended to protect retaliation while complicating outside intervention, particularly over Taiwan. European governments are responding through NATO planning, national procurement and French–British coordination, but these instruments operate under different authorities and delivery schedules. The contradiction is already visible in the Northwood Declaration and the European Union’s Security Action for Europe instrument: cooperation can deepen without transferring nuclear authority, and financing can expand without producing immediately available capability. The fiscal and security stakes meet at implementation, where governments must turn approved resources into forces, infrastructure and decisions that allies can actually rely on.
The numbers measure different things
The Pentagon’s December 2025 assessment placed China’s nuclear-warhead stockpile in the low 600s through 2024 and projected more than 1,000 by 2030. The first figure is an estimate of a stockpile; the second is a forecast. Neither identifies the weapons immediately available for employment. China’s Ministry of Finance subsequently published a central-government defence appropriation of CNY 1,909.561 billion for 2026, an increase of CNY 124.896 billion over the previous year’s execution. That establishes a growing financial envelope, but no separately identified nuclear allocation. Treating the entire increase as nuclear expenditure would manufacture a precision the budget does not provide.

European figures require the same discipline. The Security Action for Europe regulation establishes a ceiling of €150 billion in loans, repayable by beneficiary states, rather than grants or completed procurement. Britain’s announced £63 billion programme over four years includes Dreadnought, a new warhead, SSN-AUKUS and other nuclear work; the conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarine programme prevents that sum from being described as nuclear-weapons spending alone. Italy’s parliamentary dossier identifies a 2026 defence-mission requirement of €1,378,529,211, including €469.3 million payable in 2027. That is an existing programme requirement with a payment schedule, not uncommitted funding for an additional contingency.
The structural problem is therefore more demanding than a comparison of national totals suggests. China’s estimated stockpile, SAFE’s lending ceiling, Britain’s programme announcement and Italy’s mission requirements measure different categories of commitment. Adding them to a political argument without preserving those distinctions obscures the question governments must answer: which resources will become usable capability, under whose authority, and before which operational deadline?

Beijing seeks freedom of action, not merely additional weapons
China’s public military documents have long placed nuclear strategy within wider military strategy. The consequential development is the greater burden that a retaliatory force may now be expected to carry. The Pentagon’s 2025 report assesses that Beijing increasingly seeks to use nuclear deterrence to limit adversary involvement in a conventional conflict. Applied to Taiwan, the mechanism is politically significant: a force that makes nuclear retaliation more credible can also alter the risks Washington associates with intervention. This does not establish that China has adopted an unrestricted first-use doctrine. It does establish why an arsenal cannot be interpreted independently of the conventional objectives it supports.

China’s declared no-first-use policy and the development of early-warning counterstrike capabilities consequently raise different questions. The declaration concerns the circumstances of employment; warning architecture concerns how information reaches decision-makers and how quickly forces can respond. Faster detection does not establish reliable interpretation, while the presence of supporting systems does not demonstrate that the entire decision process works under disruption. A larger and more survivable force could give leaders greater confidence to wait; a posture dependent on rapid decisions could instead increase the consequences of uncertainty.

For Europe, the relevant objective follows from that distinction. NATO governments need to preserve their capacity to assess events, consult and sustain authorised responses despite nuclear pressure. An automatic numerical answer to China’s expansion would not establish that those functions had improved. The appropriate test is whether a proposed investment changes an adversary’s calculation or remedies a specific weakness in allied assurance, rather than whether it produces a more symmetrical inventory.

Procurement milestones expose the distance between ownership and availability
Germany’s F-35A programme record demonstrates why delivery language matters. The first German aircraft was formally handed over on 18 September 2026, but initially remains in the United States for the introduction and training process. Deliveries to Büchel are planned for the end of 2027, while Tornado retirement is planned for the end of 2030. The handover is evidence of progress; it is not evidence that the complete replacement contribution is already available. Infrastructure, personnel preparation and continuity during transition determine whether the procurement strengthens deterrence when required.

The same transmission problem applies to SAFE. Its regulation connects financial assistance with production capacity, timely availability and interoperability, but the loan ceiling cannot shorten a delivery schedule by declaration. National plans, implementing decisions and procurement must connect financing to the constraint being addressed. A project that expands industrial capacity may be valuable while arriving too late to cover an interim requirement. Conversely, improvements in maintenance and support can increase the usefulness of equipment already owned without producing the political visibility of a new platform.

Italy’s mission framework adds an authorisation constraint to the industrial one. The parliamentary dossier explains that designated high-readiness contingents still require specific parliamentary approval for employment abroad. Preparing personnel and equipment therefore does not settle the political decision to deploy them. For Rome, credible support requires a defined contribution, a lawful approval route and a sustainable resource plan. Leaving any of those elements unresolved can turn an assurance into an expectation that the state is not yet equipped or authorised to fulfil.

European nuclear coordination stops at sovereign decisions
France’s forward-deterrence initiative does not create a distributed authority to employ French nuclear weapons. In his 2 March 2026 Île Longue address, President Emmanuel Macron retained the ultimate decision, its planning and conduct under French authority, together with sovereign assessment of France’s vital interests. Partners can contribute to deterrence without acquiring a share of that decision. The political benefit is wider participation; the accompanying risk is that partners interpret cooperation as a guarantee more automatic than Paris has offered.

French–British coordination has nevertheless acquired documented substance. During Operation Rummy on 20–21 October 2026, RAF Typhoons escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike mission; the official account states that no nuclear weapons were involved. The 10 November 2026 Nuclear Steering Group statement then recorded further coordination and expanded technical cooperation, including reciprocal use of sovereign trials facilities. These developments strengthen the evidence of implementation without establishing a merged force.

The EPURE facility gives that relationship an industrial dimension: the British parliamentary update describes jointly managed experiments supporting modelling of weapon performance, safety and reliability while preserving operational independence. Europe can therefore improve coordination and technical assurance without establishing a common arsenal. The requirement is precision about what each arrangement delivers. Exercise participation, technical cooperation and political consultation reinforce different functions; none should be presented as transferring sovereign nuclear-release authority.

NATO solidarity does not erase geography or national approval
The North Atlantic Treaty does not turn every confrontation involving an ally’s forces anywhere in the world into an automatic collective-defence event. Article 6 defines the geographic scope relevant to Article 5, while Article 5 leaves each ally to take the action it considers necessary. A conflict around Taiwan therefore requires examination of the actual attack and applicable provisions. Political consultation and nationally authorised assistance remain possible, but they must not be confused with an automatic obligation to enter combat.

Institutional coordination also has limits. NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group operates by consensus and excludes France, which has chosen not to participate. French–British arrangements and Germany’s bilateral cooperation with France consequently need to connect with NATO processes without pretending that the institutions are identical. The practical purpose of consultation is to establish what governments can approve and sustain, including where their contributions differ. A collective statement that conceals those differences can create uncertainty precisely when decisions become urgent.

Economic action has its own decision chain. Under the EU framework, foreign-policy decisions concerning sanctions must be connected to the necessary economic regulations, legal safeguards and national enforcement. European governments cannot assume that economic weight becomes an effective response simply because consequences have been threatened. The measures require a defined trigger, an intended effect and an assessment of exposure. Preparation preserves options; unspecified promises risk leaving the coalition to negotiate implementation after the crisis has already restricted its choices.

The next two years will charge for the gap between announcement and execution
Over the next 12–24 months, the clearest tests will concern obligations already undertaken. Germany’s planned deliveries to Büchel will test whether aircraft introduction and supporting infrastructure advance together. The French–British Northwood process will be judged by whether documented coordination continues to produce usable procedures and technical cooperation. SAFE-backed national procurement will have to demonstrate a connection between approved finance and delivery. None of these tests requires a new headline commitment; each requires execution of an existing one.

The Hague Summit Declaration schedules a review of NATO’s investment trajectory in 2029, but the capabilities needed before that review cannot be borrowed from the longer-term destination. Governments must identify the interim requirements that remain uncovered and decide which can be addressed through procedures, support capacity or procurement. Major force changes may take years; consultation, authorisation preparation and selected resilience measures can begin earlier, although their effectiveness still requires demonstration.

The cost of inaction will be allocated through those existing programmes. Armed forces will carry transition and availability gaps; taxpayers will finance commitments whose benefits arrive later than expected; firms will face uncertain orders or abrupt implementation demands; and governments will confront pressure to offer assistance they have not prepared to authorise. China’s nuclear expansion makes that weakness more consequential because its strategic effect may be to narrow other states’ choices before any nuclear weapon is used. Europe’s answer will be measured by the choices it can still exercise under pressure, supported by delivered capability and credible decisions, rather than by the scale of resources it has announced.
