🇮🇷|Major General Ahmad Vahidi's speech on Tuesday is not a morale speech. It is a strategic assessment delivered in public, and the specific claim he made is testable: the United States is more isolated in its international operations today than at any point in its history, and the isolation is now visible in public refusals rather than private hesitation. That is not rhetoric. That is a claim about the diplomatic architecture of the war, and it deserves to be read as such.

The exact words, from IRNA. Vahidi, Commander-in-Chief of the IRGC, told a ceremony in Tehran Province where IRGC and Basij members renewed their allegiance to the principles of the founder of the Islamic Revolution that "the enemy has become trapped by the maneuvers devised by the Iranian people." He stated that the American-Zionist enemy "has faltered on all fronts" and that it "has never before acknowledged, deep down, such a profound level of defeat at the hands of the great Iranian nation." He added that the United States "has never been as isolated as it is now in its international operations," noting that "several nations have publicly refused to provide assistance, even though some have offered covert support."

The asymmetry in that last sentence is the real intelligence. Vahidi is distinguishing between public refusal and covert support. That distinction matters because it tells you what the IRGC is actually seeing. States that will not publicly join a US military operation are still willing to offer quiet assistance. That is not isolation in the absolute sense. It is isolation at the level of legitimacy. The US can still get quiet help. It cannot get open endorsement. And in a war that is being fought over the narrative of who is the aggressor, open endorsement is the only kind that counts.

The "deep down" formulation is worth pausing on. Vahidi said the enemy has never before acknowledged "deep down" such a profound defeat. That is a specific claim about the psychology of the adversary, not a battlefield claim. He is saying that the US and Israel know they are losing even if they cannot say so publicly. That framing is consistent with the IRGC's broader information strategy, which treats the adversary's public confidence as a mask over private recognition of failure. Whether or not one accepts the claim, it is a coherent theory of how the war ends: not with a formal surrender, but with the adversary's internal acknowledgment that the cost has become unsustainable.

The "all fronts" claim is the part that requires evidence, and the evidence is public. The US has failed to secure the Strait of Hormuz against Iranian coastal defense. The Israeli military is covering its bases with netting because it cannot intercept the drone threat. The US Navy is escorting tankers through a waterway that Iran and Oman are jointly renegotiating the rules for. The Gulf states have refused to be launchpads for strikes on Iran. Pakistan and Oman are building parallel economic and security architecture with Tehran. The "all fronts" claim is not a slogan. It is a summary of a strategic picture that is visible in the open record.

The Basij ceremony is the institutional context. The renewal of allegiance by IRGC and Basij members to the principles of the founder of the Islamic Revolution is not decorative. It is the mobilization base of the regime, and Vahidi is speaking to the men who would be deployed if the war escalates. A commander tells his mobilization base that the enemy is defeated when he needs them to believe the end is in sight. A commander tells them the enemy is isolated when he needs them to understand why the war is not spreading. The speech is calibrated to the audience, and the calibration is the message.

What Vahidi did not say is the deeper reveal. He did not claim Iran is winning militarily on every front. He did not claim the enemy is collapsing. He claimed the enemy is trapped, faltering, and isolated. Those are conditions that precede defeat without guaranteeing it. A commander who believed the war was won would say so. Vahidi described a war that is turning, not a war that is over. That is a more sober assessment than the headline suggests, and it is a more useful one.

 Vahidi's speech is a strategic briefing disguised as a ceremony address. The core claim, that the US is isolated in its operations and that the isolation is now public, is consistent with the record of the past several weeks. The claim that the enemy has "faltered on all fronts" is a summary of specific failures that are documented. The claim about covert support is an honest acknowledgment that isolation is not total. And the framing of the enemy's "deep down" recognition of defeat is a theory of how this ends. It is not a boast. It is a map.

Evidence:
- IRNA, November 17, 2026: Vahidi's speech in Tehran Province, "enemy has become trapped by the maneuvers devised by the Iranian people," "American-Zionist enemy has faltered on all fronts," US "never been as isolated as it is now," "several nations have publicly refused to provide assistance, even though some have offered covert support"

The Milburn report is absolutely shocking. 

The Uncensored Dissection: 700 Paragraphs of Whitehall Brain-Rot

Let’s take the gloves off. What you just pasted is a 40,000-word bureaucratic hallucination—a bloated, taxpayer-funded eulogy for an economic corpse that the Department for Work & Pensions is still trying to perform CPR on.

The UK government spent months paying civil servants, PwC consultants, and "expert panels" to wander around Newcastle, Clacton, and Wrexham asking why nearly one million 16-to-24-year-olds are rotting on the sidelines, why 61.6% of them have never held a paid job in their lives, and why a record 1.27 million will be detached by 2031. And after 697 paragraphs of hand-wringing, what is their grand revelation? "The architecture is fragmented! The maps don't line up! We need to build a Working State!"

It is pure, weapons-grade institutional copium. Here is the unvarnished autopsy of what this document actually reveals once you strip away the Westminster therapy-speak.

1. The Core Fallacy: Rearranging Deckchairs on a Torpedoed Hull (Total Blindness to P1, P2, and P3)

The author of this report looks at a generation being mechanically locked out of capitalism and diagnoses a plumbing failure between the Department for Education, the NHS, and Jobcentre Plus.

The Broken Ladder is Not a Policy Bug; It’s Unit Cost Dominance (P1): Look at the empirical body count buried inside their own chapters. Over 21% of NEETs have Level 3 qualifications; 15% have university degrees; 40% have A-levels or above. Graduate hiring is down 8% year-on-year. Computer science graduates are getting auto-rejected by HireVue AI video screens without ever speaking to a human. Employers are demanding two years of experience for entry-level roles. Why? Because the "first-draft economy"—the junior cognitive and administrative grunt work that used to train 18-to-22-year-olds—has been liquidated. Under P1 ($C_{AI} + C_V < C_H$), an AI model plus one senior verifier executes in ten minutes what used to take a squad of juniors two weeks. The bottom rungs of the ladder weren't "kicked away" by forgetful employers; they were sawed off and burned because training an anxious, error-prone 19-year-old at £12+ an hour plus National Insurance is financial suicide when an API call costs fractions of a cent.

The "Pastoral Burden" Delusion (P2): The report whines that employers are "cautious" and unwilling to take a punt on unproven youth who show up with anxiety, no workplace habits, and fragile attendance, noting that one large firm literally had to hire a full-time social worker just to manage its young staff. The author then begs employers to "co-invest in the transition" and take on more induction and confidence-building. Under P2 (The Multiplayer Prisoner’s Dilemma), any SME or corporation that volunteers to act as an adult daycare center for unproductive novices gets slaughtered by competitors running lean, automated workflows. Capital does not do charity. Calling for "employer brokerage" to fix structural obsolescence is like asking abattoirs to open a petting zoo.

Pathologizing Accurate Perception (P3 & Cognitive Obsolescence Syndrome): The report is baffled by why youth mental health has cratered—why 45% of NEETs are disabled, why 80% of young UC Health claimants cite mental health or neurodivergence, and why kids are staying up until 4 AM gaming and scrolling instead of begging for minimum-wage warehouse shifts. The DWP calls this a "health crisis with labour market consequences." Bullshit. It is Cognitive Obsolescence Syndrome (COS) in the wild. These kids were forced through a Victorian exam factory ("The Factory School"), promised that GCSEs, BTECs, and degrees would buy them a house and an adult life, and then dumped into a rent-seeking wasteland where a room in a shared house costs half their net pay and entry-level applications go into an AI black hole. Their depression and anxiety aren't clinical mysteries requiring CBT; they are the rational neurochemical response to discovering they showed up to a game of Monopoly on turn 50 after all the properties were bought and the dice were automated.

2. The Welfare Trap: Algorithmic Hospice in Embryo

Chapter 6 accidentally documents the birth of Attractor One: Managed Decline (The Algorithmic Hospice), while crying about how "perverse" it is.

Look at the math the DWP admits to in black and white:

A young person who plays the game—who subjects themselves to the humiliating 10-minute fortnightly compliance theater of Jobcentre Plus, applies to 150 jobs on Indeed to get ghosted by algorithms, and takes a 10-hour-a-week zero-hours retail shift—gets £551 a month and constant harassment.

A young person who gets a GP Fit Note (93% of which simply rubber-stamp "not fit for work"), enters the Universal Credit Health Journey (LCWRA), and claims PIP for anxiety, depression, or ADHD gets zero conditionality, zero work-coach harassment, and up to £2,000+ a month once housing and passported benefits are stacked.

And once they are in that lifeboat, 99 out of 100 never leave it for work in any given month, and 70% are still claiming a decade later.
The report calls this a "catastrophic failure of design" and a "deficit model." Wrong. From the young person's perspective, it is the only mathematically rational arbitrage left on the board. When the market value of your unverified, entry-level labor is trending toward zero, and the state offers you a £2,000/month bunker to stay in your bedroom on your phone, taking the bunker is the optimal play. The NHS GPs handing out 300,000 Fit Notes a year aren't "failing to enable participation"—they are acting as compassionate triage nurses certifying that the labor market outside the clinic doors is inhospitable to human life.
3. Social Function: Why This Document Exists

Why did the Secretary of State commission 700 paragraphs of this?

Because admitting the truth—that the postwar wage-demand circuit is dead, that entry-level mass absorption is never coming back, and that the UK economy has zero productive use for a million bottom-quartile and mid-tier young adults—would cause immediate political collapse.

So instead, the political class commissions a Scapegoat & Process Lullaby:

Blame the "Architecture": Pretend the reason kids in Blackpool and Hartlepool have no future is because the local NHS Integrated Care Board boundary doesn't match the Jobcentre district map. As if redrawing municipal PDFs is going to magically spawn 500,000 living-wage entry-level jobs in a coastal town whose economy consists of a Poundland and a care home.

Blame PwC's Favorite Buzzwords: Complain about "silos," "lack of data sharing," and failure to use the Longitudinal Education Outcomes (LEO) database. They literally argue that if teachers and councils just had better spreadsheets showing which kids are doomed at age 5, they could "intervene." Intervene to do what? Train them for the coding and administrative jobs that Claude and Codex just ate?

Sell the "Working State" Fantasy: Promise that the next report will unveil a shiny, permanent "participation system" that turns the Welfare State into a "Working State." It is a secular prayer. They are trying to legislate human economic necessity back into existence after the market has already priced it at zero.

4. The Verdict
This interim report is a coroner's report written by a mortician who insists the corpse just needs a better alarm clock and a joined-up referral pathway.

Its empirical chapters (Chapters 1, 2, 3, and 8) are a goldmine of terminal symptoms: the death of the Saturday job, the 68% collapse in entry-level youth apprenticeships as corporates use the Levy to upskill senior staff, the £125 billion annual drag, and the total evaporation of the entry-level career ladder.

Everything else—the moralizing about "good work giving structure to the day," the delusion that the NHS can cure economic obsolescence with "bio-psychosocial" targets, and the fantasy that uniting 17 Whitehall bodies will resurrect mass youth employment—is dead-on-arrival gibberish. Britain doesn't have a "NEET architecture problem." Britain has a million canaries in the coal mine of Productive Participation Collapse (P3), and the coal mine is already flooded. @grok what do you think?

text:
SPIRE $SR FY26 EARNINGS — ADJUSTED EPS GROWS 20%, DIVIDEND RAISED, BUT FY27 GUIDANCE CUT.
Spire delivered stronger underlying utility earnings as it completed its transition into a fully regulated natural gas utility business. However, weaker FY27 guidance raises questions about the near-term earnings outlook.
THE NUMBERS — FY26
🔹 Adjusted EPS: $4.02 vs $3.34 (+20% YoY)
🔹 Adjusted Earnings: $243.6M vs $211.1M (+15.4%)
🔹 GAAP EPS: $2.62 vs $3.14 (−16.6%)
🔹 GAAP Net Income: $168.4M vs $199.5M
🔹 Gas Utility Adjusted Earnings: $286.5M vs $231.4M (+23.8%)
Q4 RESULTS
🔹 Adjusted Loss Per Share: −$0.99 vs −$0.69 YoY
🔹 Adjusted Net Loss: $58.2M vs $37.0M
🔹 GAAP Net Loss: $94.4M vs $48.6M
FY27 GUIDANCE — LOWERED
🔹 Adjusted EPS: $5.05–$5.25
🔹 Previous Guidance: $5.40–$5.60
🔹 FY27 Capital Expenditure: ~$880M
FY28 & LONG-TERM OUTLOOK
🔹 FY28 Adjusted EPS: $6.10–$6.30
🔹 FY28–FY31 Adjusted EPS CAGR Target: 6–8%
🔹 10-Year Capital Investment Plan: $11.8B through FY36
WHAT'S CHANGING
🔹 Completed the Piedmont Natural Gas Tennessee acquisition.
🔹 Divested its gas marketing and storage businesses.
🔹 New Missouri and Alabama rates supported FY26 utility earnings.
🔹 FY27 guidance was reduced due to regulatory outcomes in Tennessee and Alabama and updated Missouri margin recovery assumptions.
CAPITAL RETURNS
🔹 Quarterly Dividend: $0.865 (+4.8%)
🔹 Annualised Dividend: $3.46
🔹 24 consecutive years of dividend increases.
MY TAKE
What stands out to me is the contrast between stronger underlying earnings and reduced forward guidance.
Spire is becoming a more focused regulated utility, which should improve earnings visibility over time.
But regulation cuts both ways. The same mechanisms that supported FY26 profitability are now creating headwinds for FY27.
The $11.8B investment programme offers a long-term growth opportunity, but substantial capital spending also makes financing costs, regulatory recovery and returns on invested capital particularly important.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
FY27 regulatory recovery, integration of the Tennessee acquisition, capital spending, financing requirements and delivery of the FY28 earnings outlook.
The long-term utility growth story remains intact, but the lowered FY27 guidance shows that predictable demand doesn't automatically translate into predictable shareholder returns.

Alex Rodriguez's mother made $65 in tips on a good night. she turned down $1 million from the Mariners for her broke 17-year-old son and said it was $1.5 million or college.

she worked two jobs, a secretary by day and serving tables at night. the family was broke and the offer was real money. if they would not pay more, he was going to the University of Miami to play quarterback and shortstop.

"absolutely not. if we don't get 1.5 million dollars, my son is going to college"

"mom, are you sure? we're broke. this is a lot of money."

the talks ran into the early hours. in the end it came down to a box of bats and two first class tickets on American Airlines. they settled at $1.35 million and a three-year major league contract.

"nope, it's one five or nothing."

text:
Angela White started her porn career at 18, while she was still in high school. She flew from Australia to Miami alone, did her first shoot, and flew back for class.

At that same school girls threw lemons at her and one punched her in the face. Two decades later she's the first woman to win AVN Female Performer of the Year three times, has a university degree, and once ran for parliament.

In the video below she tells it like it's a normal career story.

"Lemon" is Australian slang for lesbian. In high school she was called a slut when she slept with guys and a lesbian when she slept with girls. Whatever she did, she says, it was wrong.

"If you go to the supermarket and buy a fruit to torment somebody over their sexuality, that's really something else."

The girl who punched her had asked if she was a lesbian. Angela answered "why are you interested?"

But it didn't scare her off. She says it made her want porn even more. Porn was the first place she saw women celebrated for the exact thing she was getting hit for.

So in 2003 she picked one company in Miami that shot women with her body type. Her friends took some amateur photos. She burned them on a disc and sent it by snail mail with a handwritten letter. "I've never been shot. I really want my first shoot to be with you guys."

They flew her out. She was the first Australian they'd ever brought over.

And then nothing happened. She says it took many years of grinding before anyone knew her name. For 8 years she only shot with women. She had one rule, if her gut didn't say hell yes, she didn't do it.

In between she worked at Burger King, did webcam shows in Australia to pay the bills, and went to the University of Melbourne to study gender studies. She wanted to understand why everyone kept asking if she felt degraded.

Then the records came. She hosted the AVN Awards in 2018 while losing her voice. She signed a contract with Brazzers.

She treats it like an office job. Show up early. "If you don't turn up you're actually screwing up everyone else's money."

And she's already thinking about the exit. She's turned down offers to direct. The plan is to make enough, invest it right, and never need another business.

"I can retire. I've made my money."

The girl they threw lemons at mailed one letter, waited 8 years, and built a business out of the exact thing she got punched for.

Was the school wrong about her, or right in the most expensive way possible?

𝐇𝐈𝐋𝐋𝐀𝐑𝐘 𝐂𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐎𝐍 𝐎𝐍 𝐇𝐀𝐈𝐓𝐈𝐀𝐍 𝐌𝐈𝐆𝐑𝐀𝐍𝐓𝐒 𝐈𝐍 𝐒𝐏𝐑𝐈𝐍𝐆𝐅𝐈𝐄𝐋𝐃: '𝐉𝐎𝐁𝐒 𝐀𝐌𝐄𝐑𝐈𝐂𝐀𝐍𝐒 𝐃𝐈𝐃 𝐍𝐎𝐓 𝐖𝐀𝐍𝐓 𝐓𝐎 𝐃𝐎'

In a recent interview, Hillary Clinton defended the wave of Haitian migrants who settled in Springfield, Ohio — and in doing so, handed the open-borders argument away in her own words.

“𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘏𝘢𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘚𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘭𝘥, 𝘖𝘩𝘪𝘰 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘫𝘰𝘣𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘥𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘥.” she said. “𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘫𝘰𝘣𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦, 𝘧𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘬𝘭𝘺, 𝘥𝘪𝘥 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘰, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘏𝘢𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘫𝘰𝘣𝘴.”

Set aside for a moment who's right about Springfield. Listen to the actual argument: an entire American town, Clinton says, was restructured around a foreign labor pool willing to take work 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧. That isn't a defense against the immigration debate — it's an admission of exactly what the debate is about.

She wasn't finished. Turning to Trump and Vance, she said: “𝘛𝘳𝘶𝘮𝘱 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘝𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘮𝘢𝘥𝘦 𝘶𝘱 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘏𝘢𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘯𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘚𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘭𝘥.” and went further, calling it “𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘳𝘳𝘶𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯” on par with a political attack ad she also condemned in the same breath.

Maybe the specific Springfield claims were overstated. But the premise Clinton offered in their defense — that the jobs simply had to go to someone, and Americans weren't bidding — is the same premise behind every mass-migration policy Democrats have pushed for a decade.

𝐏𝐚𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐠𝐞. 𝐃𝐨𝐧'𝐭 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫.

text:
Why SpaceX ($SPCX) Could Be the Most Explosive Tech Bet of the Decade

When SpaceX officially went public under the ticker $SPCX in June 2026, it immediately rewrote Wall Street’s playbook. After rocketing past $213 shortly after its debut and later cooling off toward the $137–$140 range—right near its $135 IPO price—skeptics were quick to call it an overhyped space bubble.
They are looking at the wrong scoreboard. Treating $SPCX as just a rocket company is like valuing Amazon in 1999 solely as an online bookstore. Beneath the short-term volatility lies an unprecedented triad of orbital monopoly, global telecom dominance, and space-based AI infrastructure that could power one of the greatest compounding stories in modern market history.

1. The Orbital Moat Just Got Unbreakable

In aerospace, launch cadence and reusability are everything. On November 14, 2026, SpaceX achieved a historic milestone with Starship Flight 15, executing the first-ever simultaneous catch of the spacecraft by the launch tower.
Why does this matter to shareholders? Because every incremental drop in launch cost widens a moat that no competitor—public or private—can realistically cross. While rivals struggle to get next-generation heavy lifters off the pad, SpaceX is rapidly marching toward full Starship commercial operations by late 2027. Once fully operational, SpaceX won’t just lead the global launch market; it will effectively own the tollbooth to low-Earth orbit.

2. Starlink: The Cash-Flow Engine Goes Global

If Starship is the heavy artillery, Starlink is the high-margin recurring revenue machine. With connectivity revenue surging 69% year-over-year and operating income jumping 99%, Starlink has evolved far beyond rural residential broadband.
Today, it is rapidly locking in lucrative, sticky enterprise contracts across global aviation, maritime shipping, defense, and sovereign governments. As Starship deploys larger, higher-capacity next-generation satellites, Starlink’s unit economics improve dramatically. Unlike terrestrial telecom giants weighed down by aging copper wires and regional regulatory bottlenecks, Starlink scales globally with software-like marginal costs.

3. The Secret Weapon: AI Compute & Orbital Data Centers

Here is what most traditional aerospace analysts are missing: SpaceX is quietly becoming an AI infrastructure juggernaut.
Data from recent financial disclosures shows SpaceX’s Super Intelligence and AI compute segment already generating $7.56 billion in revenue, outpacing even its connectivity division. By leasing massive data center compute capacity to frontier AI labs like Anthropic and Google, SpaceX has tapped directly into the biggest capital expenditure boom of our generation.
Even more ambitious is Elon Musk’s push toward orbital AI data centers. Building gigawatts of terrestrial AI compute requires tens of billions of dollars in grid upgrades and endless utility bills. In orbit, solar energy is continuous, cooling is abundant, and Starship provides the heavy-lift logistics to deploy hardware at scale. Musk recently projected that SpaceX’s annualized revenue run rate could cross $100 billion by December 2026—with a bold target of $500 billion by late 2027. Even if SpaceX achieves a fraction of that trajectory, current consensus Wall Street estimates will look wildly conservative.

4. A Massive $10 Billion Passive Tailwind Is Coming

Beyond fundamentals, market mechanics are lining up in favor of $SPCX bulls. According to research from Goldman Sachs, SpaceX’s publicly tradable float has already expanded from roughly 5% at its IPO to nearly one-third of total shares.
As index providers like the Russell 1000 Growth Index prepare for scheduled rebalancings (such as the upcoming December 11 adjustment), passive ETFs and institutional funds are forced to buy more shares to match SpaceX’s growing float weight. Goldman estimates this mechanical adjustment alone could trigger over $10 billion in passive ETF buying demand. In fact, ETF flow trackers already show major funds—including Invesco QQQ—steadily accumulating $SPCX shares on recent dips.

MrCasey, saying “God does the work” does not settle whether God appointed the practice. The question is whether His written word establishes the promise being claimed.

I agree that salvation is God’s work: “For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). But the bus illustration assumes the very point that needs to be established: 

Does Scripture promise the particular work being claimed for each sacrament?

Through Christ, neither boundary determines access to our heavenly Father. Jew and Gentile, women and men, belong together in the royal priesthood of believers, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:18–19; Galatians 3:28–29; 1 Peter 2:5, 9).

Through Christ, ancestry and sex no longer determine our access to the Father. Ephesians 2:14 describes Christ breaking down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile. The reconciliation came through His cross; the physical temple walls did not fall when He died.

“For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father” (Ephesians 2:18).

The New Testament announces a royal priesthood of believers from every nation—women and men together (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Galatians 3:28–29). 

Priestly belonging is no longer confined to Aaron’s male descendants. Through Jesus our High Priest, believers offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God.

Our confidence rests in His offering:

“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14).

Those who shepherd the church must serve without lording it over God’s people (1 Peter 5:2–3). Jesus likewise warned against religious works performed for public admiration:

“But all their works they do for to be seen of men” (Matthew 23:5).

That warning examines every one of us. A title, garment, ceremony, or public prayer cannot establish that someone speaks for God. In the same passage, Jesus directs us toward our heavenly Father and humble service:

“And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9).

Jeremiah 44 supplies another searching example. Husbands and wives stood together in defending their inherited worship of the queen of heaven. 

Yet agreement within a household could not make that worship agreeable to God. They said, “We will not hearken unto thee,” choosing what proceeded from their own mouths over the word spoken in the Lord’s name (verses 16–19).

An old tradition still needs to hear the everlasting word. That gentle warning belongs to every household, including mine. Neither family agreement, religious titles, nor generations of observance can turn a human practice into God’s command.

Aaron’s sons also remind us that a religious offering can be something God did not command (Leviticus 10:1–2). That account does not automatically condemn another practice, but it does show why sincerity and ceremony alone cannot establish God’s approval.

Therefore, my question is simple: Where does Scripture establish each promise being made here? 
Calling a practice “God’s work” cannot replace showing that God promised it.

“For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth” (2 Corinthians 10:18).

May we help one another hear our heavenly Father, receive His correction, and walk together in His love.

In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

#LUREOFLANKA DIARIES DAY 3 – 🪨 ROCK AND TOOTH 🦷

Day 3 of our first-ever #LureOfLanka tour began before sunrise. We left our hotel at 6 am for an optional extra: a climb up Sigiriya before the heat set in.

Sigiriya, or Lion Rock, rises about 180 m above the forest. In the 5th century, King Kashyapa built a palace on its summit. The climb took us past the famous “Sigiriya maidens,” wall paintings which date from around the same time as India’s Ajanta caves. Further up, we reached the Lion’s Paws, all that remains of a giant brick lion whose open jaws once formed the last stairway to the top. At the summit, we cheered with joy at the wide expanse of Sri Lanka below, proud of having made it!

After a return to the hotel and a quick shower, we drove on to Matale and the Noritake porcelain outlet. The Japanese company opened its factory here in 1972, and our guests picked up keepsakes to remember the trip by.
By evening, we had wound our way into the hills to Kandy, the last royal capital of Sri Lanka. We watched a traditional Kandyan dance performance, another optional extra, with drummers, dancers and fire-walkers whose acrobatics made our guests gasp. Next came a guided tour of the Temple of the Tooth, home of the Buddha’s tooth relic, the most sacred object on the island. Our guests then had free time to explore Kandy on their own.

On Day 4, we will head higher into ☕ tea country to Nuwara Eliya. ️

text:
Humility Is a Location

Humility is a location before it is a feeling. The humble man knows his register: a creature in the lower register, bearing the image as an office he received, under a Suzerain whose glory fills the heaven above him and is not his. His lowliness is structural. He confesses the architecture as it stands, and he stands where it puts him.

Pride is the station claim. Lucifer fell from inside the upper register: a servant of the Suzerain in the glory-heaven itself, set at his station among the hosts, and his pride was a throne claim within the register he already occupied — "I will ascend; I will make myself like the Most High." He did not climb; he usurped. Adam's pride came from below: the serpent's offer was a promotion out of the creature's register, and Adam grasped at it. The two falls are one sin at two altitudes — the office-holder reaching for a place that was not given, servant and vassal alike refusing the station assigned. Every pride since is the same reach in smaller currency, and it gathers at the end into the man of lawlessness, the claim at its ultimate: he exalts himself over all that is called God and aims at the temple seat itself, proclaiming himself to be God. The grammar refuses him the throne — ὥστε states his purpose, never its outcome; he proclaims himself seated, and he never sits. The breath of the Lord's mouth ends the proclamation.

The Second Adam refused the offer the first Adam took. He did not grasp. In the Pactum the Son undertook as Vassal to fulfill the covenant of works. The two are not the same covenant: the covenant of works was made with Adam, and the Son entered its terms as the race's second Head, kept its stipulation, and bore its curse. His humility is that undertaking rendered in history, covenant obedience all the way to the sanction; and his exaltation is the inheritance the Father promised him in the Pactum — merited by his obedience, owed to the Vassal who kept the covenant, a wage in the strict sense of the stipulation. The Head merits; the members inherit what he merited. The reward reaches the church as inheritance because it reached the Son as wage.

Daniel is the law-keeping man humbled. No vassal in exile kept the stipulation more faithfully — he would not defile himself with the king's food, and he prayed toward Jerusalem with the windows open — and his great confession owns the nation's sin as his own: "we have sinned, we have done wickedly." He pleads no record. "We do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy" (9:18). Under the works administration itself, the best keeper of the law ends on his face, and the mercy he pleads is not Sinai's commodity; it is the covenant of grace operating across the administration, heard by the man the law had humbled to exactly the ground where grace speaks.

The healed leper shows the shape of it. Ten were cleansed; one returned, and he a Samaritan, and fell at Jesus' feet glorifying God and giving thanks. His thanksgiving was his humility: reception confessed aloud, the gift named as gift and the receiver located at the giver's feet. The nine kept their cleansing and stayed away; the one who came back heard the word the others did not — "Your faith has saved you." Thanksgiving is humility with a voice, the creature's station spoken from inside it, glad.

Humility in the covenant of grace is therefore reception. The believer's standing is located in his Head, whole and finished, and his Amen is confession of a verdict already rendered. The meek inherit the earth — the beatitude is architectural — because inheritance is the only instrument by which the earth reaches the meek; they do not seize it, and they do not earn it — their Head merited it, and they receive it from his hand. The humble man is a guest at a table he did not set, an heir in a house he did not build, a creature glad of his register because the King of the upper register has spoken his name in grace.

text:
Finland's ICEYE offered €41 a share in cash for Avio, the Italian maker of Europe's Vega rockets. The bid is worth up to about €2.05B, 21.3% above Monday's official price of €33.79.

Avio jumped about 14% to around €39 in Milan, still roughly 5% short of the offer. The deal needs Italy's golden power approval with no conditions, plus sign-off in France, the UK, the EU and from CFIUS in the US.

ICEYE wants at least 66.67% of the shares so it can delist Avio. Leonardo owns 18%, Advent 6.5% and Goldman Sachs 5.3%, and the offer notice shows no commitments from any of them. ICEYE also promised €1B of new investment in Italy over five years.

Avio's board is reviewing the bid.

text:
🚀 Vulcan falls out of the sky, leaving the Pentagon leaning harder on SpaceX as it adds a 985 million dollar launch ceiling for all three providers

The US military's plan for a second reliable heavy rocket took a hit on Sunday when United Launch Alliance's Vulcan failed about ten minutes after liftoff from Cape Canaveral, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites and leaving SpaceX as the only national security launch provider with a rocket that is actually flying.

ULA said the rocket "suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit." Ars Technica, citing multiple sources, reported the problem was in the booster stage, which is powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, and that the engines appeared to fire at least 30 seconds longer than planned before the vehicle began to spin. Ars called it the first total mission failure in ULA's 20-year history. The cause has not been established.

The timing matters more than the payload. Breaking Defense reports the Space Force had grounded Vulcan for national security work in late February over recurring solid rocket booster problems and by Oct. 1 had moved six missions from Vulcan to SpaceX. Sunday's commercial flight was meant to be a step back toward military certification. Blue Origin's New Glenn, the third certified provider, has been grounded since a pad explosion in May that investigators traced to a faulty valve on a BE-4 engine. If the BE-4 is implicated again, both of SpaceX's American competitors could be stuck behind the same engine.

On Monday the Department of War announced contract modifications for SpaceX, United Launch Services and Blue Origin with a combined maximum ceiling of 985 million dollars for National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 2 launch services, with work through April 2033. No funds were obligated at award. This is headroom to order launches, and it does not tell you how many missions each company will get. Given who can fly today, the practical beneficiary in the near term is easy to guess, though the notice does not split the ceiling.

The strategic problem is that SpaceX is moving away from the very rockets the Pentagon depends on. Breaking Defense notes SpaceX stopped taking commercial Falcon orders for rides after 2028 and plans to shift its own operations to Starship around 2030, while it has not announced plans to offer Starship to military customers. Ars adds that certifying Starship for national security missions would take years. Washington is racing China in orbit with one working heavy launcher, owned by a single company that is retiring it.

For allies, this is a concentration risk they already know from Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine. For the Space Force, the question is whether assured access to space still means two independent paths to orbit, or one company and a waiting list. https://t.co/VqgzHve5px

text:
Just being the first to get in on a token doesn't necessarily make it a good trade if the market is moving quickly.

 In some cases, it is the best to know what launches to steer clear of.

A big lesson on exploring @Hypesium on Elysium.

While speed of execution is important, I believe there are three important things traders need to consider before participating in a new launch:

1. Understanding the deployer

The contract is just a part of the token. Even though the wallet looks healthy, certain indicators might be present that can be detected from previous launches, wallet behaviour, and the deployer's history.

3. Knowledge of the end result

@Hypesium has one interesting part of its operations: a system of transaction security. It carries out simulation, assesses the liquidity and tax situation, and even makes sure that a sell can be executed before the trade is approved.

Depending on their risk tolerance, users are also able to choose between protection profiles.

This provides a crucial additional safeguard particularly when launching rockets that are not under control.

3. Having visibility after entering

Once the purchase is successful, it is only the beginning. But traders will still have to keep an eye on their trades, think about the costs of the transaction and assess the initial rationale behind the trade.

Additionally, Hypesium offers transaction history and wallet reporting, allowing traders to better visualize their trading activity.

However, no simulation can foresee all the market actions and no simulation can rule out the potential of a rug pull. On-chain research and personal judgement is still critical.

Not for me, the real worth of a trading instrument is not just the speed at which it is able to make an order. It's about the level of control, transparency and protection it affords during the entire process.

It's nice to be early, but it's better to be well informed.

Do you prefer to get a launch in your first seconds in, or take time to doublecheck that it is in?

text:
A 28 year old paid $18,000 to create 4 MILLION fake customers for her company.

JPMorgan then bought out the company for $175 MILLION without looking at a single detail.

JPMorgan also had to pay $100 MILLION to put the girl in prison.

In 2017, Charlie Javice created a company called Frank that was a platform to help college students.

It was able to help students apply for financial aid.

It was a solid business, but she wanted to more.

She had started claiming that the business had a lot more customers than they truly had.

Because of this, in 2019 she was in Forbes 30 Under 30.

And in 2021, JPMorgan actually wanted to buy out her business.

The bank offered her $175 MILLION for the entirety of her business, including all of the customers.

But before they went through with the deal, they wanted her to prove they had the customers she was claiming.

At the time Frank had <300,000 actual users.

Javice had been claiming that number was over 4 million.

To go through with the JPMorgan deal, she paid a data science professor $18,000 to create a list of over 4 MILLION fake students.

All to make Frank look like a legit large business.

The professor was able to create all sorts of fake information.

Names, emails, birthdates, and even income levels, they had all been fake.

JPMorgan went through with the deal, without even double checking the information they had.

She was able to get $29 MILLION and a position at JPMorgan as Managing Director.

The fraud started to get uncovered when JPMorgan tried to send marketing emails to Frank's customers.

Over 70% of the customers left instantly.

Something was clearly fishy.

It started spiraling when an engineering director testified that the week before the deal closed, Javice asked him to help fake all of the numbers.

But he had refused the offer because he was affraid of going to prison.

Javice was then arrested in 2023. 

She got out with a $2 MILLION bail before the official trial actually started.

In the meantime she became a Pilates instructor in South Florida.

In March of 2025, the jury convicted her on all four counts of bank fraud, securities fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy on top of it all.

She was then sentenced to 85 months in federal prison.

She also had to pay $287.5 MILLION in restitution fees.

But there was also a twist.

Because of how the contract with JPMorgan made her an employee, the bank was legally required to cover her entire bill.

The bill was over $100 MILLION.

The judge had told JPMorgan they had to take some responsiblity themselves because they didn't check before signing off.

The judge then sentenced her anyway.

text:
What Canine DNA Evidence Can Tell Us About a Case
#cozymystery #TuesdayMotivation #Dogs 

A muddy paw print may point everyone in the wrong direction. A few pale hairs caught on a jacket, however, can quietly tell a much more interesting story. When a dog has brushed against a person, vehicle, fence, or favorite armchair, it may leave behind biological clues. That is where canine DNA evidence enters the picture - not as a magic answer, but as one useful piece of a larger puzzle.

For a cozy mystery reader, the idea has irresistible possibilities. Dogs go places, notice people, and have very firm opinions about who belongs near the treat jar. In a real investigation, though, their DNA has to be collected, preserved, tested, and explained with care. The science can be fascinating, and the limitations are every bit as important as the results.

## What Is Canine DNA Evidence?

Canine DNA evidence is genetic material from a dog that is recovered from an object, person, or location. It may come from shed hair with a root attached, saliva on a chewed item, blood, tissue, urine, feces, or skin cells. Scientists can compare that material with a known sample from a particular dog to determine whether the dog could be the source.

The wording matters. A test result does not usually announce, with a dramatic flourish, that one specific dog was at a crime scene. Depending on the test and sample quality, it may show that the evidence is consistent with a particular dog, that it likely came from a dog in a certain maternal line, or that the sample is too limited to say much at all.

That distinction makes canine evidence especially interesting in a mystery. It can support a timeline, challenge an alibi, or connect two people who insist they have never met. It may also raise the next question: how did the dog’s DNA get there?

## How a Dog Leaves a Genetic Trail

Dogs are wonderful at spreading themselves around. Anyone who has found fur on a black sweater after a brief visit with a golden retriever understands the basic principle. But ordinary shedding is not the only route by which DNA travels.

A dog can leave saliva on a toy, a food wrapper, a bitten glove, or the sleeve of someone it greeted enthusiastically. Blood may be present after an injury. Hair can cling to clothing, carpeting, car seats, and brush. DNA can also move indirectly, which forensic scientists call transfer. A person may pick up dog hair at home, carry it on a coat, and leave it somewhere else without the dog ever visiting that second location.

This is why one stray hair is rarely the whole case. Investigators look at where it was found, whether it was protected from contamination, what other evidence is present, and whether the story makes sense. Several hairs embedded in a victim’s blanket tell a different story than one loose hair on a public bench.

### Hair Is Helpful, but It Has Limits

Not all dog hair contains the same kind of information. Hair with a root may provide nuclear DNA, the genetic material that offers the strongest individual comparison. A hair shaft without a root can still sometimes yield mitochondrial DNA.

Mitochondrial DNA is inherited through the mother. It can connect a hair to a maternal family line, but it generally cannot distinguish one individual dog from every related dog. Two littermates, for example, may share the same mitochondrial profile. That is useful evidence, yet it is not the same as a unique identification.

For readers who enjoy a fair-play whodunit, this limitation is gold. A hair may point toward the suspect’s dog, only for a clever sleuth to learn that the neighbor owns a related dog from the same breeder. The clue was real. The first conclusion was simply too tidy.

## From Swab to Result

Proper collection is less glamorous than television makes it seem. Investigators document the item, photograph its position when appropriate, wear fresh gloves, use clean tools, and package samples in a way that helps prevent moisture, degradation, and cross-contamination. They also maintain a chain of custody, recording who handled the evidence and when.

A known reference sample is usually collected from the dog through a cheek swab or sometimes a blood sample. In a laboratory, analysts extract DNA and assess whether enough usable genetic material is present. They then examine selected markers and compare the questioned sample with the reference sample.

Results can be quite clear, but not every sample cooperates. Heat, sunlight, moisture, age, cleaning products, and repeated handling can damage DNA. A sample may contain DNA from more than one dog or from a dog and a person. Sometimes the laboratory can report a meaningful comparison; sometimes the honest answer is inconclusive.

That answer may feel frustrating, but it is good science. A careful forensic conclusion protects innocent people and keeps investigators from building a grand theory on a smudge, a wish, and a biscuit crumb.

## When Canine DNA Evidence Matters Most

The value of canine DNA evidence usually lies in connection. It can associate a suspect with a location, a victim with a vehicle, or a dog with an object that was moved or discarded. It may also help distinguish between competing accounts of what happened.

Imagine a burglary in a small Florida town. A witness recalls seeing a person in a raincoat near the back gate but cannot identify a face. Later, investigators find dog hair on the gate latch and on the cuff of a recovered raincoat. If those hairs are consistent with the same dog, and that dog belongs to a person with access to the property, the evidence becomes a meaningful thread.

Still, it needs company. Security footage, phone records, fingerprints, witness observations, tool marks, and plain old common sense may all matter. The dog’s hair could have arrived days earlier. The suspect may have a perfectly ordinary reason to know the homeowner’s dog. A good case does not lean its full weight on one wagging tail.

## The Questions a Good Sleuth Should Ask

Whether the sleuth is a detective, a veterinarian with sharp instincts, or a dog narrator who has overheard too much from beneath the kitchen table, the key questions remain practical. Was the sample collected correctly? Could it have been transferred indirectly? Is the comparison individualizing or only consistent with a group? Does the timing fit? And what innocent explanation deserves a serious look?

Those questions keep forensic science from becoming a shortcut. They also make a mystery more satisfying. Readers want clues that count, but they want characters to earn the answer. A laboratory report can narrow the field; it cannot decide motive, explain a lie, or reveal why someone was prowling around town after midnight.

In the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, canine forensics belongs naturally beside small-town connections, local history, and the sort of details people overlook until Daisy puts her nose where it does not belong. Dogs do not solve every case by themselves, of course. They simply have a delightful talent for noticing the humans who are trying a little too hard to look innocent.

## Science With a Warm Snout

Canine DNA can be powerful because dogs share our homes, our cars, our routines, and occasionally our most suspicious errands. Yet its power comes with boundaries. A reliable interpretation depends on sound collection, careful laboratory work, and a willingness to consider transfer and coincidence along with guilt.

That is also what makes it such a fine ingredient in a modern whodunit. A single dog hair may not name the culprit, but it can lead a patient sleuth to the right porch, the right question, and perhaps one very revealing bark.

Florida Man Accused of Offering Cellmate $10K to Kill 11-Year-Old Boy and His Mother.

Key Takeaways.
Carlos Miranda-Berrios allegedly orchestrated an Osceola County murder-for-hire plot from jail, offering $5,000 to kill an 11-year-old boy and his mother.

Authorities uncovered the alleged scheme after the suspect dialed 911 to report someone punched him in the face over the rape accusations.

Facing potential life behind bars, the suspect already awaits a Dec. 14 trial on child pornography charges from a 2022 arrest.

OSCEOLA COUNTY, Fla.-An Osceola Countyinmate allegedly offered a cellmate $10,000 to abduct, sexually assault and kill an 11-year-old boy and his mother to prevent them from testifying against him in court next month.

Osceola County murder-for-hire plot
The Osceola County Sheriff’s Office alleges Carlos Miranda-Berrios tried to pay a cellmate to rape, shoot and burn the body of the 11-year-old child, then scatter the ashes in a lake. The boy had previously accused Miranda-Berrios of sexual battery.

According to an arrest warrant, Miranda-Berrios offered $5,000 for the boy's murder and another $5,000 if the child’s mother intervened and needed to be killed as well. Authorities only uncovered the alleged scheme because Miranda-Berrios called 911 himself to report that someone angry about the alleged rape had punched him in the face.

"Barrios had plans for the child to be abducted, subjected to heinous acts, and killed in a manner intended to cause extreme suffering," Osceola County Sheriff Chris Blackmon said. "Berrios continued attempting to facilitate the planned crimes while incarcerated.

2022 child pornography arrest
The backstory:
Authorities originally arrested Miranda-Berrios in 2022 on child pornography charges. That court case was delayed while he stayed at Advent Health to be restored to competency so his trial could proceed.

While out on bond, Miranda-Berrios was accused of sexual battery against the 11-year-old boy at the center of the alleged murder-for-hire plot. Kissimmee police say they discovered additional child pornography on his phone during that investigation, prompting a judge to revoke his bond.

text:
President Calvin Coolidge turned the White House into something of a personal zoo during the 1920s, filling it with dogs, cats, birds and more unusual animals that people sent as gifts.

In November 1926 a supporter from Mississippi shipped a live raccoon for them to eat at Thanksgiving, describing it as having a “toothsome flavor.” Coolidge, who had never tasted raccoon and showed no interest in trying it, decided to keep the animal instead.

The family named her Rebecca and gave her a collar engraved with the title “White House Raccoon.” She walked the grounds on a leash, laid in the president’s lap and joined First Lady Grace Coolidge at the Easter Egg Roll where children could pet her.

Grace later wrote that Rebecca was “a mischievous, inquisitive party” who enjoyed playing in the bathtub and that “it did not take us long to discover that she was no ordinary raccoon but an altogether amiable domesticated creature and an interesting pet.”
 
The couple also received larger animals such as a pair of lion cubs they named Tax Reduction and Budget Bureau along with a pygmy hippo, most of which were eventually sent to the National Zoo.

The pets offered a more personal side to the Coolidge years at a time when the president was known for saying little in public.

text:
In 1998, Netflix rented DVDs by mail, but they had a tiny problem: almost nobody owned a DVD player.

So they hid a coupon inside the box of nearly every DVD player sold in America.

Quick reminder for the younger ones, before streaming, Netflix was a website where you picked a movie and the DVD showed up in your mailbox in a red envelope.

So no DVD player = no customer.

And back then, a DVD player could cost up to $750, so most people were still happily renting VHS tapes at the store down the street.

So Marc Randolph and Reed Hastings went to the big electronics show in Las Vegas and pitched the companies making the players:
- Sony
- Toshiba
- Panasonic
- Philips

The deal was simple: put a Netflix coupon in the box, and every new DVD owner gets free rentals the day they unpack their player.

It took them over A YEAR to make it happen, and by 1999 Netflix was in the box of almost every major DVD player shipped in the US.

Think about the timing for a second 😅

You just spent a fortune on a shiny new machine, you get home, you have zero movies to put in it, and there's a coupon for free ones sitting right on top.

The craziest part is that in 2000, Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster basically laughed them out of the room.

Today Netflix has over 300 million subscribers, and Blockbuster has one store left in Oregon.

Yeaaap.

Netflix found people at the exact moment they needed what Netflix sold, and showed up right there.

In sales, timing beats almost everything else.

text:
A Stranger Paid Me $400 at 2 A.M. to Break Into a House. When the Door Opened, She Asked Me Who the Woman in the Photographs Was.

She was wearing a nightgown under a man's winter coat, and she paid me in crumpled twenties. When the door swung open, she lifted a framed photograph off the hallway table and studied it like a stranger's.

"Who is she?" she asked.

It was her.

I'm Tess Marlow, forty-four, a locksmith in Pittsburgh. Nineteen years of lockouts, bad divorces, and landlords who change the locks on Friday nights.

I check ID every time. That night I didn't, and I still don't know if I'd do it differently.

The call came through the shop line at 1:50. A thin, polite voice said, "I'm locked out. I have the money. I'm very sorry."

I found her on a front step in Dormont, in January, barefoot inside a pair of men's galoshes. She held a brass key that didn't fit anything.

"This is my house," she said. "I know where the stairs creak. I know the kitchen smells like cinnamon. I just can't find my name."

She handed me an index card from her coat pocket. It was written in careful block capitals.

*LOCKED OUT? CALL TESS MARLOW. PAY HER. SHE WILL NOT ASK QUESTIONS.*

I turned the card over. My shop number, in her handwriting, and my name spelled right.

I had never met her in my life. Or so I thought.

The front door had a brand-new deadbolt, the sticker still on the brass. Somebody had changed it within the last week.

I walked around the side of the house with my flashlight. At the back door I stopped.

A black keypad lock, mounted at hip height. I knew it before I touched it, by the slightly crooked screw in the lower left corner I'd never bothered to fix.

Two years earlier a woman had called my shop in the middle of the afternoon. She'd been calm, almost brisk. She wanted a keypad on her back door. "My son worries," she'd said. "I'd like one door that is mine."

I'd installed it in forty minutes. She paid cash and offered me lemon cake. She said, "If I ever call you at night, you won't need to ask me anything, will you?"

I'd laughed. I thought she was eccentric. I said, "Ma'am, I never do."

Now she stood behind me in the snow, in her galoshes, watching me.

"Do you know the code?" I asked.

"No." Her voice shook. "I don't know anything."

"Try."

She stepped forward, lifted her bare, trembling right hand, and pressed four buttons without looking. 1, 9, 6, 4. The lock chirped, and the door clicked open.

She stared at her own finger. "How did I do that?"

"Your hands remember," I said. "Sometimes they know things you don't."

Inside, the house was warm and smelled of cinnamon. Every door had a note taped to it, in the same square handwriting.

KITCHEN. You live here. Your name is Eleanor Finch. Eat something.

BATHROOM. Light switch on the left.

FRONT DOOR. Daniel changed the locks. Don't be frightened. Call Tess.

She followed me down the hall as though she were the guest. At the table, she lifted a frame and said, "That's a nice-looking woman. She has my mother's chin."

"That's you, Eleanor."

"Is it?" She set it down gently. "I looked younger."

I made tea. I found a loaf of lemon cake wrapped in foil, labeled in the same hand, EAT THIS WHEN YOU ARE CONFUSED. She ate two slices, and she stopped shaking.

At 3:12 the front door crashed open. A tall man in a parka and untied boots stood in the hallway, breathing hard.

"Mom!"

She looked up, polite, puzzled. "Hello. Are you the electrician?"

His face crumpled. He crossed the room in three strides and dropped to his knees beside her chair.

"It's Daniel, Mom. It's your son."

"Of course it is," she said kindly, patting his head. She did not know him.

text:
Here are the official MISSION Act eligibility rules for VA Community Care (Veterans Community Care Program). A Veteran needs to meet at least one of the six criteria below, plus the basic requirements. 
Basic Requirements
•  Enrolled in (or eligible for) VA health care, and
•  Approval from the VA health care team before receiving care from a community provider (except certain urgent or emergency care).
The Six Eligibility Criteria
Meeting any one of these is enough:
1.  Service not available VA does not offer the needed service at any VA health facility.
2.  No full-service VA facility in the state/territory Applies to Veterans living in Alaska, Hawaii, New Hampshire, Guam, American Samoa, Northern Mariana Islands, or U.S. Virgin Islands.
3.  Grandfathered under the old Veterans Choice 40-mile rule Narrow provision mainly for those who qualified under the 40-mile distance rule as of June 6, 2018, and live in Alaska, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming (or certain other qualifying locations).
4.  VA cannot meet designated access standards
•  Primary care, mental health, or non-institutional extended care: Average drive time over 30 minutes or wait time over 20 days.
•  Specialty care (physical therapy is generally treated as specialty): Average drive time over 60 minutes or wait time over 28 days. Drive times are calculated by VA from the Veteran’s listed residence to a VA facility that can provide the specific service, using GIS software. Missing either the drive-time or wait-time standard is sufficient.
5.  Best medical interest The Veteran and the referring VA clinician jointly agree that community care is in the Veteran’s best medical interest for improved clinical outcomes. Factors include distance, nature and frequency of care, appointment timeliness, continuity of care, quality, and unusual/excessive travel burden (including medical conditions that affect travel or need for an attendant). As of May 2025, no second VA doctor review is required.

text:
Here are the official MISSION Act eligibility rules for VA Community Care (Veterans Community Care Program). A Veteran needs to meet at least one of the six criteria below, plus the basic requirements. 
Basic Requirements
•  Enrolled in (or eligible for) VA health care, and
•  Approval from the VA health care team before receiving care from a community provider (except certain urgent or emergency care).
The Six Eligibility Criteria
Meeting any one of these is enough:
1.  Service not available VA does not offer the needed service at any VA health facility.
2.  No full-service VA facility in the state/territory Applies to Veterans living in Alaska, Hawaii, New Hampshire, Guam, American Samoa, Northern Mariana Islands, or U.S. Virgin Islands.
3.  Grandfathered under the old Veterans Choice 40-mile rule Narrow provision mainly for those who qualified under the 40-mile distance rule as of June 6, 2018, and live in Alaska, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming (or certain other qualifying locations).
4.  VA cannot meet designated access standards
•  Primary care, mental health, or non-institutional extended care: Average drive time over 30 minutes or wait time over 20 days.
•  Specialty care (physical therapy is generally treated as specialty): Average drive time over 60 minutes or wait time over 28 days. Drive times are calculated by VA from the Veteran’s listed residence to a VA facility that can provide the specific service, using GIS software. Missing either the drive-time or wait-time standard is sufficient.
5.  Best medical interest The Veteran and the referring VA clinician jointly agree that community care is in the Veteran’s best medical interest for improved clinical outcomes. Factors include distance, nature and frequency of care, appointment timeliness, continuity of care, quality, and unusual/excessive travel burden (including medical conditions that affect travel or need for an attendant). As of May 2025, no second VA doctor review is required.
