text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

text:
🗣 The Irish News view:

A survey of young people about their attitudes to the Irish language offers a refreshing antidote to the toxicity at Stormont around cultural issues.

The headline finding is that more than a quarter of post-primary pupils from a Protestant background said they would like to learn Irish.

But only 8%, and just 11% of those of no or other religions, actually have cúpla focal.

Just over half of Catholic pupils in the Young Persons’ Behaviour and Attitudes Survey, published by the Department for Communities, said they could understand, speak, read or write Irish to some level.

The figures will not come as a surprise to anyone involved in the promotion or teaching of Irish, which has enjoyed an explosion of interest in recent years, including in areas not traditionally associated with the native tongue.

The most prominent of these has been east Belfast, where Irish language project Turas has confirmed that many of its learners are Protestants.

They are attracted for a range of reasons, but among them is a growing realisation that this beautiful language is as much a part of their cultural heritage as it is for Catholics.

Irish has deep roots within the Protestant and Presbyterian traditions, which played an important role in its preservation during the 18th and 19th centuries, and it still surrounds us in place names and the words and idioms we use in daily speech.

It is therefore all the more dispiriting that Irish has repeatedly been dragged into the ‘culture wars’ that have so soured relations at Stormont.

The latest example was a petition of concern tabled by the DUP to block a bill on Irish-medium education, which Gavin Robinson explicitly linked to his party’s efforts to punish Sinn Féin over Drumcree.

Irish language signage is also a regular source of contention, while the petty withdrawal of a relatively small sum for Gaeltacht bursaries was among the reasons cited for the collapse of the Assembly in 2017.

The reality, away from tribal exchanges in assembly and council chambers, is there is a growing interest in identity and history and people on the ground are far ahead of their politicians.

Fascinatingly, the survey found that while 26% of Protestant pupils expressed an interest in Irish, a quarter of Catholic pupils said they would like to learn Ulster-Scots.

The results make a strong case for expanding the availability of classes in schools and communities so that everyone has an opportunity to explore the richness and diversity of our shared cultural heritage.

The lesson from young people is clear: language can and should be a bridge between communities, not another weapon in old political battles.

text:
✝️ SAINT OF THE DAY

St. Elizabeth of Hungary: Love Made Visible

Honoring the saints who show us the way.

📅 November 17 | St. Elizabeth of Hungary

Hungarian Princess | Served in present-day Germany
A loaf of bread, offered with kindness, can mean more than a meal. It can tell someone: You matter. Your suffering has been noticed.

Today’s image captures the spirit of St. Elizabeth of Hungary, whose love for Christ became visible through her care for people in need.

Born in 1207, Elizabeth was the daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary. Sent to Thuringia as a child, she later married Ludwig IV, its ruler. Together, they had three children.

Elizabeth used her resources to provide food, clothing, and relief for the poor. She visited people in their homes and personally attended to their needs. Her husband supported her generosity.

Then, in 1227, Ludwig died while traveling to join a crusade. Elizabeth was widowed at about twenty, with three children. She subsequently lost the security of her home at Wartburg and endured a period of serious hardship. Her life held both profound love and painful loss. Pope Benedict XVI(https://t.co/vLcvX4Wk8J)

After receiving a financial settlement, Elizabeth used her resources to establish a hospital at Marburg. Inspired by the Franciscan way of life, she embraced simplicity and devoted herself to serving the sick and those pushed to society’s margins. She died in 1231, aged just twenty-four. Irish Franciscans[Irish Franciscans](https://t.co/NI0dicbGU8), Vatican News(https://t.co/9cycIWEVwI)

The Scripture featured in today’s image expresses the invitation her life places before us:

“Children, let us love not in word or speech but in deed and truth.”
— 1 John 3:18(https://t.co/R1wLQhu45z)

Elizabeth’s story invites us to consider what love looks like in practice.

It may look like bringing groceries to a struggling family, accompanying someone to an appointment, listening to a grieving friend, or giving an exhausted caregiver a little time to rest.

Sometimes, we are carrying burdens of our own. We may feel tired, anxious, or unsure whether we have enough to offer. We can ask the Holy Spirit for wisdom, strength, and a compassionate heart. God can work through the care we offer while also helping us receive the support we need.

Within our families, children learn generosity when they see us notice another person’s needs and respond respectfully. Sharing a meal or helping a neighbor together can become a lesson in faith they remember.

🌿 Today, let us make love visible:
• Offer practical help to someone facing hardship.
• Visit or contact someone who is sick, grieving, or lonely.
• Share useful food, clothing, or resources through a trusted ministry.
• Choose one act of service to carry out as a family.

🕊️ Whose burden could I help lighten today?

🙏 Lord Jesus, give us hearts that recognize Your presence in those who suffer. Through Your Holy Spirit, strengthen us in our own trials and guide us toward generous, practical care. Bless struggling families, comfort those who grieve, and help us make Your love visible through our daily actions. Amen.

St. Elizabeth of Hungary, pray for us.

— A Striving Pilgrim
One faithful step at a time.

#SaintElizabethOfHungary #SaintOfTheDay #CatholicX #AStrivingPilgrim

text:
MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system | Massachusetts Institute of Technology, ScienceDaily

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?"

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

"Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

text:
New study finds children and teens reason differently about participation trophies | Eric W Dolan, PsyPost

Children as young as 7 and teenagers largely agree that reserving trophies for top finishers motivates athletes to try harder and feel prouder than handing out participation awards to everyone, according to a new study published in Developmental Science. Yet only adolescents consistently predicted negative side effects from winner-only awards, expecting them to encourage cheating and physical risk-taking. Teenagers’ personal preferences for competitive versus inclusive trophy systems also aligned with how fast they believed they could run, suggesting that self-interest begins shaping views on fairness by adolescence.

At the end of many youth sports seasons, leagues choose between two competing rules for handing out awards. Inclusive, or egalitarian, reward systems give every participant the same recognition simply for showing up and taking part, whereas selective, or merit-based, systems reserve prizes for top performers based on measurable results.

Supporters of participation trophies argue that inclusive recognition fosters belonging and acknowledges effort, while critics contend that giving everyone the same prize dilutes achievement and dulls motivation. Selective trophies spark parallel disagreements between advocates who see them as fair recognition for excellence and critics who worry they create pressure to take unethical shortcuts or risk injury.

“Although these debates largely take place among adults, children are the ones who experience these reward systems,” study lead author Shuai Shao, who conducted the research at the University of California, San Diego, and is now at Boston College, told PsyPost. “We wanted to understand how children and adolescents themselves think about the implications of these reward systems and how their reasoning changes across development.”

Developmental psychology research indicates that children begin weighing individual performance alongside strict equality during elementary school. While preschoolers often default to splitting items evenly, a 2016 experiment with 3- to 8-year-olds found that by age 8, children reliably accepted harder work as a fair reason to give one person a larger share while rejecting purely selfish requests. By adulthood, people’s views on fairness also tend to reflect their own personal standing, as a 2014 study of adults showed that individuals tend to favor equal or performance-based reward rules depending on whichever arrangement benefits them personally.

Most childhood studies, however, have examined one-time decisions about how to divide toys or snacks rather than how broader institutional rules influence emotions and behavior. In a 2025 study of workplace pay systems by the same researchers, children as young as 7, adolescents, and adults expected employees to work harder when pay depended on output rather than being divided equally, a finding the new study set out to replicate in a new setting.

That left an open question: would young people anticipate a wider range of trade-offs when the prize was a trophy rather than money? The researchers tested whether children and teenagers expect winner-only trophies not only to increase effort and pride, but also to encourage cheating and physical risk-taking, and explored whether young people’s confidence in their own athletic ability relates to which trophy system they prefer.

The researchers recruited 87 young people from the southwestern United States during 2024 and 2025, divided into two age brackets. The sample included 43 children aged 7 to 9 (with an average age of about 8.4) and 44 adolescents aged 15 to 18 (with an average age of about 16.9).

Those group sizes exceeded the 32 participants per age bracket needed to reliably detect medium-sized departures from an even 50-50 split. Five additional participants who missed at least one comprehension question were excluded in accordance with the study’s preregistration, a public research plan filed in advance and posted online alongside the data and analysis code.

Trained experimenters interviewed the 7- to 9-year-olds in person at local parks, while the teenagers completed an online survey featuring the exact same scenarios and wording. Every participant learned about a school holding two separate running events, each with 10 runners completing a single lap around a soccer field. In the “Trophies for All” event, everyone received a trophy just for showing up, whereas in the “Trophies for Winners” event, only the top three finishers received a trophy.

After the two events were introduced in randomized order, participants answered eight two-option questions presented in a fixed sequence across four areas: personal effort, pride, morality, and physical risk-taking. Each area included one positively framed question and one negatively framed question so that results would not depend on question wording alone.

Participants chose which event would make runners run faster or not try very hard, and which would make them feel more special or feel less proud after getting a trophy. They also predicted in which race runners would cheat to win or follow the rules, and in which they would risk getting hurt to win or focus on staying upright to avoid falling down.

While the main statistical tests comparing choices against random guessing were preregistered, the researchers noted that their specific expectations about age differences were not formally laid out in advance. The younger age group was included partly to explore when teenage-like reasoning begins to appear. Participants also completed an exploratory, non-preregistered section in which they chose which of the two races they would personally like to join and rated how fast they ran compared with peers their age on a five-point scale from “much slower” to “much faster.”

Because every core question offered a choice between the two events, random guessing would yield a 50% split. Compared against that 50% baseline, both age groups strongly linked selective trophies to greater effort: 72.1% of children and 100% of adolescents predicted that runners would run faster in the “Trophies for Winners” race, and large majorities in both groups likewise expected runners in the “Trophies for All” race to put in less effort.

Both groups also viewed selective awards as more emotionally meaningful than participation awards. Specifically, 81.4% of children and 95.5% of adolescents predicted that runners would feel more special after receiving a trophy in the winners-only event, and the exact same percentages expected recipients in the all-trophies event to feel less proud. Teenagers were more uniform in their answers than children on three of those four questions, though both age groups stood well above chance.

When the questions turned to rule-breaking, however, the two age groups diverged. Nearly all adolescents (95.5%) predicted that runners would be more likely to cheat in the “Trophies for Winners” event, and 68.2% expected runners in the “Trophies for All” event to be more likely to follow the rules. Among 7- to 9-year-olds, 65.1% chose the winners-only race for cheating and 62.8% chose the participation race for rule-following, neither of which was statistically significant compared with a 50-50 split. When the two age groups were compared directly, the smaller gap on rule-following was not statistically significant, unlike the much wider age gap on cheating.

Predictions about physical safety showed a similar age split. Every adolescent (100%) expected runners in the winners-only race to risk getting hurt in order to win, and 68.2% expected runners in the participation race to prioritize avoiding falls. Children’s answers hovered near an even split on both items (58.1% and 51.2%) and were not statistically significant; between age groups, the gap on avoiding falls was also not statistically significant, unlike the wide gap on risking injury.

Follow-up Bayesian analyses pointed the same way. That statistical check weighs how strongly data favor random guessing versus a real effect. For children’s risk-taking answers, the results leaned toward genuine chance responding rather than an undetected effect.

Shao emphasized how early this reasoning appears. “Even young children recognize that different reward systems can have different consequences,” he said.

In the exploratory questions about personal preferences, 62.8% of children and 63.6% of adolescents picked the “Trophies for Winners” race. Neither split was statistically significant, though both leaned toward the competitive race. Both groups rated their own running speed slightly above average on the five-point scale, and the difference between children’s average score (3.63) and adolescents’ average score (3.30) was not statistically significant.

Even so, perceived running ability related to event choices very differently depending on age. Among adolescents, higher self-rated running speed was associated with a greater likelihood of preferring the competitive “Trophies for Winners” event over “Trophies for All.” Among 7- to 9-year-olds, self-rated running speed showed virtually no connection to which race they wanted to join.

According to the authors, the core results indicate that an intuitive expectation linking merit-based rewards to harder work and stronger pride is already established by age 7, extending beyond money to symbolic awards like sports trophies.

To explain why only adolescents consistently anticipated cheating and physical risk-taking, the researchers suggest that teenagers draw on broader personal experience with competitive pressure and peer norms. Because young children are routinely taught by adults to follow rules and avoid danger, the authors also propose that predicting how a prize could motivate cheating or recklessness may require mentally setting aside everyday rules to imagine alternative scenarios, a skill known as counterfactual thinking that develops gradually across childhood.

The preference pattern also surprised the team. “We were surprised to find that adolescents who saw themselves as fast runners were more likely to prefer the event where only winners received trophies,” Shao noted. “This suggests that by adolescence, individuals may begin to prefer the reward system that best aligns with their self-interest.”

Because the study did not directly measure why participants favored one race over the other, the authors note that the exact reasons behind the teenage shift toward self-interest remain open to interpretation. They point to two possibilities: adolescents may grow more attentive to how reward rules align with their own chances of winning, or they may become more sensitive to social comparison and competitive standing among peers. Younger children, the researchers suggest, may instead approach the choice more aspirationally, picking whichever setup sounds appealing in the moment rather than weighing their actual odds of finishing in the top three.

As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Participants predicted how fictional runners would feel and behave in a brief story rather than competing for trophies themselves, so the findings capture young people’s beliefs about reward systems rather than how trophies affect real-world behavior on the field.

“For example, children might expect performance-based trophies to encourage greater effort, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they would work harder themselves under such a system,” Shao explained. “Nevertheless, understanding how children reason about different reward systems is important because these beliefs are likely to shape their preferences and how they approach situations involving rewards and competition.”

Comparing two separate age groups at one point in time also cannot directly track how individual children’s reasoning changes as they grow up, and the younger participants were interviewed in person at parks whereas the teenagers completed the survey online.

The wording of two questions may have nudged participants’ answers as well, since asking where runners would cheat or risk getting hurt “to win” echoed the framing of the “Trophies for Winners” event. Future studies using more neutral phrasing, such as asking what runners might do “to get a trophy,” could help rule out that possibility. Researchers could also examine whether young people reason the same way in settings where merit is more subjective than a footrace, such as school classrooms, or in hybrid sports leagues that give participation medals to everyone alongside larger trophies for top finishers.

Beyond refining survey scenarios, the team hopes to test how real-world prizes influence young people’s emotions and actions. “A key next step is to understand how participation-based versus performance-based reward systems affect children’s actual behavior, and whether those effects match expectations,” Shao said. “More broadly, we are interested in how the incentives children encounter shape their affect, behavior, cognition, and development.”

For parents, coaches, and educators deciding how to recognize young participants, the study points to the unspoken signals built into everyday awards. “One thing we hope this study highlights is that the way adults design reward systems can communicate meaningful messages to children about what is valued,” Shao added. “Whether a trophy goes to everyone or only to the top performers, children notice the difference, and their interpretations and beliefs may shape how they approach rewarded activities.”

text:
Her family has been Mormon since Brigham Young. At 8 her parents made her get baptized so they wouldn’t be shamed, and at 16 she had to move out over boys. Now she’s in the top 0.01% on OnlyFans, does whatever you can imagine and makes about $10K a day. Her parents have no idea:

Nobody has recognized her yet.

Her name is Kit, she’s 28 and grew up in Ventura County, California. Both of her parents were born Mormon. She says she felt cut off from the church since she was tiny, and it put her at war with her family.

At 7 she told her grandma she wouldn’t be getting baptized. Grandma wrote in the family journal that Kit was just being humble. Her dad was furious, because a kid who skips baptism shames the whole family at church. Her mom told her she couldn’t do this to her dad.

“So I didn’t really have a choice.”

As a teen she started exploring boys and her own body. Her dad was worried sick about her eternal soul. At 16 she moved in with her grandma in Idaho.

Her parents offered to pay for college if she gave two years to a Mormon mission, with someone watching her every move. She said no, rented a little room from an elderly couple and worked as a personal trainer, barely scraping by.

In the video below she explains how one TikTok live changed everything, and why her family still has no clue.

Viewers on her fitness live told her to start an OnlyFans. She was planning a PhD and was scared it would wreck her career in academia. She did it anyway.

“I made over $10,000 my first month. Changed my life.”

She pulled her grad school application and went back for a math degree. Now she’s in the top 0.01% of creators on the site, with no agent.

“A lot more than 10,000 a month.”

Asked if it’s closer to 10,000 a day, she laughed and said it depends on the day. Her content has no limits, and she shoots with partners.

“If I’m going to make porn, I’m going to make porn.”

Her parents moved out of state. She says the photos of her around their house are so weird that nobody ever connects them to her.

Some say a church that forces 8-year-olds into baptism and only pays for college in exchange for a mission built her this exit. Others say the day somebody shows her dad a link, no math degree is going to matter.

Did the church push Kit into this, or was she always going to end up here?

DoorDash agreed to pay Instacart $1.25 billion if antitrust review sinks their deal, and now it knows who's doing the reviewing.

The Justice Department will look at the roughly $17 billion purchase, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Regulators clear the vast majority of deals without changes.

Instacart's own exit fee is $650 million, owed if it walks away for a better offer, per the merger filing with the SEC.

The filing gives the deal 12 months to close, with up to four automatic three-month extensions if antitrust approval is the only thing left. States like New York and California can bring their own challenges.

He was sure his wife was sleeping with a coworker. Her family says he showed them a gun and offered cash for a hitman to kill the guy. Then she vanished and her body was never found. A jury convicted him of murder and he got 25 to life. He swears he didn’t do it and she ran away:

He says he’s waiting for her to show up so they let him out.

His name is Larry Millete. His wife Maya was a mom of three from Chula Vista, California. In 2020 he got it in his head that she was having an affair with a guy from work.

Larry went to online spellcasters, people who sell magic spells. He paid for love spells to keep her, curses on the coworker, and then spells to hurt Maya so badly she’d have to depend on him.

By December she’d decided to divorce him. On January 7, 2021, hours before she was last seen, he texted his boss that he was shaking inside, ready to snap and about to lose it. Then Maya was gone. No phone, no money moving, no body.

Prosecutors say he killed her and buried her in the desert. In July a jury took about six hours to convict him of first-degree murder. On November 2 the judge gave him the max, 25 to life.

His own daughter read a statement in court.

“As a human being, unforgivable. As his daughter, I cannot stop loving him.”

The day after his sentencing Larry gave his first TV interview, from inside the jail. In the video below he goes through the case line by line and has an answer for everything.

The gun and the hitman? He calls it a lie.

“That’s just fabricated. They would say anything to try to get me in here.”

Asked what shocked him most at trial, he didn’t talk about his missing wife. He talked about the affair, and kept saying he was embarrassed.

He still thinks Maya just took off and is hiding somewhere.

“It’s not that difficult to stay hidden, even here in the United States.”

He says he’s doing all this for his three kids. The judge put a 10-year protective order between him and them.

Some say there’s no body, no weapon and no confession, and a man got 25 to life over spells and text messages. Others say a husband who paid for curses on his wife, then lost her without a trace, doesn’t get the benefit of the doubt.

Is Larry Millete a killer taking Maya’s grave to prison, or a man convicted without a body?

text:
Supreme Court Punts on DEI Grants, Forces Taxpayers to Keep Funding California Ideology

The Supreme Court declined Monday to hear the Trump administration's appeal in Trump v. Thakur, leaving intact a Ninth Circuit ruling that blocks the termination of roughly $59 million in University of California research grants tied to diversity, equity and inclusion, gender ideology, and environmental justice themes.

After President Trump issued executive orders shifting federal priorities away from these initiatives, agencies including the National Science Foundation and National Endowment for the Humanities used keyword searches to identify and end projects promoting the disfavored viewpoints. District Judge Rita Lin and the Ninth Circuit called this likely unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment. The justices offered no explanation and no noted dissents. The case returns to the lower court with the funding still flowing.

This is not a victory for free speech. It is a victory for the idea that researchers have a constitutional right to keep collecting taxpayer checks for political projects the elected administration no longer wants to subsidize. Competitive federal grants are limited public funds, not entitlements. Presidents and agencies routinely set priorities; that is the point of executive authority over spending. Treating a decision to stop paying for DEI studies as censorship turns the First Amendment on its head and hands activist courts veto power over policy.

The Ninth Circuit has long been the most reliably left-leaning circuit in the country. By refusing to intervene, the Supreme Court lets that circuit shield ideological research at a massive public university system while the rest of the country is told to move on from race preferences and gender ideology. Taxpayers remain on the hook for projects selected in part because they advanced the very concepts the administration campaigned against and ordered ended. The broader fight over federal research funding will continue, but Monday's inaction is a clear win for the status quo the Trump team tried to change.

text:
THE US$60.68 MILLION PRESIDENTIAL JET: WHERE IS THE PRINCIPLE?

Yesterday, 16th November 2026, the Minister for Government Communications, Hon. Felix Kwakye Ofosu, announced that the Ghana Air Force has taken delivery of a brand-new Falcon 6X presidential jet, acquired under a contract worth a staggering US$60.68 million.

This development raises serious questions about the consistency, credibility and principles of the government.

During the debate on the 2026 Budget, the Minority raised concerns about the government’s plans to acquire presidential aircraft. The Majority disputed our characterisation of the proposed expenditure and sought to justify the acquisition.

Indeed, it was suggested at the time that the procurement and delivery process would take several years, giving the strong indication that the aircraft would not be delivered during President Mahama’s tenure.

Yet, yesterday, barely a year later, the aircraft has been delivered. How does the government explain this remarkable turn of events?

Let us not forget that, when the NDC was in opposition, leading members of the party opposed proposals to acquire a new presidential jet, claiming that the
economic circumstances confronting the country does not justify such expenditure and that there is the need to prioritise the welfare of ordinary Ghanaians.

What has changed?

At a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living, youth unemployment remains alarmingly high, and the government’s much-touted 24-hour economy has yet to deliver its promised transformation, the administration has found the resources to acquire a luxurious presidential aircraft.

The question is not simply whether Ghana requires a safe and reliable presidential aircraft. It is whether those who condemned such expenditure when they were in opposition can now defend it without adequately explaining what has changed.

What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed.

The apparent double standards and political inconsistency are difficult to ignore.

Ghanaians deserve a full explanation of the cost, financing arrangements, procurement process and justification for prioritising this expenditure at this time.

Accordingly, the Minority Caucus on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration Committee will demand full disclosure and accountability from the government on this acquisition. We shall pursue the matter in Parliament and insist on answers regarding the total cost to the taxpayer, the financing arrangements, the procurement and approval processes, and the justification for the acquisition. We shall also demand the full documentation relating to the transaction.

The government must be prepared to account to the representatives of the people for every dollar committed to this purchase. Public expenditure of this magnitude demands transparency, accountability and rigorous parliamentary scrutiny.

Politics and public life must be anchored in at least a modicum of principle!

text:
Inbound leads who ask for sales often wait hours for a human. By then the buyer has moved on.

Alex Lindahl's GTM Engineering Newsletter wrote up how Oran Akron, VP of AI GTM at https://t.co/6TA747Kapt, rebuilt inbound so an AI voice agent calls the lead within minutes and books the meeting while they're still on the phone:

1. Pre-qualify each form fill as sales or support.
2. Research the sales lead and load that context into the voice agent before it dials.
3. Split the call across small agents: intent, qualification, commercial questions, scheduling. One agent with too many instructions hallucinated more.
4. Put a thin layer between the voice model and the calendars so it maps region and segment to the right rep and offers a few real times, not every open slot.
5. Give the agent a slice of leads first and widen it only when it matches the human team on that slice.
6. Review KPIs and automated call and email evals every morning.

Where it breaks: passing details between agents mid-call is the hard part, calling at volume gets numbers flagged as spam, and automated calls have consent rules that vary by country and state. Check those before dialing.

text:
Interesting, but more to the point, many people are going to wonder what is gootloader, and how is its infection and action prevented. 
I asked Grok, and here is what it said in that regard:
Gootloader is a JavaScript-based malware loader and initial-access framework (linked to the older GootKit family). It has been active since around 2018–2020 and is used primarily as a ransomware precursor: it gets a foothold on a machine, then operators sell access or deploy follow-on tools (Cobalt Strike, ransomware, etc.).
How it works
It spreads mainly through SEO poisoning of compromised WordPress sites rather than classic phishing emails:
1Attackers compromise legitimate WordPress sites (often via stolen credentials, vulnerable plugins/themes, or XML-RPC) and inject content optimized for specific searches.
2They target low-competition, business/legal queries such as contract clauses, NDA templates, lease agreements, or jurisdiction-specific legal forms.
3Poisoned pages rank high in Google/Bing results and appear as legitimate forum posts or document repositories that match the search.
4The page offers a ZIP archive (sometimes with anti-analysis tricks like hundreds of concatenated ZIPs). Inside is a malicious .js (JScript) file.
5When the user extracts and double-clicks the .js file, Windows Script Host (wscript.exe/cscript.exe) runs it. This downloads more payloads, establishes persistence (registry, scheduled tasks, Startup folder, etc.), and often hands off to ransomware operators.
As of October 2026, the FBI identified over 1,000 infected WordPress sites and 216 domains controlled by the Gootloader administrator, linked to over $28 million in ransomware payments (at least 44 U.S. victims and ~$28.8 million in losses; roughly 25,000 systems infected worldwide overall). It has targeted legal professionals, businesses, and even defense-related entities.
A major international disruption (Operation Endgame) in mid-November 2026 seized servers/domains and cleaned many compromised WordPress sites, but the technique can be rebuilt.
How to prevent it
Highest-impact technical control (breaks the chain for most users):
•Change the default association so .js files open in Notepad (or another editor) instead of executing via wscript.exe. Or disable Windows Script Host for standard users. This can be done via Group Policy (GPO). Red Canary and others have long recommended this against Gootloader and similar JS loaders.
Other effective steps (from FBI FLASH and industry sources):
•Windows/endpoint: Use standard (non-admin) user accounts. Restrict or block unapproved scripts/executables from user-writable locations (Downloads, Temp, AppData). Keep Defender/SmartScreen, AMSI, and tamper protection enabled. Use application control (WDAC/AppLocker) where possible. Monitor for wscript.exe/cscript.exe running .js from a ZIP/Downloads folder, especially followed by PowerShell.
•User awareness: Treat ZIP “documents” or legal/business templates from search results with extreme caution. Prefer official sources. Show file extensions in Windows so you can see it’s a .js file. Don’t open unexpected archives.
•WordPress site owners (to avoid becoming a lure or being compromised):
◦Keep WordPress core, themes, and plugins updated; remove unused ones.
◦Strong unique passwords + MFA for all admin/hosting accounts.
◦Disable or tightly restrict xmlrpc.php if unused.
◦Block PHP execution in wp-content/uploads.
◦Monitor for unexpected file/JS changes, new admin accounts, or unusual Search Console queries/indexed pages.
◦Use a WAF and integrity monitoring.
•Broader: Web/proxy filtering, DNS filtering, patching, least-privilege access, and good EDR logging help. If you suspect infection, isolate the machine, preserve evidence, and report to your local FBI field office or IC3 (https://t.co/UeeZb9Yzlq).

$GFF Q4 2026 earnings: Griffon cuts debt and boosts buybacks, but door volumes fall

Griffon, the maker of Clopay garage doors and Hunter ceiling fans, finished its shift into a building-products business with higher prices masking lower shipment volumes. Fourth-quarter revenue rose 3% to $491 million, above what the company's own unrevised annual plan pointed to, because 6% higher prices and product mix offset a 3% drop in unit volume. Chief executive Ronald J. Kramer set a fiscal 2027 plan that keeps both revenue and operating cash profit flat at $1.85 billion and $460 million.

• Q4 Continuing revenue: $𝟒𝟗𝟎.𝟗𝐌 (+3.2% from a year ago (+6% price/mix, -3% volume))
• Q4 Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟏.𝟔𝟏 (+13.4% from a year ago)
• Net debt to operating cash profit: 𝟐.𝟎𝐱 (down from 2.4x a year ago)
• FY27 Revenue and cash profit outlook: 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 ($1.85B sales and $460M adjusted EBITDA)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because a cleaner balance sheet offsets a weaker demand outlook. Extending bond maturities to 2034 and cutting debt by $364 million removed the 2028 refinancing risk, cut planned net interest to $50 million, and backed a $400 million buyback increase. The bad news: shipment volumes fell back into contraction across both residential and commercial customers, and more than $21 million of next year's interest savings comes from non-cash interest accruing on loans to the divested tool ventures by our math.

The question now is whether per-share profit growth from lower interest and share buybacks can carry the business until construction volumes recover, or if fading price gains expose shrinking unit demand in 2027. If door and fan volumes stabilize, the 26% operating cash profit margin holds and cash flows straight into buybacks; if volumes keep dropping at 3%, factory overhead will squeeze margins. Next quarter's volume and price split will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 concern eased — 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟒 𝐄𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐖𝐚𝐥𝐥
Griffon, the maker of Clopay garage doors and Hunter ceiling fans, removed its largest balance-sheet risk this quarter. Investors had worried about nearly $1 billion of senior notes due in 2028 and a credit line that would expire in December 2027 if those bonds remained unpaid.

Chief executive Ronald J. Kramer said the company "repositioned Griffon into a pure play building products company, and significantly strengthened our balance sheet by extending our bond maturities to 2034 and reducing our debt by $364 million." The cash flow statement shows $1.11 billion of new long-term debt and $1.47 billion of debt repayments during the year, which cut net debt to 2.0 times operating cash profit from 2.4 times a year ago.

That debt reduction lowers interest costs for the coming year. Management plans for $50 million of net interest expense in fiscal 2027, down $29 million from fiscal 2026, which lifts profit per share by our math even without sales growth.

What to watch: the coupon rate on the new 2034 bonds in the annual report debt footnote. A rate near the old 5.75% notes would confirm that cash interest savings match the headline drop.

🟢 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰 𝐁𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐰 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞
With the AMES tool divestitures complete and debt down to 2.0 times operating cash profit, Griffon is returning more cash to shareholders. The board added $400 million to the share buyback plan, bringing the remaining allowance to $544.8 million, and raised the quarterly dividend by 14% to $0.25 per share.

The building products maker bought back 1.6 million shares for $136.3 million in fiscal 2026 and spent another $16.9 million in the first six weeks of fiscal 2027. Since April 2023, buybacks have retired 22.1% of the share count, which helped fourth-quarter profit per share excluding one-offs rise 13.4% to $1.61 on 3.2% sales growth.

What to watch: quarterly buyback spending in the first quarter. Spending near $35 million would keep shrinking the share count by more than 2% a year while keeping debt steady.

🟢 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟔% 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Raw material costs take four to five months to reach Griffon's income statement, which squeezed full-year gross margin down by 0.9 percentage points to 46.4%. In the fourth quarter, spring price increases on garage doors caught up with those costs: cost of goods sold fell 0.7 percentage points to 53.1% of revenue, lifting quarterly gross margin to 46.9%.

Selling, general and administrative expenses (overhead and sales costs) rose 0.5 percentage points excluding one-offs to 22.9% of sales. Even so, fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA — operating cash profit before interest, taxes and depreciation — reached 26.0% of revenue, up 0.2 percentage points from a year ago despite "the unfavorable impact of decreased volume on overhead absorption, and increased material, labor and distribution costs".

What to watch: first-quarter gross margin. Holding near 46.5% would show that current door prices cover steel and labor costs without needing another round of price hikes.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐬 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭
"Griffon is well-positioned for the future, and we expect our growth to accelerate as building activity improves," Kramer said. Now that the AMES garden tool units are gone, the remaining business relies almost entirely on North American residential and commercial construction, which offers both higher margins and direct exposure to housing cycles.

This quarter's numbers show that customer demand weakened instead of improving. Fourth-quarter revenue rose 3.2% to $490.9 million "primarily due to favorable residential and commercial price and mix of 6%, partially offset by decreased volume of 3% driven by both residential and commercial".

• Fourth-quarter unit volume: down 3%, reversing the 1% volume gain in the third quarter
• Commercial volume: turned negative alongside residential doors after holding up earlier in the year
• Fiscal 2027 revenue outlook: $1.85 billion, up 0.1% from fiscal 2026 by our math
• Fiscal 2027 operating cash profit outlook: $460 million, up 0.1% from $459.6 million in fiscal 2026

The flat 2027 plan matters because the 6% price increases implemented in fiscal 2026 will pass their one-year mark over the next four quarters. Without new price increases, flat total revenue means unit volumes remain sluggish or negative for another year.

What to watch: the volume versus price breakdown in the first quarter. Another volume drop of 3% or worse as price gains fade would drag total revenue growth below zero.

🔴 𝐍𝐨𝐧-𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬
When Griffon moved its AMES garden tool businesses into joint ventures during the summer, it took much of the payment in paper rather than cash. The year-end balance sheet carries $215.6 million of related-party notes receivable (loans Griffon made to the new joint ventures) and $139.5 million of minority equity stakes, totaling $355.1 million by our math.

Those seller loans charge 10% paid-in-kind interest, meaning the borrower adds the interest owed to the loan balance instead of paying cash. In the fourth quarter, interest income jumped to $5.6 million from $0.2 million a year ago, and the cash flow statement shows $5.9 million of non-cash paid-in-kind interest deducted from operating cash flow for the year.

The company's 2027 forecast of $50 million in net interest expense is "inclusive of interest income from notes receivable". By our math, more than $21 million of that annual interest reduction is non-cash loan accrual rather than cash saved, and Griffon collects it only if the tool joint ventures eventually pay off the loans in 2029.

What to watch: the equity-method earnings line in the first quarter, once the three-month reporting lag on the joint ventures expires. Operating losses at the tool ventures would reduce reported profit and raise credit risk on the $215.6 million loan balance.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing items from prior quarters received no new figures in the fourth-quarter earnings release because Griffon now reports as a single segment.

• Hunter Fan performance and China tariffs: no standalone fan sales, volume or tariff figures were given, leaving no operational read on the $343.6 million net intangible asset balance.
• Commercial specification pipeline: management previously highlighted inquiries from data centre, semiconductor and pharmaceutical builders, but commercial volume fell in the fourth quarter with no order backlog disclosed.
• Environmental cleanup liabilities: updates on the Peekskill, Historic Potteries and Hunter Memphis sites await the annual report footnotes.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰, 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐅𝐘): $𝟐𝟔𝟕.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Full-year free cash flow — operating cash flow minus equipment spending — edged up 0.3% from $266.1 million a year ago. In the fourth quarter alone, free cash flow rose 13.5% from a year ago to $72.8 million by our math because Griffon spent $37.9 million on equipment all year against its $50 million budget.

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬, 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟏𝟖𝟑.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Unsold goods on the balance sheet rose 6.9% from a year ago, more than double the 3.2% fourth-quarter revenue growth rate, and absorbed $11.9 million of operating cash during fiscal 2026. Higher material costs and the 3% drop in fourth-quarter shipment volumes left more stock on hand at year-end.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏.𝟖𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. The building products group expects sales to match fiscal 2026's $1.85 billion, slowing from 3.0% growth this year to 0.1% by our math. As fiscal 2026's 6% price increases pass their anniversary, the flat forecast leaves little room for unit volume recovery.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 (𝐚𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀): $𝟒𝟔𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
New. Management plans for $460 million of operating cash profit, matching the $459.6 million earned in fiscal 2026 and keeping the margin at 24.9% of sales by our math. In fiscal 2026, Griffon held its $458 million target unchanged all year and beat it by 0.3%.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 (𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥. $𝟔𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐱)  ⇘ decelerating
New. Equipment spending is planned to rise 58% to $60.0 million after fiscal 2026 came in $12.1 million below its $50 million budget. Because of that catch-up spending, Griffon expects free cash flow to approximate continuing net income (about $266 million by our math from the guided lines) rather than exceed it.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞: $𝟓𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. Net interest expense is set to fall 37% from $79.0 million in fiscal 2026. The $29 million drop reflects the $363.8 million debt reduction and a full year of 10% non-cash interest accruing on the $215.6 million of loans to the AMES joint ventures.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟐𝟔.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧; $𝟏𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
New. Combined depreciation and amortization is forecast at $41.0 million, up slightly from $40.3 million in fiscal 2026 as the larger $60.0 million capital spending budget begins entering service.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐓𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: 𝟐𝟖%  ⇒ stable
New. The expected tax rate excluding one-offs stays at 28%, matching the prior year's outlook and just above fiscal 2026's 27.8% actual rate.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐱 𝐢𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕?
Fiscal 2026 grew 3% because 6% higher prices offset a 3% volume drop. With 2027 revenue planned flat at $1.85 billion as those price hikes pass their one-year mark, investors need to know whether management expects unit volumes to keep falling.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐩𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟒 𝐛𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲?
Griffon issued $1.11 billion of debt and extended bond maturities to 2034, replacing notes that carried a 5.75% rate. Disclosing the new coupon will show how much of the $50 million net interest forecast is cash debt savings versus non-cash seller note interest.

𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐌𝐄𝐒 𝐣𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐥𝐚𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠?
Griffon holds $215.6 million in seller loans and $139.5 million in equity across the two AMES tool ventures, recorded on a three-month lag. How those businesses performed in the September quarter determines what Griffon will book in its first-quarter income statement.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐇𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐅𝐚𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦 𝐚𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭 𝐠𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟒?
Combining Hunter Fan into the building products segment removed separate disclosure for a China-sourced consumer brand that took a $243.6 million write-down last year. Knowing whether fans or doors drove the 3% fourth-quarter volume drop tests whether consumer demand is holding up.

text:
My daughter is 16, and she invited two of her friends over during the school holidays to spend the afternoon.

I had no problem with it. I bought extra groceries, snacks, drinks, and told her they were welcome to stay for dinner.

The girls arrived around noon.

My daughter made them smoothies, brought out some biscuits, and spent the afternoon showing them movies and playing games.

Around 5:30, I started preparing dinner. I had planned to make rice, grilled chicken, and salad, but my daughter offered to help.

I was happy to let her.

She washed the vegetables, seasoned the chicken, and helped set the table.

When everything was ready, I called the girls to eat.

They all sat down together, and I went upstairs to take a phone call.

text:
Protest reported in Abdanan after deadly bus crash

An initial report from Abdanan says residents gathered on Tuesday, three days after a bus carrying workers from the Dehloran gas plant overturned. They were protesting what they saw as a lack of clear answers from officials about the crash.

Thirteen people died after the bus overturned on the Dasht Abbas–Mourmouri road on Saturday evening, 14 November. The Organizing Council of Oil Contract Workers’ Protests said shopkeepers in Abdanan closed their shops on Sunday in protest and to show solidarity with the families.

Ilam traffic police said on Tuesday that the bus was travelling too fast for the road conditions, that its rental contract violated passenger transport rules, and that the road lacked a proper safety barrier. Ilam’s prosecutor announced charges against the head of NGL Dehloran and the province’s roads director. In a statement published by Mehr News Agency, some of the families called for a full explanation of what happened and said they would pursue their claims through the courts.

Rivar Abdanan, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), offered his condolences to the families and the people of Abdanan and wished the injured a speedy recovery. He spoke of what he described as years of neglect and discrimination by the authorities in Abdanan and other parts of Kurdistan. Recalling how residents scattered rice outside shops during the January protests, he said they had shown that they “value dignity and freedom above all else.” 

Mustafa Hijri, secretary-general of the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan, and Amir Salimi, spokesperson for the Yarsan Democratic Party, also offered condolences in separate messages. 

The Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) raised concerns about road safety and called for those responsible for the crash to be prosecuted.

text:
With coverage of the ASEAN summit now wrapped up, attention has shifted to the upcoming APEC summit, though, in truth, much of the diplomatic spotlight had been on APEC from the outset. Trump has only heightened that interest by repeatedly bringing up North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and the possibility of meeting him in China.

But IMO, Trump’s repeated references to Kim raise concerns from Seoul’s perspective, not necessarily because of the prospect of another US-North Korea meeting, but because of the broader diplomatic context in which the remarks were made.

With Washington pursuing unprecedented trilateral talks with China and Russia, including possible nuclear arms reductions, Trump’s casual invocation of Kim risks sending a misleading signal about how North Korea fits into the emerging nuclear diplomatic landscape.

Unlike the United States, China and Russia, which are recognized nuclear-weapon states under the NPT, North Korea has no such internationally recognized status.

The concern is … placing Kim rhetorically within the orbit of great-power nuclear diplomacy could help normalize the perception of North Korea as another nuclear-armed actor whose arsenal must be managed rather than ultimately dismantled.

For Kim, even the perception of being treated as a nuclear peer could offer a diplomatic advantage without requiring any corresponding nuclear concessions.

Trump may simply be keeping the door open to renewed engagement with Kim. But the diplomatic optics are consequential, particularly when Pyongyang has consistently sought recognition of its nuclear status.

There is also a broader question of South Korea’s place in the diplomatic process. Amid the high-stakes diplomacy among major powers, Seoul’s voice risks being drowned out, even as it is on the front line of the existential nuclear threat posed by North Korea, just across the border.

text:
Mr. Tsarfati,

You claim to have received information from a very senior American source. You describe an urgent and potentially catastrophic national security threat. You then present a proposal under which Benjamin Netanyahu would remain Prime Minister for another two years, be elected President of Israel, and have all criminal indictments against him dismissed.

But what is the national security connection between these conditions?

If the issue is Israel's security and the Iranian threat, Americans should know who Gadi Eisenkot is.

Eisenkot served as the 21st Chief of Staff of the Israel Defense Forces from 2015 to 2019. He holds a Master of Strategic Studies degree from the United States Army War College.

He helped formulate Israel's military strategy and oversaw its implementation. Under his command, the IDF conducted its campaign against Iranian military entrenchment in Syria.

He worked directly with senior American military commanders. In 2016, he received the Legion of Merit for his contribution to strategic military cooperation between Israel and the United States.

After retiring from military service, he became a military fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

Alongside him is Yair Golan, a former IDF Deputy Chief of Staff and former commander of both Northern Command and Home Front Command.

Golan is a graduate of the U.S. Army War College and holds a Master of Public Administration degree from Harvard University. He also served as a military fellow at the Washington Institute.

Both men have extensive experience with regional security threats and direct professional familiarity with the American defense establishment.

Eisenkot's experience extends beyond implementing military policy. He participated in developing strategy, assessing threats, planning operations, and overseeing their execution.

This raises several fundamental questions.

What unique national security advantage can Netanyahu offer President Trump that Eisenkot cannot?

What specific military or strategic capability requires Netanyahu to remain Prime Minister?

How would dismissing Netanyahu's criminal indictments strengthen deterrence against Iran?

How would electing him President of Israel improve security along the Jordanian border or prevent a terrorist attack?

And if Netanyahu possesses knowledge or relationships essential to Israel's security, why could he not contribute them without remaining Prime Minister?

Does responsibility for national security end when a political leader joins the opposition?

Your suggestion that the democratic electoral strength of Israel's Arab citizens constitutes a security threat also requires evidence. Their right to vote is not an act of terrorism.

The importance of the American-Israeli alliance is not in question. Nor is the need for close security cooperation with President Trump.

But a strategic alliance exists between nations, not merely between two individuals.

If you believe Netanyahu is indispensable to Israel's security, explain what unique security advantage he provides and why it cannot be achieved through another government or broad national cooperation.

If that connection cannot be established, why should Israelis accept an arrangement affecting their democratic choice of leadership and the continuation of criminal proceedings against one political leader?

Israel's national security is the responsibility of every Israeli leader. It must never become a bargaining chip for securing the political or legal future of any one individual.

text:
Why the US CFTC Approved the First Blockchain Based Perpetual Futures Exchange

Global digital asset firm Backpack announced overnight that it has received official approval from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission CFTC to operate both a regulated derivatives exchange and a clearinghouse in the United States. The landmark clearance allows Backpack to offer leveraged crypto perpetual futures backed by native crypto collateral, cross margining, and 24 hour trading inside a single unified global order book. After years of watching the massive perpetual futures market flow to offshore exchanges, US regulators are now moving to bring crypto price discovery directly onshore.

In the digital asset market, perpetual futures are the primary engine of liquidity and price discovery, routinely trading several times the volume of the spot market.

Because perpetual contracts never expire and trade around the clock, they dominate global crypto volume, yet regulatory hurdles had largely kept them locked out of onshore US markets. As a result, American institutional and retail traders were either limited to standard dated futures on the CME or pushed toward unregulated offshore venues, leaving global price discovery in the hands of overseas platforms.

What separates this newly approved exchange from legacy US derivatives venues is that blockchain infrastructure is built directly into the clearing and collateral engine.

Whereas traditional US futures clearinghouses rely on fiat cash margin and legacy banking hours, the approved framework allows traders to post cryptocurrencies directly as collateral with real time risk management running 365 days a year. Even more importantly, rather than trapping US traders inside a shallow domestic only liquidity pool, the CFTC approved structure connects compliant US participants to a unified global order book, providing deep institutional liquidity from day one.

Ultimately, the CFTCs approval of the first blockchain based derivatives exchange signals a strategic push by Washington to capture the industrys largest and most profitable trading market from offshore competitors and anchor it inside the US regulatory perimeter.
