text:
🖼️ 200 FACTS ABOUT THE MONA LISA

🖼️ THE PAINTING
𝟏. The Mona Lisa is a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian Renaissance artist

𝟐. Leonardo began painting it around 1503 in Florence

𝟑. He kept working on it for many years, possibly until around 1517 or later

𝟒. It is painted in oil on a wooden panel of poplar, not on canvas

𝟓. The panel measures only about 77 × 53 cm (30 × 21 in)

𝟔. Many visitors are surprised by how small it is in person

𝟕. The poplar panel is only about 1.3 cm (half an inch) thick

𝟖. A crack near the top of the panel was stabilised long ago with butterfly-shaped wooden inserts on the back

𝟗. In Italian it is called La Gioconda; in French, La Joconde

𝟏𝟎. 'Mona' comes from 'Monna', a contraction of 'Madonna', meaning 'my lady'

𝟏𝟏. The correct Italian spelling is 'Monna Lisa'; the single-n version became common in English

𝟏𝟐. 'La Gioconda' is also a pun: 'giocondo' means cheerful or jolly in Italian

𝟏𝟑. She is shown seated, half-length, with her hands gently folded

𝟏𝟒. She sits in a loggia; the bases of two columns are faintly visible at the edges

𝟏𝟓. Behind her stretches an imaginary landscape with winding paths, a bridge, water and jagged mountains

𝟏𝟔. The horizon on the left side of her appears lower than on the right

𝟏𝟕. She wears a thin, transparent veil over her hair

𝟏𝟖. She wears no jewellery at all

𝟏𝟗. The painting has no signature and no date

𝟐𝟎. It belongs to the French state and is often called the most famous painting in the world

𝟐𝟏. Her face is lit softly from the upper left

𝟐𝟐. Begun in 1503, the painting is now more than 520 years old

👩 WHO WAS SHE?
𝟐𝟑. Most experts identify the sitter as Lisa Gherardini, a woman from Florence

𝟐𝟒. Lisa Gherardini was born on 15 June 1479 in Florence

𝟐𝟓. In 1495, at about 15, she married Francesco del Giocondo, a wealthy silk merchant

𝟐𝟔. Francesco was about 14 years older than Lisa, and she was his third wife

𝟐𝟕. Lisa and Francesco had at least five children

𝟐𝟖. Francesco probably commissioned the portrait, perhaps to mark the birth of their son Andrea in 1502 or a new family home

𝟐𝟗. Lisa was about 24 when Leonardo started painting her

𝟑𝟎. Francesco never received the painting: Leonardo kept it for the rest of his life

𝟑𝟏. In 1550, the writer Giorgio Vasari identified the sitter as Francesco del Giocondo's wife

𝟑𝟐. In 2005, a librarian at Heidelberg University found a margin note from October 1503 confirming Leonardo was painting Lisa del Giocondo

𝟑𝟑. That note, by Florentine official Agostino Vespucci, compared Leonardo to the ancient Greek painter Apelles

𝟑𝟒. In 1517, a visitor named Antonio de Beatis wrote that the portrait showed 'a certain Florentine lady', made for Giuliano de' Medici, which still puzzles historians

𝟑𝟓. Lisa spent her final years at the convent of Sant'Orsola in Florence

𝟑𝟔. She died on 15 July 1542, aged 63

𝟑𝟕. From 2011, researchers dug at Sant'Orsola looking for her remains, but no identification was ever confirmed

𝟑𝟖. Some alternative theories name other sitters, such as Isabella d'Este

𝟑𝟗. Another theory claims the painting is a disguised self-portrait of Leonardo; most experts reject it

𝟒𝟎. Some have suggested that Leonardo's pupil Salaì was a model for the face; this is unproven

𝟒𝟏. Sigmund Freud argued that the smile reflected Leonardo's memories of his mother

𝟒𝟐. Leonardo himself never gave the painting a title; its names came later

𝟒𝟑. 'La Gioconda' also means 'the Giocondo woman', after her husband's family name

🎨 TECHNIQUE & HIDDEN DETAILS
𝟒𝟒. Leonardo used sfumato, blending tones so softly that there are no hard outlines

𝟒𝟓. 'Sfumato' comes from the Italian word 'fumo', meaning smoke

𝟒𝟔. He built up the face with extremely thin, translucent layers of glaze

𝟒𝟕. A 2010 X-ray study found some glaze layers were only a few micrometres thick, far thinner than a human hair

𝟒𝟖. No brushstrokes can be seen with the naked eye

𝟒𝟗. The smile seems to fade when you look straight at her mouth and return when you look at her eyes

𝟓𝟎. Harvard neuroscientist Margaret Livingstone explained this through the way our peripheral vision picks up blurry shadows

𝟓𝟏. Leonardo studied anatomy, including the muscles of the face and lips

𝟓𝟐. Aerial perspective makes the distant mountains fade into a bluish haze

𝟓𝟑. The figure forms a stable pyramid shape, a classic Renaissance composition

𝟓𝟒. Her three-quarter pose was highly influential and was copied by many later portrait painters

𝟓𝟓. Raphael made a drawing based on it around 1504

𝟓𝟔. She has no visible eyebrows or eyelashes

𝟓𝟕. In 2007, engineer Pascal Cotte said high-resolution scans revealed faint traces of an eyebrow that had since faded

𝟓𝟖. A 2006 infrared scan by Canadian scientists showed she wears a fine gauze dress, of a type worn by pregnant women or new mothers

𝟓𝟗. The same scan suggested her hair was pinned up under a bonnet, not loose as it appears

𝟔𝟎. A 2023 study found Leonardo mixed lead oxide into the oil of the base layer, producing a rare compound called plumbonacrite

𝟔𝟏. The old varnish has yellowed, so the colours now look warmer and greener than Leonardo intended

𝟔𝟐. The sky and landscape were likely much bluer when first painted

𝟔𝟑. The whole surface is covered with a fine network of cracks, called craquelure

🧑‍🎨 LEONARDO & HIS MASTERPIECE
𝟔𝟒. Leonardo da Vinci was born on 15 April 1452 near the town of Vinci in Tuscany

𝟔𝟓. He was about 51 years old when he began the Mona Lisa

𝟔𝟔. He was also an engineer, scientist, anatomist and inventor

𝟔𝟕. Fewer than 20 surviving paintings are generally attributed to him

𝟔𝟖. Leonardo was left-handed and wrote many of his notes in mirror script

𝟔𝟗. Around the same time, he was also working on the huge (now lost) Battle of Anghiari mural in Florence

𝟕𝟎. Vasari wrote that Leonardo hired musicians, singers and jesters to keep the sitter cheerful

𝟕𝟏. Vasari claimed Leonardo worked on it for four years and left it unfinished

𝟕𝟐. Leonardo carried the painting with him as he moved between Florence, Milan, Rome and France

𝟕𝟑. In 1516, he moved to France at the invitation of King Francis I

𝟕𝟒. He lived at the Clos Lucé manor near the royal château of Amboise

𝟕𝟓. Leonardo died at Amboise on 2 May 1519

𝟕𝟔. His presumed remains lie in the Chapel of Saint-Hubert at the Château d'Amboise

𝟕𝟕. After his death, the painting may have passed to his pupil Salaì, whose 1525 estate list mentions a 'Joconda'

𝟕𝟖. King Francis I acquired it, reportedly for 4,000 gold écus

𝟕𝟗. The Prado Museum in Madrid owns a copy painted at the same time in Leonardo's workshop, probably by a pupil

𝟖𝟎. When the Prado copy was restored in 2012, a bright landscape appeared from under a later black overpaint

𝟖𝟏. The 'Isleworth Mona Lisa' is a disputed version that some claim is an earlier Leonardo; most scholars disagree

𝟖𝟐. Nude variations known as the 'Monna Vanna' were made by Leonardo's followers

𝟖𝟑. Thousands of copies of the Mona Lisa have been made over the centuries

𝟖𝟒. Raphael's 'Portrait of Maddalena Doni' borrows the Mona Lisa's pose

👑 A ROYAL JOURNEY
𝟖𝟓. The painting entered the French royal collection under Francis I

𝟖𝟔. For a time it hung at the Palace of Fontainebleau

𝟖𝟕. King Louis XIV moved it to the Palace of Versailles

𝟖𝟖. After the French Revolution, it went to the Louvre in 1797

𝟖𝟗. Around 1800, Napoleon Bonaparte hung it in his bedroom at the Tuileries Palace

𝟗𝟎. It returned to the Louvre in 1804

𝟗𝟏. During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, it was reportedly sent to the naval arsenal at Brest for safety

𝟗𝟐. In 1939, at the start of the Second World War, it was secretly evacuated from Paris

𝟗𝟑. Its wartime crate was reportedly marked with red circles to show it was a top priority

𝟗𝟒. During the war it was moved between hiding places, including the Château de Chambord and the Château de Montal

𝟗𝟓. It came back to the Louvre after the war ended in 1945

𝟗𝟔. In late 1962, it crossed the Atlantic in a climate-controlled case aboard the ocean liner SS France

𝟗𝟕. US First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy and French culture minister André Malraux helped arrange the loan

𝟗𝟖. President John F. Kennedy unveiled it at the National Gallery of Art in Washington in January 1963

𝟗𝟗. In Washington it was reportedly guarded around the clock by US Marines

𝟏𝟎𝟎. It was then shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York

𝟏𝟎𝟏. About 1.7 million people saw it during its US visit

𝟏𝟎𝟐. Before the trip it was assessed at $100 million, a Guinness World Record for the highest insurance valuation of a painting

𝟏𝟎𝟑. That is worth more than $1 billion in today's money

𝟏𝟎𝟒. It was reportedly never actually insured: the money went into security instead

𝟏𝟎𝟓. In 1974, it was shown at the Tokyo National Museum, where about 1.5 million people saw it

𝟏𝟎𝟔. On the way back from Japan, it was shown at the Pushkin Museum in Moscow, and it has not left the Louvre since

🕵️ THE GREAT 1911 THEFT
𝟏𝟎𝟕. On 21 August 1911, the Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre

𝟏𝟎𝟖. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who had worked at the museum

𝟏𝟎𝟗. He had helped build the glass cases that protected paintings at the Louvre

𝟏𝟏𝟎. On a Monday, when the museum was closed, he walked out with the panel hidden under a white work smock

𝟏𝟏𝟏. Nobody noticed it was missing until the next day, when a painter came to sketch it

𝟏𝟏𝟐. The empty frame and glass case were found abandoned in a stairwell

𝟏𝟏𝟑. The Louvre closed for a week while police searched

𝟏𝟏𝟒. The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested as a suspect and spent several days in jail

𝟏𝟏𝟓. Pablo Picasso was questioned by police too

𝟏𝟏𝟔. Police even interviewed Peruggia at his home, but did not suspect him

𝟏𝟏𝟕. Neither Apollinaire nor Picasso had anything to do with the theft

𝟏𝟏𝟖. Peruggia reportedly left a thumbprint on the case, but police failed to match it to his records

𝟏𝟏𝟗. When the museum reopened, crowds queued to stare at the empty wall where it had hung

𝟏𝟐𝟎. Peruggia kept the painting in his small Paris room for more than two years, reportedly in a trunk

𝟏𝟐𝟏. In 1913, he offered it to Alfredo Geri, an art dealer in Florence

𝟏𝟐𝟐. Geri and Uffizi director Giovanni Poggi checked it, confirmed it was real, and alerted police

𝟏𝟐𝟑. Peruggia was arrested in Florence in December 1913

𝟏𝟐𝟒. He claimed he wanted to return the painting to Italy, believing Napoleon had looted it

𝟏𝟐𝟓. He served only about seven months in jail

𝟏𝟐𝟔. Before going home, the painting was exhibited in Florence, Rome and Milan

𝟏𝟐𝟕. It returned to the Louvre in January 1914

𝟏𝟐𝟖. The theft turned the Mona Lisa into a global celebrity, as newspapers worldwide printed its image

𝟏𝟐𝟗. A popular legend says a conman named 'Valfierno' sold fake Mona Lisas during the theft, but the story is unverified

🏛️ AT THE LOUVRE TODAY
𝟏𝟑𝟎. It hangs in the Salle des États, one of the largest rooms in the Louvre

𝟏𝟑𝟏. It has been in this room since 2005

𝟏𝟑𝟐. It faces Veronese's The Wedding at Cana, the largest painting in the Louvre

𝟏𝟑𝟑. The room is in the Louvre's Denon wing

𝟏𝟑𝟒. The painting sits in a climate-controlled case, kept at about 20°C and 50% humidity

𝟏𝟑𝟓. In 2019, the case was fitted with new, clearer bulletproof glass

𝟏𝟑𝟔. A barrier keeps visitors several metres away

𝟏𝟑𝟕. The Louvre is the world's most-visited art museum, with about 8.7 million visitors in 2024

𝟏𝟑𝟖. The Louvre has said that most of its visitors come mainly to see the Mona Lisa

𝟏𝟑𝟗. Once a year, the case is opened so experts can inspect the painting

𝟏𝟒𝟎. In 2004, a team of about 39 specialists examined it in a major scientific study

𝟏𝟒𝟏. Experts have noted that the poplar panel has warped slightly over time

𝟏𝟒𝟐. Its current 16th-century-style Italian frame was donated in 1909 by the Countess of Béhague

𝟏𝟒𝟑. In 2019, it was moved temporarily to the Galerie Médicis while its room was renovated

𝟏𝟒𝟒. In January 2025, President Emmanuel Macron announced it will get its own dedicated room

𝟏𝟒𝟓. The new room is part of the 'Louvre New Renaissance' plan, expected to be completed around 2031

𝟏𝟒𝟔. The plan also includes a new main entrance to ease crowding

𝟏𝟒𝟕. Under French law, museum collections cannot be sold, so the Mona Lisa is effectively priceless

𝟏𝟒𝟖. In October 2025, thieves stole crown jewels from the Louvre's Apollo Gallery; the Mona Lisa was not affected

𝟏𝟒𝟗. Taking a selfie with the Mona Lisa is one of the most popular photo moments in Paris

🛡️ ATTACKS & DRAMA
𝟏𝟓𝟎. In 1956, a man threw acid at the painting, damaging its lower part

𝟏𝟓𝟏. Later in 1956, another man threw a rock at it, chipping paint near her left elbow

𝟏𝟓𝟐. That damage was later carefully retouched

𝟏𝟓𝟑. Since the 1950s, the painting has been kept behind protective glass

𝟏𝟓𝟒. In 1974 in Tokyo, a woman sprayed red paint at it to protest the museum's lack of access for disabled visitors; the glass protected it

𝟏𝟓𝟓. In 2009, a Russian woman threw a ceramic mug bought at the Louvre; it shattered against the glass

𝟏𝟓𝟔. In 2022, a man disguised as an elderly woman in a wheelchair smeared cake on the glass

𝟏𝟓𝟕. He shouted at visitors to think of the planet Earth

𝟏𝟓𝟖. In January 2024, two climate activists threw soup at the glass

𝟏𝟓𝟗. They said they were campaigning for a right to healthy, sustainable food

𝟏𝟔𝟎. In none of these recent attacks was the painting itself harmed

𝟏𝟔𝟏. Each incident made headlines around the world, adding to its fame

🔬 SCIENCE & MYSTERIES
𝟏𝟔𝟐. In 2005, emotion-recognition software rated her expression as 83% happy, 9% disgusted, 6% fearful and 2% angry

𝟏𝟔𝟑. In a 2017 study, people judged her smile as happy about 97% of the time

𝟏𝟔𝟒. The 'Mona Lisa effect', where eyes seem to follow you, is named after her

𝟏𝟔𝟓. But a 2019 study found she actually looks about 15 degrees to the viewer's right, so the effect doesn't really apply to her

𝟏𝟔𝟔. In 2010, an Italian researcher claimed to see tiny letters in her eyes; experts say they are just cracks in the paint

𝟏𝟔𝟕. In 2015, Pascal Cotte claimed a different portrait lies beneath the surface; the Louvre did not endorse this

𝟏𝟔𝟖. Some doctors have speculated she had conditions like high cholesterol, based on marks near her eye; these are only guesses

𝟏𝟔𝟗. Researchers have proposed real places for the background, such as the Buriano bridge near Arezzo

𝟏𝟕𝟎. In 2024, a geologist argued the landscape shows the area around Lecco, near Lake Como

𝟏𝟕𝟏. None of the proposed background locations has been proven

𝟏𝟕𝟐. The left and right sides of the landscape do not line up, which may be intentional

𝟏𝟕𝟑. In the novel The Da Vinci Code, 'Mona Lisa' is called an anagram of the Egyptian gods Amon and L'Isa; this is fiction, not history

𝟏𝟕𝟒. The term 'Mona Lisa smile' is now used for any mysterious, enigmatic smile

𝟏𝟕𝟓. Art historians still debate whether the painting was ever truly finished

𝟏𝟕𝟔. Infrared imaging has revealed Leonardo's underdrawing and changes he made while painting

𝟏𝟕𝟕. The Louvre has long been reluctant to clean off the old yellowed varnish, fearing damage to the delicate layers

𝟏𝟕𝟖. In 2004, Canadian scientists made a detailed 3D scan of the panel to monitor its condition

𝟏𝟕𝟗. In 2014, two researchers suggested the Prado copy and the Louvre original together form a 3D stereoscopic pair

🌍 POP CULTURE & LEGACY
𝟏𝟖𝟎. In 1919, Marcel Duchamp drew a moustache and goatee on a postcard of her and called it L.H.O.O.Q.

𝟏𝟖𝟏. In 1930, Fernand Léger painted 'La Joconde aux clés' (Mona Lisa with Keys)

𝟏𝟖𝟐. In 1954, Salvador Dalí posed as the Mona Lisa in a famous photo with Philippe Halsman

𝟏𝟖𝟑. In 1963, Andy Warhol repeated her image 30 times in 'Thirty Are Better Than One'

𝟏𝟖𝟒. The song 'Mona Lisa', a hit for Nat King Cole, won the Academy Award for Best Original Song for 1950

𝟏𝟖𝟓. Banksy has made several Mona Lisa parodies, including one holding a rocket launcher

𝟏𝟖𝟔. The street artist Invader's 'Rubik Mona Lisa', made of Rubik's Cubes, sold for €480,200 in 2020

𝟏𝟖𝟕. In 2021, a 17th-century copy known as the 'Hekking Mona Lisa' sold for €2.9 million at Christie's Paris

𝟏𝟖𝟖. Julia Roberts starred in the 2003 film 'Mona Lisa Smile'

𝟏𝟖𝟗. Dan Brown's 2003 novel The Da Vinci Code begins with a murder in the Louvre

𝟏𝟗𝟎. The 2006 film of The Da Vinci Code was shot partly inside the Louvre

𝟏𝟗𝟏. In the 1979 Doctor Who story 'City of Death', a villain makes Leonardo paint several extra Mona Lisas

𝟏𝟗𝟐. The 2022 mystery film 'Glass Onion' features the Mona Lisa on loan to a billionaire's island

𝟏𝟗𝟑. In 2013, NASA beamed an image of the Mona Lisa by laser to the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter near the Moon

𝟏𝟗𝟒. Elton John's 1972 song 'Mona Lisas and Mad Hatters' borrows her name

𝟏𝟗𝟓. William Gibson's 1988 cyberpunk novel is titled 'Mona Lisa Overdrive'

𝟏𝟗𝟔. Art critic Robert Hughes made a 2008 documentary called 'The Mona Lisa Curse' about art and celebrity

𝟏𝟗𝟕. She is one of the most parodied and reproduced images in history, from mugs to memes

𝟏𝟗𝟖. Her pose and gentle smile shaped the way portraits were painted for centuries

𝟏𝟗𝟗. More than 500 years after it was begun, people still travel from all over the world to see her

𝟐𝟎𝟎. In a world of selfies and screens, a small poplar panel from 1503 remains the world's most famous face

📸 Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci (c. 1503–1519), Musée du Louvre. Public domain

text:
Loan Caps Help, but Degrees Were Never Meant for Everyone
The recent price cuts and expanded scholarships at graduate programs, as Preston Cooper notes, are a useful correction to years of unlimited federal lending that let schools raise tuition while students and taxpayers carried the cost. These caps restore basic pressure: institutions must compete on value rather than assume the government will fund any price.
The deeper problem is a borrowing-dependent system that has long favored well-connected interests in government, defense, energy, and finance over the broader public. Easy access to dollar borrowing for these groups, paired with policies that serve a narrow Washington elite, has left ordinary Americans and universities alike burdened by debt and rising costs. This pattern has contributed to growing dysfunction in American political and economic life.
A university degree is not for everyone. It suits those with the intellectual capacity and realistic financial means to benefit from it. For most people, high-quality vocational education and training offer a more direct path to stable work. A college degree does not guarantee a high-paying job. Roughly 48 percent of U.S. college graduates work in positions that do not require a bachelor’s degree. The share of taxi drivers with college degrees rose from under 1 percent in 1970 to about 15 percent by 2010, and similar credential inflation appears in other occupations such as janitorial work.
This mismatch between credentials and actual job requirements is one visible symptom of a system that has prioritized borrowing and institutional expansion over broad-based economic opportunity.
Price reductions at the graduate level are a start. Lasting relief requires recognizing that not every career should run through a university and that perpetual borrowing is not a sustainable model for higher education or for the majority of Americans.
Degrees open doors for some; they should not lock everyone else into debt. Vocational pathways, not endless borrowing, remain the practical foundation for most productive lives.

text:
He said, "Honestly, businesses at your stage shouldn't be too concerned about immediate returns. You need to spend money to look like a serious brand."

I asked him whether they had studied my business finances before making that recommendation.

He said they hadn't, but that their package was designed for companies that wanted to scale.

I told them my average monthly revenue was around $28,000, with operating expenses taking up most of it. Spending $5,000 every month without a clear performance structure was a serious financial decision for me.

One of them smiled and said, "If $5,000 is difficult for you, perhaps you're not ready for the level of growth you're expecting."

That comment irritated me.

I had invited them to help grow my business, not to make me feel financially inadequate because I wouldn't sign their contract.

I asked them to leave the proposal with me.

The following morning, I received an email saying their discounted offer would expire by 5 p.m. They also mentioned that several other businesses were interested in the same package.

I declined.

Three days later, I hired a freelance marketing manager for $1,200 a month, with clearly defined deliverables and a 30-day review period.

The original agency somehow found out and sent me another email saying I had made a short-sighted decision by choosing a cheaper alternative.

They even suggested that small businesses often fail because their owners are unwilling to invest properly.

I haven't responded.

Apparently, spending $15,000 without guaranteed results is considered ambition, but refusing to sign a contract you aren't comfortable with is considered a lack of vision.

(A short story.fiction)

text:
Endometrial cancer rates are rising and affecting Native American and Hispanic women at younger ages | Phil Villarreal, Medical Xpress

While incidence rates for some cancers have declined among women, endometrial cancer, the most common type of uterine cancer, has increased substantially over the past two decades, with particularly concerning increases among Native American and Hispanic women.

New research from the University of Arizona Cancer Center found that Native American and Hispanic women were diagnosed with endometrial cancer at significantly younger ages than other racial and ethnic groups.

The study, published in the journal Cancer Medicine, reviewed records of 261 women who had gynecologic surgery from 2016 to 2021 at Banner—University Medical Center Phoenix.

Of the 168 women in that group who had endometrial cancer, Native American patients were diagnosed at an average age of 49.8 years, compared with 62 years for white patients. Hispanic patients were diagnosed at 53.7 years, compared with 61.6 years for non-Hispanic patients.

Endometrial cancer begins in the lining of the uterus, which thickens and sheds under hormonal control during the menstrual cycle. According to the American Cancer Society, endometrial cancer rates rose in the United States between 1.8% and 2.6% per year from 2013 to 2022. Recent trends show some stabilization, with current estimates of approximately 68,270 new cases of endometrial cancer per year in the U.S.

Diagnosed early, before the cancer has spread beyond the uterus, the 5-year survival rate for endometrial cancer is approximately 95%. However, not all cases are detected early, and cancers of the uterus are expected to claim more than 14,000 lives in the United States in 2026. The high incidence rate and late diagnoses contribute annually to more deaths than ovarian cancer.

"We need to rethink who we consider at risk for endometrial cancer," said Melissa Herbst-Kralovetz, the study's lead author and a professor of basic medical sciences at the U of A College of Medicine—Phoenix and a member of the U of A Cancer Center's Cancer Prevention and Control Program.

"Native American and Hispanic women in our study were diagnosed significantly younger than their white and non-Hispanic counterparts. These findings challenge the perception that endometrial cancer is primarily a disease of older, postmenopausal women."

Herbst-Kralovetz, a member of the BIO5 Institute, directs the Translational Women's Health Research Program and Women's Health Microbiome Initiative. She focuses her research on gynecologic cancers, particularly cervical and endometrial cancer, and the role of the microbiome and microenvironment in cancer risk and progression. She said that the retrospective study results need to be confirmed in larger groups.

"This study highlights the need to increase awareness of endometrial cancer risk, particularly among younger women and their providers. Native American and Hispanic women in this study were diagnosed significantly younger than their counterparts.

"The Society of Gynecologic Oncology's 2026 evidence review identified delayed evaluation of abnormal bleeding in premenopausal women as an important concern, citing research in which 36% experienced delays of more than six months before undergoing endometrial sampling.

"These findings underscore the importance of recognizing risk factors and symptoms earlier, alongside developing simple, low-cost, point-of-care diagnostic tests that can be made accessible through primary care and rural health settings. Earlier detection offers an important opportunity to reduce deaths from a cancer that is highly treatable when diagnosed at an early stage," said Patricia Thompson, deputy director of the U of A Cancer Center and professor of physiology at the U of A College of Medicine—Tucson.

The study also found that 45% of Native American patients and 21% of Hispanic patients in the study had diabetes. Obesity and diabetes are some of the primary drivers of the disease, and estrogen levels can affect the growth of the uterine lining.

"Adipose or fatty tissue is hormonally active and can produce estrogen, and metabolic conditions like obesity and diabetes can create an environment that promotes abnormal growth in the uterine lining," said Herbst-Kralovetz. "Over time, this can drive cancer development. But we need to look beyond metabolic health alone and understand how environmental, biological and social factors intersect to drive these disparities."

The research team used the Arizona Social Vulnerability Index, which draws upon census data to measure the challenges faced by people in underserved areas. The study found that patients with cancer were more likely to live in areas with housing and transportation difficulties, and more likely to lack access to a vehicle and live in crowded housing.

Herbst-Kralovetz's lab is working to develop a simple, less invasive test that could detect endometrial cancer without the need for a tissue biopsy. Her goal is to make testing more accessible through primary care offices, particularly for women in rural and underserved communities. She hopes to see greater investment in validating these tests and in building partnerships with rural health care providers to improve access to early detection when treatment leads to cure.

To reduce endometrial cancer deaths in the coming years, Herbst-Kralovetz points to bringing earlier diagnosis closer to patients. "Moving diagnostic innovation closer to primary care and underserved communities could help change the trajectory of endometrial cancer diagnoses."

text:
🤯“HOW MUCH LONGER, SVITOLINA?” — EUROSPORT SPAIN HAS A QUESTION FOR A UKRAINIAN TENNIS PLAYER.

Imagine sitting in a warm office in Spain, enjoying your morning coffee, while millions of Ukrainians are struggling with power outages, spending nights in bomb shelters and wondering whether Russian missiles will hit their homes.

And then deciding that one of the most pressing issues in tennis is why 🇺🇦 Elina Svitolina still refuses to shake hands with Russian players.

This is essentially the perspective offered by @fermurciego in his November 17 opinion column for @Eurosport_ES, titled “¿Hasta cuándo, Svitolina?” — “How Much Longer, Svitolina?”

Yes, seriously.

Apparently, after almost five years of Russia's full-scale invasion, the real question is no longer why Russia continues to attack Ukraine.

It is why Ukraine's leading tennis player still refuses to behave as though everything is normal.

Let's examine some of the most remarkable arguments in this article.

And let's see whether the journalist, and perhaps the editorial team at Eurosport, can understand why this is so deeply offensive.

1. “BUT TIME HAS PASSED.”

Murciego acknowledges that Russia's war continues and that Ukraine's suffering remains a reality.

Then he writes:

“But time has passed. The war continues, Ukraine's suffering remains a reality, and Svitolina's position remains practically unchanged.”

Read that again.

The war continues. The suffering continues. And somehow, the problem is that Svitolina's position hasn't changed.

What exactly is supposed to change? Has Russia stopped attacking Ukrainian cities? Have the missiles stopped flying? Have Ukrainian families stopped burying their loved ones? Have Ukrainian children stopped running to shelters when air raid sirens interrupt their tennis practices?

No.

But apparently, the passage of time itself is a sufficient reason for Ukrainians to reconsider their moral boundaries.

At the beginning of the invasion, Murciego suggests, Svitolina's position was understandable.

But now? Almost five years later?

Surely she should have got used to it by now.

Got used to what, exactly?

The explosions? The funerals? The destroyed homes? The nights without electricity and heating?

Or the fact that the country represented by her opponent continues to wage war against her homeland?

How incredibly convenient it must be to measure someone else's suffering in years and conclude that it has lasted long enough to become less important than sporting etiquette.

2. “I DON'T INTEND TO ENGAGE IN POLITICS OR ATTEMPT AN EXERCISE IN EMPATHY.”

This is perhaps the most revealing part of the entire article.

Murciego openly admits that he is probably not equipped to understand what Ukrainians are experiencing.

He says he doesn't know what it means to live for years with the fear of your country being bombed.

And then proceeds to explain why Elina Svitolina should change her behaviour.

Think about that.

He admits that he cannot fully understand her circumstances, yet feels qualified to judge how she responds to them.

Perhaps that is precisely where the problem begins. If you cannot understand what someone is living through, maybe the first step should be to listen.

Not lecture. Not question how long their position should last. Not explain to them that a handshake would be a beautiful gesture of humanity.

Empathy is not something you can simply skip because it makes your argument more complicated.

And if empathy is beyond the scope of your article, perhaps judging the moral choices of someone living through a war should be too.

3. “WHAT FAULT DOES MIRRA ANDREEVA HAVE?”

Another central question in the column.

The journalist reminds readers that Mirra Andreeva was only 14 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

And asks what responsibility she could possibly bear for her government's decisions.

But here is a question in return:

Where exactly did Elina Svitolina accuse Mirra Andreeva of being personally responsible for the invasion?

Where did she say that Andreeva should be held accountable for every Russian missile? Where did she demand that Andreeva be punished for the actions of Vladimir Putin?

She didn't.

Svitolina simply refuses to exchange traditional gestures of sporting friendship with players representing Russia and Belarus.

That is her position. It has been explained repeatedly. And it has remained consistent.

You can acknowledge that Andreeva is not personally responsible for Russia's invasion while also respecting Svitolina's decision not to participate in gestures that would make the situation appear normal.

These two things are not mutually exclusive.

But the article presents them as though they are.

As though recognizing Andreeva's lack of personal responsibility automatically creates a moral obligation for Svitolina to shake her hand, congratulate her or publicly acknowledge her.

It doesn't.

4. “A GESTURE OF ADMIRATION, RESPECT AND HUMANITY.”

This is how the journalist describes Andreeva's words to Svitolina during the WTA Finals trophy ceremony.

Andreeva congratulated the Ukrainian on her season and praised her achievements after becoming a mother.

Beautiful words, certainly.

But let's consider the context.

Andreeva knows perfectly well that Ukrainian players do not exchange handshakes or traditional public congratulations with Russian opponents.

She knows why. The entire tennis world knows why.

Yet she chose to publicly address Svitolina during the ceremony.

We cannot know what Andreeva intended. But we can question whether this was truly the most considerate thing to do.

Because the consequences were entirely predictable.

Andreeva was celebrated for her supposed display of extraordinary sportsmanship. Svitolina was criticized for not responding in the way people expected.

The Russian player became a symbol of class and maturity. The Ukrainian player became the target of another wave of criticism.

And somehow, Eurosport's journalist looks at this situation and decides that Svitolina is the one who needs to learn a lesson in humanity.

5. SHOULD SVITOLINA JOIN VLADIMIR PUTIN IN CONGRATULATING ANDREEVA?

There is one particularly important detail missing from this discussion.

On November 16, Russian President Vladimir Putin officially congratulated Mirra Andreeva on winning the WTA Finals.

The congratulatory message was published by the Kremlin.

Putin praised her victory, her determination and her contribution to Russian tennis. And this was not the first time Russia's president had publicly recognized Andreeva's sporting achievements.

In September 2025, Putin signed a decree awarding Andreeva the Medal of the Order “For Merit to the Fatherland”, First Class, following her silver medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

Yes, the same Vladimir Putin who ordered Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The same president whose armed forces continue to attack Ukrainian cities, destroy civilian infrastructure and kill Ukrainian citizens.

And now Fernando Murciego is asking why Elina Svitolina didn't congratulate Andreeva.

So what exactly is being suggested here?

Should Svitolina now line up alongside Vladimir Putin to congratulate the Russian tennis player? Should she join the chorus of congratulations coming from the Kremlin?

Should she put aside everything happening in her country and publicly applaud the same athlete whom Putin has already honored with a state decoration and congratulated on her latest triumph?

Is that really what the international tennis community expects from Ukraine's leading player?

Let's be absolutely clear.

We are not suggesting that Andreeva is responsible for Putin's decisions.

But how can anyone demand that a Ukrainian athlete ignore this context?

For people watching from peaceful countries, these may be nothing more than sporting congratulations. For Ukrainians, the name Vladimir Putin carries an entirely different meaning.

It is associated with the invasion of their homeland, destroyed cities, lost lives and years of suffering.

And yet the outrage is directed at Svitolina because she didn't congratulate a Russian tennis player.

Not at the war. Not at the destruction. Not at the Russian president who has just publicly celebrated the victory.

At Elina Svitolina.

How extraordinary.

6. “PERHAPS GREAT CHANGES BEGIN WITH SMALL INDIVIDUAL GESTURES.”

This is the journalist's proposed path towards reconciliation.

A handshake. A smile. A few kind words. Perhaps that is how peace begins.

Really?

Ukrainian athletes have been explaining their position for almost five years. And Russian missiles have continued to hit their country for almost five years.

Do you genuinely believe that the missing ingredient in this tragedy is Elina Svitolina's willingness to congratulate a Russian tennis player?

Ukraine does not need a symbolic handshake. Ukraine needs Russia to stop attacking it.

Ukrainian children do not need tennis players to demonstrate friendship in front of television cameras. They need to be able to attend school and tennis practice without fearing Russian drones.

Ukrainian families do not need lectures about reconciliation. They need their homes, their electricity, their heating and, above all, their loved ones to be safe.

One of the people who helped Svitolina prepare for these WTA Finals was 🇺🇦 Sergiy Stakhovsky.

A former professional tennis player who spent more than four years serving in Ukraine's Defence Forces.

While others continued their tennis careers, he helped defend his country.

And now we are supposed to believe that the important moral question surrounding Svitolina is whether she politely congratulated her Russian opponent?

Are you serious?

7. “HOW MUCH LONGER, SVITOLINA?”

Let's finally answer the question that Murciego chose as his headline.

How much longer?

As long as Elina Svitolina considers it necessary.

As long as she chooses to maintain that position.

And certainly not until a journalist sitting thousands of kilometres away decides that enough time has passed.

The most remarkable contradiction in the article is that its author explicitly acknowledges that nobody has the right to demand that Svitolina change her position.

And then spends an entire column explaining why she should.

You cannot acknowledge someone's right to make a personal moral choice and then criticize them for exercising it simply because their choice makes you uncomfortable.

And there is one more question we would like to ask.

DEAR EUROSPORT SPAIN, IS EVERYTHING ALL RIGHT WITH THIS EDITORIAL POSITION?

Does your editorial team genuinely believe that the passage of time makes Ukraine's suffering a less compelling reason for refusing a handshake?

Is the problem really that Ukrainian players continue to maintain their position?

Or is the problem that Russia continues to give them every reason to maintain it?

Perhaps, following this logic to its absurd conclusion, Ukraine should simply stop resisting so that everyone in the tennis world can finally stop worrying about these uncomfortable handshakes?

Would that make the trophy ceremonies more pleasant? Would that solve the problem for tennis commentators?

Of course, we are not suggesting that Eurosport supports Russia's invasion.

We are asking why this column places the burden of changing behaviour on the Ukrainian athlete rather than recognizing the circumstances that have made her position necessary.

Yesterday, we published a long explanation of why this situation is so much bigger than tennis.

We wrote about Ukrainian families waking up to explosions.

About children training on tennis courts while air raid sirens sound. About sporting facilities destroyed by Russian attacks. About the people who have spent years defending their country.

And about the extraordinary lack of empathy shown towards Ukrainian athletes by those who insist on treating this war as an inconvenience to normal sporting relationships.

Today, a column published by Eurosport Spain has demonstrated exactly why that explanation was necessary.

We understand that people who have never experienced war may find it difficult to comprehend the choices Ukrainians make.

But difficulty understanding something is not an excuse for dismissing it.

And it certainly does not give anyone the right to decide when another person's suffering has lasted long enough.

Fernando Murciego, you ask: “How much longer, Svitolina?”

We have a question for you.

How much longer will parts of the tennis world continue demanding gestures of reconciliation from Ukrainians while Russia continues destroying their country?

And why is it always the Ukrainians who are expected to take the first step?

The next time you sit down to write about Elina Svitolina, perhaps consider what her family, her friends, her compatriots and millions of Ukrainian tennis fans are living through.

Not what you imagine they should be feeling after almost five years. What they are actually experiencing today.

Because while you are discussing the beauty of a handshake, someone in Ukraine may be sitting in a cold apartment without electricity, listening to explosions and hoping to survive another night.

For Ukrainians, this has never been just about tennis.

And until you understand that, perhaps the question shouldn't be “How much longer, Svitolina?”

Perhaps it should be: “How much longer until we finally show Ukrainians some empathy?” 🇺🇦

Charley Reese's final column for the Orlando Sentinel... He has been a journalist for 49 years. He is retiring and this is HIS LAST COLUMN.

Be sure to read the Tax List at the end.

This is about as clear and easy to understand as it can be. The article below is completely neutral, neither anti-republican or democrat. Charlie Reese, a retired reporter for the Orlando Sentinel, has hit the nail directly on the head, defining clearly who it is that in the final analysis must assume responsibility for the judgments made that impact each one of us every day. It's a short but good read. Worth the time. Worth remembering!

545 vs. 300,000,000 People
-By Charlie Reese

Politicians are the only people in the world who create problems and then campaign against them.
Have you ever wondered, if both the Democrats and the Republicans are against deficits, WHY do we have deficits?
Have you ever wondered, if all the politicians are against inflation and high taxes, WHY do we have inflation and high taxes?
You and I don't propose a federal budget. The President does.
You and I don't have the Constitutional authority to vote on appropriations. The House of Representatives does.
You and I don't write the tax code, Congress does.
You and I don't set fiscal policy, Congress does.
You and I don't control monetary policy, the Federal Reserve Bank does.
One hundred senators, 435 congressmen, one President, and nine Supreme Court justices equates to 545 human beings out of the 300 million are directly, legally, morally, and individually responsible for the domestic problems that plague this country.
I excluded the members of the Federal Reserve Board because that problem was created by the Congress. In 1913, Congress delegated its Constitutional duty to provide a sound currency to a federally chartered, but private, central bank.
I excluded all the special interests and lobbyists for a sound reason. They have no legal authority. They have no ability to coerce a senator, a congressman, or a President to do one cotton-picking thing. I don't care if they offer a politician $1 million dollars in cash. The politician has the power to accept or reject it. No matter what the lobbyist promises, it is the legislator's responsibility to determine how he votes.
Those 545 human beings spend much of their energy convincing you that what they did is not their fault. They cooperate in this common con regardless of party.
What separates a politician from a normal human being is an excessive amount of gall. No normal human being would have the gall of a Speaker, who stood up and criticized the President for creating deficits.. ( The President can only propose a budget. He cannot force the Congress to accept it.)
The Constitution, which is the supreme law of the land, gives sole responsibility to the House of Representatives for originating and approving appropriations and taxes. Who is the speaker of the House?( John Boehner. He is the leader of the majority party. He and fellow House members, not the President, can approve any budget they want. ) If the President vetoes it, they can pass it over his veto if they agree to. [The House has passed a budget but the Senate has not approved a budget in over three years. The President's proposed budgets have gotten almost unanimous rejections in the Senate in that time. ]
It seems inconceivable to me that a nation of 300 million cannot replace 545 people who stand convicted -- by present facts -- of incompetence and irresponsibility. I can't think of a single domestic problem that is not traceable directly to those 545 people. When you fully grasp the plain truth that 545 people exercise the power of the federal government, then it must follow that what exists is what they want to exist.
If the tax code is unfair, it's because they want it unfair.
If the budget is in the red, it's because they want it in the red.
If the Army & Marines are in Iraq and Afghanistan it's because they want them in Iraq and Afghanistan ..
If they do not receive social security but are on an elite retirement plan not available to the people, it's because they want it that way.
There are no insoluble government problems.
Do not let these 545 people shift the blame to bureaucrats, whom they hire and whose jobs they can abolish; to lobbyists, whose gifts and advice they can reject; to regulators, to whom they give the power to regulate and from whom they can take this power.
Above all, do not let them con you into the belief that there exists disembodied mystical forces like "the economy," "inflation," or "politics" that prevent them from doing what they take an oath to do.
Those 545 people, and they alone, are responsible. They, and they alone, have the power.
They, and they alone, should be held accountable by the people who are their bosses. Provided the voters have the gumption to manage their own employees... We should vote all of them out of office and clean up their mess!

Charlie Reese is a former columnist of the Orlando Sentinel Newspaper.
What you do with this article now that you have read it... is up to you.

text:
WRAP: WrapShield Puts Numbers Behind the Frenel Opportunity

WRAP’s updated product page goes beyond the November 16 announcement, publishing specific drone-detection, classification and tracking claims. The next test is whether those results can be independently validated and converted into defense contracts.

November 17, 2026

WRAP Technologies’ updated WrapShield product page provides something shareholders have been waiting for: measurable performance claims for Frenel’s TPiCore thermal-polarimetric technology, accompanied by a more clearly defined hardware and operational architecture.

The November 16 announcement established that Frenel had integrated its technology into an existing military-grade electro-optical gimbal, completed environmental certification and conducted a weeklong deployment at an active border installation. The product page goes further, describing what the technology has reportedly accomplished in field testing.

According to WRAP, TPiCore demonstrated nano-drone detection at 400 meters, drone-versus-bird classification at 500 meters and continuous tracking through clutter at distances of 500–750 meters below the treeline. The company also describes the ability to identify manufactured objects concealed in vegetation and detect RF-silent or pre-programmed drones without relying on radio-frequency emissions.

These are potentially consequential capabilities because the counter-UAS problem is increasingly defined by small, inexpensive aircraft operating at low altitudes, often against cluttered backgrounds and without conventional command-and-control transmissions.

Traditional RF-based detection can be effective against drones that emit recognizable signals. It cannot depend on those signals when an aircraft operates autonomously or maintains radio silence. Passive optical sensing provides another means of detecting and classifying threats, but conventional thermal imaging can struggle when objects share similar apparent temperatures with their surroundings.

Frenel’s approach adds polarization information to thermal imagery, seeking to distinguish materials, surfaces and manufactured objects that might otherwise blend into the background.

The important development is that WRAP is now attaching specific performance distances to that proposition.

The hardware story is equally relevant. Frenel has integrated its TPiCore thermal channel and NVIDIA Jetson edge processing into a dual-channel EO gimbal manufactured by an unnamed defense supplier. WRAP says the underlying platform is already approved for and used by military customers, including the U.S. Army, while the integrated configuration completed MIL-STD-810 environmental and IP67 ingress-protection certification in October.

The company also reports a July 2026 deployment at an active border installation, operating for one week in dusty conditions and temperatures reaching 124°F.

That is meaningful engineering progress. Military customers generally procure qualified systems, not isolated sensing concepts. Integrating a new capability into established hardware can reduce some of the mechanical, environmental and procurement obstacles associated with introducing an entirely new platform.

But the underlying gimbal’s existing military service record should not be confused with Army adoption of Frenel’s modified configuration.

Nor should the published performance figures be mistaken for independently verified operational results. WRAP has not provided the underlying test reports, detection probabilities, false-alarm rates, target specifications, sample sizes or environmental conditions needed to fully evaluate the claims. The page references February drone-detection footage, ground-gimbal evaluations and other field scenarios without establishing that every result was achieved by the same configuration.

Those distinctions matter.

A claimed ability to distinguish drones from birds at 500 meters is particularly interesting, but its operational value depends on how consistently the system makes that distinction across different targets, weather conditions and backgrounds. Likewise, tracking through clutter at 500–750 meters becomes much more significant when accompanied by track persistence, classification confidence and reliable handoff to an existing command-and-control system.

WRAP also describes the polarimetric signature as potentially resistant to spoofing and jamming. That is an attractive proposition for electronically contested environments, but the suggestion that such signatures may be unspoofable remains a claim requiring rigorous adversarial testing.

The broader WrapShield architecture is organized around Detect, Orchestrate and Respond, with human authorization retained throughout the decision chain. Frenel provides the passive detection component, while WRAP intends to connect sensing, classification, tracking and threat prioritization to appropriate response capabilities.

The commercial opportunity lies in making that entire chain work within systems government customers already operate.

For shareholders, the next milestones are now more specific: publication of supportable operational trial results, identification of the gimbal manufacturer, completion of the anticipated U.S. demonstration, validation of sensor-to-command-system integration and disclosure of an actual customer or procurement agreement.

The contractual economics also remain important. Frenel’s pre-existing relationships and WRAP’s commercialization rights mean that technical success must still be connected to revenue attributable to WRAP.

Nevertheless, the progression is meaningful. The discussion has moved from what thermal polarimetry might accomplish to what WRAP now claims it has demonstrated, using identifiable performance distances and an environmentally qualified hardware configuration.

The company has put numbers behind the technology. Now those numbers need to withstand independent evaluation, operational qualification and customer scrutiny.

If the reported detection, classification and tracking capabilities prove repeatable, Frenel could offer a differentiated sensing component for the increasingly difficult counter-drone threat environment.

WRAP has advanced the engineering case. The next milestone is proving the operational case—and converting it into commercial value for common shareholders.

Sources:

https://t.co/p21I8ZAUWQ

WRAP Technologies — November 16, 2026 announcement:
https://t.co/LNTMjcxI88

Disclosure: The author holds a long position in WRAP Technologies (NASDAQ: WRAP).

Bulgaria, Slovakia, Hungary, and (to a more limited extent) Poland have recently suspended or halted forms of military support for Ukraine. The Czech Republic has also opted out of major new collective funding packages. Several other European countries have provided little or no lethal aid throughout the war due to neutrality or policy. 
Recent suspensions or significant reductions
•  Bulgaria: In November 2026, Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced that Bulgaria would no longer supply weapons or ammunition from its military stockpiles and would end financial support for lethal weapons (including via the European Peace Facility). Reasons cited include a large budget deficit and depleted reserves. Bulgaria had earlier been a major supplier of Soviet-standard artillery shells and fuel. It has withdrawn from the “Coalition of the Willing” and continues to offer only humanitarian, medical, and energy-related assistance. 
•  Slovakia: Under Prime Minister Robert Fico, Slovakia ended state-funded military aid (including weapons from army stocks) after his return to power. In January 2026 and repeatedly since (including in November 2026), officials confirmed no further military support, no troops, and no participation in loans or guarantees covering weapons. Fico has framed this as opposition to “war loans” and a preference for diplomacy. Slovakia continues limited humanitarian aid (e.g., generators, locomotives, and medical/shelter funding in late 2026) and has allowed some commercial activity, but not government military transfers. 
•  Hungary: Hungary has refused direct military aid since the start of the full-scale invasion. This policy continues under the new government of Prime Minister Péter Magyar (who took office in 2026 after Viktor Orbán): no weapons, no troops, and no transit of lethal arms through Hungarian territory. Support is limited to energy and humanitarian assistance. Hungary did lift its long-standing veto on EU European Peace Facility reimbursements in mid-2026 (unblocking funds for other donors), but it has not begun providing bilateral military aid and has opted out of new collective NATO/EU military financing packages. 
•  Poland: On 13 November 2026, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that Poland would pause further contributions to NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme, which funds purchases of U.S. weapons (especially air defence and ammunition) for Ukraine. He cited a high budget deficit and Poland’s already very high domestic defence spending. Poland continues other military support and remains one of Ukraine’s strongest backers overall; the pause applies specifically to additional PURL funding. 
•  Czech Republic: It has declined to participate financially in major new NATO packages (such as a €70 billion plan) and has previously indicated limits on further direct transfers from its own stocks. It prioritises its own defence needs and certain joint European projects while continuing some non-military assistance.
Countries with minimal or no lethal aid throughout
Hungary, Austria, Switzerland, Malta, and Cyprus have provided essentially no lethal military support (Austria and Switzerland cite neutrality; Malta and Cyprus are non-NATO EU members with limited capacity). Ireland has provided very limited military-related assistance consistent with its neutrality policy. 

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius recently said Germany can no longer supply additional Patriot systems or interceptor missiles from its own stockpiles.

text:
Staff Sergeant Jared C. Monti was a U.S. Army forward observer assigned to Headquarters and Headquarters Troop, 3rd Squadron, 71st Cavalry Regiment, 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division. A veteran of deployments to Kosovo and Afghanistan, he returned to Afghanistan in February 2006 for his second combat tour.

In June 2006, Monti helped lead a 16-man reconnaissance patrol during preparations for Operation Gowardesh Thrust in Nuristan Province. The team, consisting of scouts, snipers and forward observers, moved for three days through mountainous terrain near the Pakistani border to establish an observation position on Mountain 2610. Their mission was to gather intelligence and direct artillery and mortar fire against insurgent positions threatening a larger American operation in the valley below.

On June 21, after an aerial resupply exposed the patrol’s position, approximately 50 insurgents attacked from the surrounding terrain with PK machine guns, rocket-propelled grenades and small-arms fire. Monti directed his soldiers into defensive positions behind large rocks and began calling for mortar support as enemy fighters advanced to within roughly 50 meters.

During the engagement, Private First Class Bradbury, one of the patrol’s squad automatic weapon gunners, was wounded and left in open ground about 20 meters from the defensive position. Monti repeatedly called out to him until he answered. Although another team leader offered to attempt the rescue, Monti insisted on going himself.

He handed his radio to Sergeant Grzecki, transferring his call sign, Chaos 3-5, before moving into enemy fire. His first attempt brought him within a few meters of Bradbury, but heavy machine-gun fire forced him back. He tried again and was driven into cover by another burst of small-arms and RPG fire.

For his third attempt, Monti coordinated covering fire with Sergeant John Hawes, who had only one 40mm grenade remaining for his M203 launcher. As Hawes fired toward the enemy position, Monti ran from cover once more. An RPG exploded in his path, mortally wounding him just short of the soldier he was trying to reach.

Monti remained conscious briefly and asked that his parents be told he loved them. He died on the mountainside at age 30. Bradbury was eventually rescued by other members of the patrol after darkness fell.

Monti was posthumously promoted to Sergeant First Class the following day. On September 17, 2009, President Barack Obama presented the Medal of Honor to his parents, Paul and Janet Monti, at the White House.

text:
Airlines expect a lot of understanding from their customers but it's a shame that understanding rarely seems to work both ways

I was flying back from West Palm Beach on Sunday when our flight was canceled. We were fortunate enough to get seats on another flight, likely due to my Fiancé's airline status, but plenty of other passengers weren't so lucky.

Once we boarded, we found ourselves sitting on the plane with no air conditioning being told it would come on once the aircraft started moving, directly after being told we didn't know when we would take off.

The whole experience got me thinking about how one sided the relationship between airlines and its customers has become.

Over the past several months, we've seen some extraordinary airfare increases. Airlines have been quick to point to higher fuel costs and operational pressures but it's difficult to believe those factors alone explain some of the prices passengers are being asked to pay.

Then there's the cost of flexibility. 

Need to change your flight? Expect to pay for it

Need to travel at short notice? You'll often pay significantly more

But when an airline cancels your flight, delays your departure, or leaves you sitting on a hot aircraft, suddenly we're all expected to appreciate how complicated the airline business is.

I live in Charlotte, North Carolina, which makes this even more frustrating. Charlotte is one of American Airlines' largest hubs, and consistently ranks among the more expensive major airports in the country for domestic fares. The hub model works incredibly well for connecting passengers, but for those of us who actually live here, the lack of competition on many direct routes means we're often paying a substantial premium just to fly from our local airport.

@AmericanAir has built an incredibly strong position in Charlotte, and commercially, you have to admire that, but there's a difference between having pricing power and taking advantage of customers who have very few alternatives.

I'm certainly not against airlines making money. They're complex, capital intensive businesses with enormous operating costs, and profitability matters, but if you're going to charge premium prices, customers should reasonably expect a level of service and accountability that reflects that.

Most passengers understand that things go wrong. Weather happens, aircraft develop faults, and schedules get disrupted. That's not really the issue.

What frustrates me is that when customers need understanding, the airlines point to their terms and conditions. When airlines need understanding, they expect customers to be patient, flexible, and grateful for whatever solution they're offered.

It seems we've reached a point where airlines expect customer loyalty without feeling much obligation to earn it.

Week 11 Fantasy Defense Writeups
1. Texans Defense vs. Colts: Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter need to be a full go, but ultimately I want that pass rush against Daniel Jones, who has been atrocious this season.

2. Bills Defense vs. Dolphins: Buffalo is a massive favorite and their pass rush will have a trench advantage in this contest.

3. Steelers Defense at Eagles: The Steelers are coming off a bad loss, where their defense had one of their worst performances in recent memory. They are in a bounce back spot against the Eagles very messy offense led by Joe Milton.

4. Chiefs Defense vs. Cardinals: Carson Beck had a moment or two last week, but Kansas City is positioned to win with some distance, and the idea of Beck being forced into a late-game negative game script is very appealing.

5. Bears Defense vs. Saints: I could see the Bears demolishing the Saints coming off their bye, which came off a very messy Sunday night game against Tampa.

6. Jaguars Defense at Giants: The Jaguars front four will have an advantage in this contest, against what is generally a volatile Giants offense. That said, I could see this being a fairly contested, kind of ugly game.

7. Broncos Defense vs. Raiders: I like Fernando Mendoza, but after getting the Seahawks in his first start, he doesn’t get a very good draw in his second at Denver, where the Broncos front will have a trench advantage. This is also a situation where the Raiders will likely have no running game, and their below average wide receiver group has a really bad matchup here.

8. Vikings Defense at 49ers (SNF Mexico City): The Kyle Shanahan vs. Brian Flores chess matchup is one of the best the league has to offer, but I was pretty surprised at how disruptive the Cowboys pass rush was last week. Minnesota is radically more disruptive than Dallas (though the 49ers will game plan around that better than basically anyone).

9. 49ers Defense vs. Vikings (SNF Mexico City): I was very disappointed in the 49ers defense last week in Dallas, but I could see them bouncing back against the Vikings on a neutral field, in what should be a close game.

10. Bengals Defense at Commanders (MNF): The Bengals front four will have a trench advantage in this contest.

11. Chargers Defense vs. Jets: If Geno Smith plays, I don’t really want to mess with the Chargers defense. If Cade Klubnik does, I did not like what I saw out of him last week.

12. Cowboys Defense vs. Titans: Obviously no one wants to play the Cowboys defense in fantasy, because their downside is they get you negative points. But on a week where 6 teams are on a bye, the Cowboys are a large favorite, at home, in a game they pretty much have to win. I’ll take that over some of the other mediocre options on the slate.

I will post a fantasy playoffs lookahead for defenses later today

text:
The False Gospel of Zionism and John Hagee

"I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel: which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ. But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed." — Galatians 1:6-9

Paul doesn't hedge. Another gospel, then accursed, twice in four verses. Not a difference of emphasis. Accursed.

John Hagee has taught for forty years that Jews don't need to become Christians. Not a footnote in an end times chart. Doctrine, organizational policy, a book written to prove it. And almost nobody noticed he built a second door into the kingdom.

Houston Chronicle, 1988: "I'm not trying to convert the Jewish people to the Christian faith... trying to convert Jews is a waste of time. Jews already have a covenant with God and that has never been replaced by Christianity."

That's an argument from failure. It didn't work, so it needn't be done. The Great Commission now has an exemption clause.

"The law of Moses is sufficient enough to bring a person into the knowledge of God until God gives him a greater revelation. And God has not."

Five words carry the whole thing: and God has not.

His 1987 book: "Let us put an end to the Christian chatter that 'all the Jews are lost' and can't be in the will of God until they convert to Christianity!" A 1994 letter: "If God blinded the Jewish people to the identity of Jesus as Messiah, how could He send them to hell for not seeing what he had forbidden them to see?"

Good question, honestly. It assumes the blindness in Romans 11 is total, so unbelief isn't guilt, it's incapacity, and incapacity isn't damnable.

Then he institutionalized it. CUFI's first rule was "no proselytizing at our events. CUFI exists only to honor and support the Jewish people, never to convert them." No altar call, no follow up, no urgency. You could sit in that church for years and never be told you must be born again.

2007, In Defense of Israel: "The Jews were not rejecting Jesus as Messiah; it was Jesus who was refusing to be the Messiah to the Jews." "How can the Jews be blamed for rejecting what was never offered?"

If that holds, everything follows. Judaism isn't incomplete, it's an alternate arrangement. Two covenants, two doors, same room.

The objection is that Jesus said no man comes to the Father but by Him. Hagee's answer is timing: "All people will gain entrance into heaven through Christ. The question is one of timing."

Now the text.

Peter at Pentecost, to an all Jewish crowd: "let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ" (Acts 2:36). Three thousand baptized that day, every one of them a Jew. If evangelizing Jews is a waste of time, the church was born in a waste of time.

Jesus, to the men with roots in Judaism and a faith structure: "if ye believe not that I am he, ye shall die in your sins" (John 8:24).

Hebrews 8:13: "In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old." Hagee says the schoolmaster is sufficient. Paul says its job was to hand you off.

Chosen for what? "They are not all Israel, which are of Israel" (Rom 9:6). Paul prays "that they might be saved" (Rom 10:1). Why pray for people who already have it?

Hagee isn't a heretic in the Trinity denying sense, and he made evangelicals care about a people most had ignored. But Paul's test in Galatians 1 isn't whether a message is gospel adjacent. It's whether it's the gospel.

A message that says a Jew can die outside of Christ and be fine is not the one Peter preached at Pentecost.

Not a development. Not an emphasis. Another gospel.

In September 2022, https://t.co/wKgGzUGR5Y raised $150 million at a unicorn valuation.

Its users had exchanged more than 2 billion messages with its bots in five months. By October 2024 it had 20 million monthly active users. Lightspeed, a16z, SV Angel. Over $193 million raised.

In August 2024, Google struck a $2.7 billion deal to license its models. The founders went back to Google.

That is what safety looks like in AI. A giant pays billions for your technology. The market has priced you.

Then the lawsuits came. Families alleged the bots had contributed to the deaths of teenagers.

The company stopped training foundation models. Its general counsel became interim CEO.

On October 13, 2026, https://t.co/wKgGzUGR5Y filed for Chapter 11 in Delaware. Liabilities: $50 million to $100 million.

The stalking-horse bidder is Disney. The offer: $20 million. For that, Disney gets a non-exclusive perpetual license to the technology.

Non-exclusive. Disney is not even buying it outright.

The company's own statement on what happens if no better bid arrives: "the platform will be wound down."

Two years. From $2.7 billion to $20 million. The asset did not break. It did exactly what it was built to do. It made people attach to it.

That was the product. That was the liability.

The bots worked. That was the problem.

text:
Elon Musk lost a $56 billion pay package to a man who owned 9 Tesla shares. A judge voided the deal, then ordered Tesla to pay that man's lawyers $345 million, after they asked for $5.6 billion.

Then Delaware's Supreme Court gave it all back. By then the package was worth $139 billion. The man with 9 shares got $1.

In the video below, Musk walks on stage right after shareholders voted for his pay a second time: "Hot damn, I love you guys."

In 2018 Tesla's board offered Musk options on 304 million shares, about 9% of the company, if Tesla hit a set of huge targets. It hit every one.

Richard Tornetta, a former heavy metal drummer with 9 shares, sued that same year.

In January 2024 a Delaware judge struck the deal down and called it "unfathomable."

His lawyers asked for $5.6 billion in fees. The judge called that a windfall and gave them $345 million.

In June 2024 shareholders voted for the package again. In December the judge rejected it again.

Musk moved Tesla's legal home from Delaware to Texas.

On December 19, 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed it, unanimously. Throwing the deal out, it said, left Musk "uncompensated for his time and efforts over a period of six years." The lawyers' fee was cut by about 80%. Damages: $1.

Musk said he was "vindicated."

9 shares froze the biggest paycheck in history for 7 years. The final bill for the man who started it: $1.

Did the system protect shareholders, or did 9 shares nearly cost Musk $139 billion?

text:
29-year-old Sky kept shooting up into the same wound on her thigh until you could see her femur. The bone was fracturing on its own. Doctors begged to amputate, she kept signing herself out and leaving. When they finally cut off her leg, the rot moved to her hand. Then Sky died.

Sky was 29. "Some days I feel like I'm 25 and some days I feel like I'm 70."

The xylazine in her d*pe left wounds up and down both legs. So she started shooting up between them. Then inside them. She didn't want to make new ones. The wounds connected and turned into one giant hole.

She picked one spot on her thigh and kept going there. It ate away. And ate away. Until you could see her femur. The bone was fracturing on its own.

She went to the hospital again and again. Every time they wanted to amputate. Every time she said no and walked out against medical advice.

The last time she couldn't even stand up out of her chair.

The surgeon said if he cleaned it, there would be nothing left of her leg. "Thin like a piece of paper." He didn't understand how she was still walking on it. She signed the papers. Within 20 minutes she was in surgery.

The leg was gone. The xylazine wasn't. Methadone and Suboxone don't even touch it.

Then it moved to her hand. And she doesn't even inject there. A finger swelled up. A blister. A hole in her palm "like someone stabbed me." The finger turned purple, then green. She walked into the University of Maryland hospital and said she was 90% sure it was gangrene.

The doctor showed her something white inside the wound. "Is that my bone?" "No, that's your tendon. Your bone is right behind it." He said they should amputate the finger and move her pinky closer to her middle finger.

She walked out again.

Now she keeps the hand wrapped in gauze with a shirt over it. So flies don't land on it and lay eggs.

Sky is dead now.

Some people will say xylazine is a poison nobody asked for, and Sky was a sick girl the system let rot one limb at a time. Others will say she was offered help every single time and chose the needle over her own leg.

Victim of the drug, or a girl who chose this until the end?

text:
Justin Jefferson holds the record for the most receiving yards anybody has had in their first six NFL seasons, and his scholarship to LSU came down to whether he passed one English class.

Chris Hummer of 247Sports went back through the recruitment after Jefferson's last college season, because his own company had been part of getting it wrong.

In the 2017 class, the 247Sports Composite had Jefferson 2,164th in the country. Rivals made him a two star. ESPN did not rate him at all. The Top247 gave him three stars for a while before his senior year, and that was the highest any service ever put him.

Outside LSU, the only schools in a power conference that offered him were Northwestern and Tulane.

He had arrived at Destrehan High School at about 175 pounds. His coach, Stephen Robicheaux, described him as stick like, and said the athleticism was obvious to anyone who watched him anyway.

Robicheaux gave two reasons nobody came for him, and the second one explains more than the first.

"Everybody that came around the school thought he was going to LSU."

His older brothers had both played there, Jordan at quarterback and Rickey at defensive back. Recruiters saw the surname, assumed the family had already decided, and spent their time elsewhere. He was ignored for looking like somebody else's business.

The offer from LSU was conditional. Ed Orgeron told Robicheaux that Jefferson would have a scholarship if he graduated and met the admission requirements, and Jefferson still needed one more English course to qualify. Nobody knew whether he was going anywhere until that summer.

He passed it and enrolled, then played two games as a freshman and did not catch a single pass all year.

The year after that he led LSU with 54 catches for 875 yards. The year after that he caught 111 passes for 1,540 yards and 18 touchdowns, and in the playoff semifinal against Oklahoma he had 14 catches for 227 yards and four touchdowns, all four of them before halftime, which no player in the history of the College Football Playoff had done.

LSU won the national title and he turned professional two days later.

Minnesota took him 22nd overall in 2020, using the pick they had gotten for trading Stefon Diggs to Buffalo.

Six seasons on, he has 579 catches and 8,480 yards, and nobody in the history of the league has had more of either in their first six years. In 2024 he signed for $140 million with $110 million guaranteed.

Barton Simmons, who runs scouting at 247Sports, did not dress it up when Hummer asked him about it.

"We obviously missed."

Every recruiting service in the country graded that class, and the thing that nearly stopped him was a high school English credit.

text:
Adam Thielen's only college scholarship offer was for $500.

Nobody drafted him. He had an internship lined up in case his NFL tryout didn't work out.

He grew up in Detroit Lakes, Minnesota, a Minnesota Vikings fan who copied Cris Carter's sideline catches in his backyard. As a senior, he weighed barely 160 pounds.

Minnesota State, a Division II school in Mankato, was the only school that offered. In Thielen's words, the coach called and said, "We got 500 bucks for you. Come to Mankato."

He went undrafted in 2013, paid his own way through a regional combine, and earned a tryout at the Vikings rookie minicamp.

He ran a 40-yard dash that turned heads, and the Vikings signed him. He turned down the internship.

He spent his first year on the practice squad. He went on to make two Pro Bowls and climb into the Vikings' all-time top tier in catches and touchdowns.

The kid from Detroit Lakes ended up starring for the team he grew up cheering for.

text:
8 years ago today, I was on a long Asia trip. 

3 weeks between India & Thailand.

Flew to India and met my dad for a bit while we explored northwestern parts of the country - Rajasthan was magical. This was the last time I’ve been to India but I’ve been many times before. I then decided to pay $800 (hotel and flight package) and visit Thailand for a week by myself. 

It was a crazy trip…I was only 24. 

- went into a cage with a Tiger

- fined for not wearing a helmet on my moped by the local police

- explored beaches, ate good food

- did what the locals did 

- did things I shouldn’t be too specific on 

- lost control of my parked moped and accidentally lunged into a walking pedestrian. Luckily, she was not hurt. I almost passed out because I was so nervous. I’ve seen those shows “Locked Up Abroad” She was a New Jersey resident and was visiting the country. I offered to take her to the hospital and pay for the visit and she declined. I think she was more concerned at how nervous I was. Either way, we departed ways and I had to go to a local garage to get the moped fixed before the rental company saw it and charged me a copious amount of money because I was a tourist. I visited a few local moped shops and got one to fix it for a $100. He changed a few fenders and changed the headlight. I returned it to the company without an issue.

The point is you shouldn’t wait. Doing things alone became a source of enrichment for me. Especially, traveling to different countries. I had fun, got myself into a little trouble and more.

I also have stories for days from my personal experiences. That’s something that’s priceless as I get older. 

Memories are not monetary but they’re also a form of wealth. Money is physical but memories are mental.

Live Now! 

From Miami Vice to Nash Bridges How a Yellow ’Cuda Became Don Johnson’s Co Star!  #NashBridges #PlymouthCuda #MiamiVice 

The yellow Plymouth ’Cuda in Nash Bridges practically shared top billing with Don Johnson. Seven years after Miami Vice ended, the man who played Sonny Crockett was back on prime-time TV, swapping a white Ferrari Testarossa for a yellow American muscle car and the streets of San Francisco.  

In this episode of The Cars The Star!, I trace the Barracuda from its beginnings as a sporty fastback based on the Plymouth Valiant to the four-headlight ’Cuda we remember from the show. I also look at why the crew repainted the cars before filming the pilot, how several Plymouths played the same yellow convertible, and why Nash’s car meant so much to him.  

Then there’s the auction story. One intact screen car sold for $23,000 at the 2001 props auction. Don Johnson’s ’Cuda fetched a reported $148,500 at Barrett-Jackson in 2003. 

The burned car from the series was offered at the props sale too, with charred seats, a smashed windscreen and its bonnet detached. How much it made and where it went afterwards remain a mystery.  

Which keys would you take for the afternoon? Crockett’s white Testarossa or Nash’s yellow ’Cuda?  Sources featured in the video - 2001 auction preview, including the burned ’Cuda - The $23,000 props auction result - The $148,500 Barrett-Jackson sale — see the 2003 entry - Behind the scenes with the original production cars - The 2012 eBay listing write-up and dealer photos

text:
For 21 years, Make-A-Wish has had a special place in my heart.

I’ve seen what happens when a child who’s spent far too much of their young life in hospital rooms, enduring needles, treatments, fear, and uncertainty, suddenly has something wonderful to look forward to.

I’ve seen what a wish can mean to a family that’s been through hell.

And after 21 years, it still gets me. Every single time.

This Thursday, we’re holding our annual KRLD Make-A-Wish Radiothon. And I’m asking you for something before I ask anyone for a donation.

Would you please pray for us?

Pray that God opens hearts. Pray that our listeners respond generously. Pray that the stories we share reach the people who need to hear them. Pray that we raise more money than we ever imagined possible.

Because right now, 1,100 children across North Texas are waiting for their wishes.

Those aren’t just numbers on a fundraising goal. They’re real kids. Real families. Moms and dads who would give anything to take away their child’s suffering, even for a little while.

I know money is tight for a lot of people. I know we’re all being pulled in a hundred different directions.

But I also know what can happen when people come together to do something extraordinary for a child.

A wish doesn’t cure cancer. It doesn’t erase a diagnosis.

But it can give a child something illness has stolen: the freedom to dream about tomorrow.

And sometimes, tomorrow is exactly what a family needs to believe in.

Please pray that Thursday is an extraordinary day for these children.

We’ll be broadcasting live all day from NFM at Grandscape in The Colony.

If you feel led to help, you can donate at https://t.co/M72B8x1wzH.

And whether you can give a dollar, a hundred dollars, or simply offer a heartfelt prayer, thank you.

After 21 years, I still believe in the power of a wish.

And I still believe in the power of prayer.

Sometimes we hear about an event only after it has ended. But it can be hard to search for something we don't yet know exists.

Using tomorrow's deadlines and yesterday's beginnings as a starting point, this project brings together opportunities, events, and creative work from across the United States. By placing different fields side by side, we hope to help you discover things beyond your usual interests.

For example, someone looking for a poetry call might notice a pottery workshop. “I could try making that myself.” A small discovery like that might become something to look forward to on a day off.

You are free to take part, share something with a friend who might enjoy it, or simply browse for pleasure.

For readers outside the United States, we hope these glimpses of what people are making, sharing, and enjoying bring life in different communities a little closer.

Something you would not normally have searched for happens to catch your eye today. It might lead to a new interest, another option, or a conversation with someone. We share this list in the hope that these chance encounters can open a few more possibilities in everyday life.

Announcements and promotions related to the listed items are welcome in the comments. Please also let us know if you spot an error or a change.

Wishing you a better day ahead. Please take good care of yourself.
